News.title: Andy Burnham Cabinet picks – live: New PM brings Angela Rayner back into Government
News.content:
New Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has made sweeping changes to the Cabinet — bringing back Angela Rayner and appointing the experienced John Healey as Chancellor of the Exchequer

Andy Burnham has made his first Cabinet appointments — bringing back Angela Rayner to the fold.

The new Prime Minister has also opted for John Healey as his Chancellor and Ed Miliband as Foreign Secretary. Ms Rayner, who was deputy leader of the Labour Party until she quit amid her stamp duty error, is now the Housing Secretary.

Mr Healey replaces Rachel Reeves in the post with the latter confirming her departure from the Cabinet on social media this afternoon. David Lammy has also gone, vacating the deputy prime minister post, a role to which he was appointed by Keir Starmer last year.

Mr Miliband has been appointed Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs. He takes over from Yvette Cooper as Foreign Secretary in Mr Burnham's Cabinet. Mr Miliband, who also served as leader of the Labour Party from 2010 to 2015, was energy secretary in Mr Starmer's government. Ms Cooper herself is now Health Secretary, a position Wes Streeting held for nearly two years.

Other major figures from the Starmer era have been sacked, including Peter Kyle who was Business Secretary. His replacement is yet to be confirmed. Mr Healey, however, recently resigned as Mr Starmer’s defence secretary in a row over military funding.

But Shabana Mahmood has been reappointed Home Secretary by Mr Burnham. Ms Mahmood, MP for Ladywood, Birmingham, first took on the role in September 2025, replacing Ms Cooper in Mr Starmer's first reshuffle.

Talking today without a lectern or notes, in a huge move away from tradition, Mr Burnham, 56, spoke for 10 minutes and used the opportunity to outline his vision for the UK. He made several vows, stressing his first action will be to set out a plan to end rough sleeping. Minutes after this vow though, his Housing Secretary - Steve Reed OBE - quit.

News.title: Donald Trump shares details of first call with new Prime Minister Andy Burnham
News.content:
Donald Trump shares details of first call with new Prime Minister Andy Burnham

Donald Trump has shared details of his first conversation with the UK's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and has hinted at a meeting in the "not too distant future"

View Image Donald Trump hinted at a meeting with Andy burnham in the "not too distant future" (Image: CameraSport via Getty Images)

Donald Trump has commented on his first phone call with Andy Burnham.

‌



The US president was the first call Burnham made after entering Number 10 as the new prime minister.

‌



Taking to Truth Social Trump wrote: "I had a very good conversation with the new Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, Andy Burnham. We discussed many subjects, including the outstanding relationship we have had with the UK. We will be meeting in the not too distant future for topics of mutual interest. The Prime Minister has got a big job ahead of him, but he will be able to do it and, of course, the U.S.A. will be there to help!

‌



"We discussed North Sea Oil, Trade, the Military Alliance, Demining of the Hormuz Strait, and many other topics. The call was interesting, and went very well. I wished Prime Minister Burnham, GOOD LUCK AND GODSPEED! President DONALD J. TRUMP"

New Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has made sweeping changes to the Cabinet — bringing back Angela Rayner and appointing the experienced John Healey as Chancellor of the Exchequer.

News.title: Former Miss Universe Jamaica contestant dies suddenly at 35 as tributes pour in
News.content:
Former Miss Universe Jamaica contestant dies suddenly at 35 as tributes pour in

The Miss Universe Jamaica organisation announced the death of the actress and dancer a social media tribute - her cause of death has not been disclosed

View 3 Images LaToya Malcolm has passed away at 35 (Image: LaToya Malcolm/Instagram)

A former Miss Universe Jamaica finalist has passed away at 35.

‌



The Miss Universe Jamaica organisation announced the death of actress and dancer, LaToya Malcolm, on Saturday in a social media tribute.

‌



Her cause of death was not disclosed.

‌



View 3 Images The Miss Universe Jamaica organisation announced her death in a social media tribute (Image: Instagram)

"We are deeply saddened by the passing of Miss Universe Jamaica alumna LaToya Malcolm," the organisation wrote.

It went on to say that she would "never be forgotten."

‌



LaToya competed in the 2024 Miss Universe Jamaica pageant, where she was one of the competition's standout contestants.

She was grieving the loss of her father during the event. LaToya later won the Miss Jamaica Bikini International title and dedicated her win to her dad in a heartfelt message.

Outside of pageantry, LaToya was an an actress and dance instructor.

Article continues below

View 3 Images LaToya Malcolm competed in the 2024 Miss Universe Jamaica pageant (Image: Instagram)

She was also invested in the Transition Project, a program that helps underprivileged teenagers prepare for adulthood.

Current Miss Universe Jamaica titleholder, Gabrielle Henry, was among those paying tribute. She said LaToya's passing is a "a great loss" whose impact and voice "will not be forgotten."

News.title: Doorbell footage shows brazen woman swiping pints of milk at 5am from doorstep
News.content:
Doorbell footage shows brazen woman swiping pints of milk at 5am from doorstep

Doorbell footage from a resident in Bearwood, Birmingham, showed a woman dressed only in underwear walk down her driveway and allegedly grab two bottles of milk

Woman in black underwear caught on doorbell camera snatching milk

Footage shows the bare-faced cheek of a woman who appeared to snatch two bottles of milk from a doorstep wearing just underwear.

‌



A resident from the Bearwood area of Birmingham was surprised to find her milk delivery missing but was even more taken aback when she found out what had happened.

‌



She checked her doorbell footage and allegedly discovered that a woman dressed only in skimpy black underwear and flip flops had made off with the bottles at around 5am in the morning.

‌



The alleged offender could be seen strolling up the driveway, picking up the bottles and walking off calmly before she seemed to show more haste when she got to the main road.

View 2 Images A woman was seen taking two bottles from a doorstep (Image: Birmingham Live)

UK airline issues ‘urgent’ plea as key flights cancelled READ MORE :

UK weather maps turn volcanic red for next 31C heatwave with 19 counties above 30C READ MORE :

The resident took to Facebook to show what had happened and others also reported their milk had gone amiss recently, reported BirminghamLive.

‌



The householder said: "We were very frustrated to see it on our doorbell as have two young children, but you hope it’s someone in such desperate need they resort to stealing.

"Why in her underwear we do not know! Makes us think twice about getting milk delivered as it has happened several times in our area recently."

West Midlands Police confirmed that it received a report of stolen milk at 5.10am on Friday, July 17, and has appealed to the public for information

‌



View 2 Images The woman was caught on doorbell footage (Image: Birmingham Live)

Its statement said: "Anyone with any information is asked to contact 101 or use the Live Chat option on our website quoting crime number 20/328342/26."

Meanwhile, a resident in the Cotteridge area of Birmingham has also complained about milk bottles being stolen from their driveway and he said he had stopped the milk delivery.

‌



The man wrote on Facebook: "Same again this morning. Milk deliveries have been stopped. It’s now being investigated and they have asked for the footage. I’d advise everyone contact their milk companies."

While a person replied: "Might sound and look trivial to some but this is someone's livelihood our tracksuited tea-leaf is impacting.

"No doubt the milk delivery company put a lot of time and effort into developing the round. Only for someone to tear it all up." And a further reply read: "Have you got the video of him walking up to the doorstep? someone may recognise them."

News.title: 'Significant' search launched for man missing at popular lake in Wales
News.content:
'Significant' search launched for man missing at popular lake in Wales

Police helicopter and divers have reportedly been seen at Llyn Geirionydd after a man went missing at the 45-acre lake on the slopes of the Carneddau mountains in Snowdonia

View 2 Images Llyn Geirionydd near Trefriw has been the site of a major search (file photo) (Image: Ian Cooper/North Wales Live)

Police are still searching for a man who went missing at a lake yesterday with police divers and helicopters reportedly joining the hunt.

‌



The alarm was raised on Sunday evening at Llyn Geirionydd, a 45-acre lake nestled on the lower slopes of the Carneddau mountains in Snowdonia, Wales.

‌



The alarm was raised at approximately 7.10pm with emergency services called to the lake. North Wales Police has confirmed that, despite searches conducted throughout the night, the man has yet to be found. His family has been notified.

‌



Search efforts are set to continue at the lake, the force said, with an "increased emergency service presence" amid the ongoing search operation.

Locals reported seeing a helicopter circling the lake at around 8pm. Meanwhile one witness described a "significant emergency response" and another said police divers were at the scene.

‌



View 2 Images The scenic lake has proved very popular with tourists (Image: Ian Cooper/North Wales Live)

The body of a 21-year-old man was recovered from the lake just 11 days ago. Llyn Geirionydd is a popular destination for watersports enthusiasts. The lake draws kayakers to its waters and holds the distinction of being the only lake within Eryri National Park where speedboats are permitted, reports North Wales Live.

North Wales Police is urging members of the public to stay clear of the lake while the search continues. A spokesperson said: "Immediate family have been informed and are being supported.

Article continues below

"We ask members of the public to avoid the area today to allow emergency services to continue their work.

"Anybody who was at the lake yesterday evening who hasn't already spoken to police should contact us."

News.title: Donald Trump vows Iran will 'pay' after killing of US soldiers
News.content:
Donald Trump vows Iran will 'pay' after killing of US soldiers

The US president issued more threats towards the Islamic Republic following the deaths of US troops in Iran

View 3 Images Trump has vowed revenge against Iran for the killing of US service personnel (Image: Getty Images)

Donald Trump has vowed that Iran will pay for the killing of US troops “many times over” following the deaths of three service personnel in recent days.

‌



The president issued the warning after the American military launched a further wave of strikes, sparking retaliatory attacks by Tehran.

‌



The ongoing clashes and the collapse of the interim ceasefire deal have fuelled fears of a return to a full-blown conflict.

‌



US Central Command said two soldiers were killed in Jordan on Friday while defending against Iranian ballistic missile and drone attacks.

It was subsequently announced a service member had died in Iraq during the “controlled detonation” of a downed Iranian drone.

Some 17 US troops have been killed since the start of the war.

‌



Writing on his Truth Social platform, Mr Trump said: “Every time Iran kills an American Soldier they will pay for that killing many times over!”

He added that this “directive” had been passed on to defence secretary Pete Hegseth and top US general Dan Caine as well as other military commanders.

‌



White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt has said Mr Trump will attend Dover Air Force Base in Delaware on Tuesday evening for the return of the fallen service personnel.

Iranian authorities have said said at least 50 people have been killed and more than 500 wounded in the latest rounds of US strikes.

Shortly after Mr Trump’s warning, the US defence department posted on X a drawing of a soldier in revolutionary-era battledress carrying a musket, with the message: “We untie the hands of our warfighters to intimidate, demoralise, hunt and kill the enemies of our country. No mercy.”

‌



Meanwhile, Tehran has continued to target shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the US enforce a restored naval blockade of Iranian ports as both sides wrestle for control over the contested Gulf waterway, which is vital to global energy supplies.

View 3 Images This undated image provided by the U.S. Army shows Pvt. Isabella Gonzales, 19, of Carrollton, Texas. (Image: U.S. Army via AP)

The fighting has caused maritime traffic using the channel to plummet, leading to renewed concerns over the impact on economies around the world, including the UK.

‌



The situation in the Middle East and the movement of shipping through the strait was among the topics discussed by newly installed Prime Minister Andy Burnham and the US president in a phone call soon after his arrival in Downing Street.

The strait had been open before the war was launched by the US and Israel on February 28.

In response to the offensive, Tehran effectively closed the waterway to maritime traffic, which disrupted global oil and gas supplies and drove up fuel and food prices.

‌



View 3 Images This undated photo provided by the U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command shows 1st Lt. Tyler James Feehan (Image: U.S. Army Space and Missile Defe)

Despite the initial ceasefire deal with the US, known as the memorandum of understanding, Iran continued to exert leverage over the sea route by demanding ships seek permission to transit, raising the threat of future charges and attacking vessels.

Tehran claims it controls the channel, while this is disputed by the US and other countries, which cite international law on freedom of navigation.

Article continues below

US secretary of state Marco Rubio has said the US is still open to negotiating with Iran but that “it has to be real”.

He said: “We’re going to continue to respond. If the door opens to diplomacy — if the guys that want to do something productive for Iran win and take control of that system, or take control of the negotiations — that’ll be a very positive development.”

However, he pointed out currently “that’s not where we are”.

News.title: Wandsworth residents brand structure 'IKEA Bridge' after council's £600,000 paintjob
News.content:
Wandsworth residents brand structure 'IKEA Bridge' after council's £600,000 paintjob

Wandsworth Council said the work on two railway bridges at on East Putney Underground Station cost £600,000, a restoration residents in the southwest London district have blasted

View 2 Images The expensive makeover has sparked backlash (Image: Cllr George Crivelli / SWNS)

Residents have been left outraged after a council spent £600,000 painting a railway bridge.

‌



Wandsworth Council spent the hefty sum repainting two railway bridges at East Putney Tube station in southwest London as part of upgrade works, including “pigeon-proofing” the metalwork. But locals say the new blue and yellow colour scheme resembles IKEA branding - and even HSS Hire.

‌



The paintjob was carried out in March under the borough’s previous administration, before local elections took place in May. Now, residents have branded the new look a “shame”.

‌



Emma, 38, who has lived in the area for eight years, said the colours were “out of character” for Putney, replacing the bridges’ previous muted red paint. She said: “I just think it’s a bit of a shame they’ve gone for this garish colour palette that’s not in keeping with the surrounding area. It’s all just become a bit of a in terms of the IKEA bridge.”

View 2 Images Conservative ward councillor, George Crivelli believes the bridge is too bright (Image: Cllr George Crivelli / SWNS)

Gran refuses to sell patch of garden to save ancient oak from £45,000,000 Hereford Bypass READ MORE :

Dad scoffs record number of fish fingers after making strange vow on The 1% Club READ MORE :

Council officers said the bridges, which are owned by Network Rail and Transport for London, were repainted to a specification recommended by the local authority. They also confirmed the work was not legally required but was considered “capital maintenance”.

‌



Conservative ward councillor and cabinet member for children George Crivelli said: “I think it’s a bit too bright, and not in keeping with the local area. My main concern about it was that, in effect, one councillor has decided the colour scheme on it.

“What I would have liked was that we actually maybe consulted local residents on it.”

While welcoming the repainting work, he added: “I’m very pleased to see the bridge being repainted, and I’m very pleased to see it being cleaned up, but a lot of people think it’s a bit garish, and I have to say I’m inclined to agree on that.

Article continues below

“People call it the IKEA bridge, I’ve heard people say it looks like an IKEA bridge. Perhaps it’s not really in keeping with the East Putney area overall. The only positive thing about those bright colours is that I suppose it will fade over time, won’t it?”

Responding to the backlash last month, a senior transport planner at the council said there were “no plans to revise the design”, adding that the number of negative comments was “relatively few given the very large numbers of local residents and station users.”

A Wandsworth Council spokesperson said: “The cost was £600,000 and the project was completed in May 2026.”

News.title: 'Andy Burnham draws line under Starmer era with Cabinet overhaul - and shocks with Chancellor pick'
News.content:
The clear-out of Keir Starmer's allies was swift and brutal.

Some Westminster wags branded it the "night of the long eyelashes" as Andy Burnham dispensed with the services of a string of top ministers in a clear break with the Starmer era.

Steve Reed, David Lammy, Darren Jones, Peter Kyle, Liz Kendall, Lord Hermer - all close to the former PM - were among those told their time was up.

Rachel Reeves fought hard to stay on as Chancellor but she was too closely tied to the Starmer project, particularly its most totemic failure - the cut to the winter fuel allowance. It is understood that she declined the offer of another big Cabinet job.

‌



Uncertainty over Burnham's pick for Chancellor created a state of hysteria in Westminster. Speculation lurched from initial favourite Ed Miliband to Shabana Mahmood, who was confidently tipped by much of the media in the days running up to Burnham's arrival in Downing Street.

Hope for income tax cut for lower earners as Burnham prepares cost of living blitz READ MORE :

View 2 Images Former Defence Secretary John Healey was named Chancellor in a surprise move (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

But it was John Healey, the ex-Defence Secretary, who was handed control over the nation's purse strings. Mahmood stays on as Home Secretary with a mandate from the PM to deliver her hard-line immigration reforms, while Miliband becomes Britain's top diplomat.

Awkwardly, the pair ended up walking up Downing Street together to learn their fate - but still shared a quick hug.

‌



Healey's appointment as Chancellor was a surprise to many but perhaps it shouldn't have been. The well-liked Labour veteran served in the Treasury under Tony Blair and Gordon Brown, and is seen as a safe pair of hands.

Burnham says he wants to avoid division between Labour's different tribes - despite carrying out a purge of the Starmerites that could set up trouble ahead.

Much of the briefing about the next Chancellor fixated on whether Miliband was too left-wing or whether Mahmood was too right wing. Healey is not aligned to one faction.

The PM's team are clear he wants an experienced and trusted figure in the Treasury to deliver his vision. Healey, a Yorkshire MP, shares his concern about deindustrialisation, the cost of living and backing British industry.

‌



Healey's record as a housing minister, and his commitment to overhauling forces accommodation, while he was at the Ministry of Defence, clearly chimes with Burnham's desire for a council house building boom.

Healey's decision to resign over defence spending will put him under pressure to find cash for the armed forces. But his parting swipe at "Treasury orthodoxy" show he's a safe pick with an edge - one who won't spook the markets but can help to drive through radical reforms.

It is a blow to Miliband, who coveted the job of Chancellor, and played a pivotal role in the new PM's rise to power. For months he was Burnham's most powerful friend in Westminster, and is said to have been the first Cabinet Minister to privately urge Keir Starmer to resign.

But Burnham appears to listened the backlash and handed him another great office of state instead. Whether it is a consolation to Miliband remains to be seen.

‌



He rewarded loyalty elsewhere by appointing key ally Louise Haigh, as First Secretary of State and Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster. The former Transport Secretary, who was sacked by Starmer over a historic fraud conviction, is now one of the most powerful people in Government.

Lucy Powell, another ally, becomes Education Secretary - and one of his right-hand women, Anneliese Midgley, was named as Chief Whip.

Angela Rayner is back in Government in her old role, Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government. She fought hard to win back this brief, which is a key priority for Burnham.

The PM kept Pat McFadden at the Department of Work and Pensions, in a sign of his commitment to fixing the welfare system and getting young people into work. He also moved experienced minister Yvette Cooper to the Department of Health, where she will drive much-needed reforms to the broken social care system.

‌



The Cabinet continues to take shape but these appointments show us what the PM's key priorities are.

And while he has packed his Cabinet with experienced people, there is only one vision here - and it's his.

News.title: Burnham pledges to 'bring back hope' as he makes Healey chancellor
News.content:
Andy Burnham pledged to "bring back hope" to Britain, as he began his tenure as prime minister by appointing Labour stalwart John Healey as chancellor.

In his first speech to the nation in Downing Street, Burnham said he wanted to bring forward the "biggest changes in the last 40 years" to British politics.

He outlined his intention to unveil a 10-year "new plan for Britain" later this year, explaining this would lay out a path to where he believes "we all want Britain to be".

Burnham promised to make announcements this week to "give people some breathing space now, some help with the cost of living" and explain how he would pay for them.

Burnham also started making cabinet appointments after removing loyalists of former PM Sir Keir Starmer. Out went Rachel Reeves as chancellor, David Lammy as deputy prime minister and justice secretary, and Steve Reed as communities secretary.

Healey, who quit Sir Keir's government due to a row over defence spending, was in as chancellor.

With Burnham saying he wants to honour the UK's commitments on defence spending, Healey will face the challenge of finding the extra money he believed the last government failed to deliver to keep the UK safe.

Speaking to broadcasters, Healey said the pair will "work in lockstep to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty" and on how they will "make life more affordable for working people right across the UK".

Ed Miliband moves from energy secretary to foreign secretary, replacing Yvette Cooper who is now the health secretary.

Miliband told the BBC it was the "honour of my lifetime" to become foreign secretary, a role his brother David held between 2007 and 2010.

Shabana Mahmood remains as home secretary and Louise Haigh takes on the role of Burnham's fixer across government, serving as first secretary of state, chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster and minister for the Cabinet Office.

Angela Rayner returned to a cabinet job as housing secretary, a role she previously held in Sir Keir's government. She stood down in September 2025 after admitting she underpaid stamp duty on her Â£800,000 flat in Hove.

Wes Streeting, the former health secretary who at one stage was seen as a possible leadership challenger, is the new defence secretary.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch welcomed Burnham to his new role but said he has not "set out a clear plan for government".

She said "Britain needs a leader who can take difficult decisions, not a people pleaser" and criticised him for "promising to undo Margaret Thatcher's policies".

News.title: Man, 28, charged with murder of Ann Widdecombe
News.content:
A 28-year-old man has been charged with the murder of Ann Widdecombe, police and prosecutors have said.

Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, is set to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

Counter Terrorism Policing said "determining the motivation, including any possible political motivation" remains "an active avenue" of investigation.

Kerry was initially arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July, before being additionally arrested on 13 July on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.

Widdecombe, 78, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman, was found dead on Thursday 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries.

In a statement read outside New Scotland Yard, Laurence Taylor, head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing said: "I want to make it very clear that our investigation into [Kerry], determining his motivations and any wider activity he may have been involved in is continuing."

"As with all murder investigations, understanding the 'why' is a key part of our enquiries," he said, adding that it was "a particularly intensive and complex investigation".

Taylor said it remained the case that investigators were not looking for anyone else in connection with the incident.

He added that counter terrorism teams have gathered "a huge amount of information" over the last week, leading to more than 800 lines of enquiry.

The investigation, which remains ongoing, has been led by Counter Terrorism Policing South East, supported by Devon and Cornwall Police.

Frank Ferguson, of the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS)'s special crime and counter terrorism division, said: "Our prosecutors have worked closely with the police to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court, and we will continue working with them as their investigation progresses."

"We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial," Ferguson said.

"It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings."

News.title: Kevin Keegan, Liverpool footballer who managed England and Newcastle United, dies aged 75
News.content:
Former England captain and manager Kevin Keegan has died at the age of 75, seven weeks after he revealed he had been diagnosed with stage four cancer, his family have confirmed.

One of English football's most decorated players, Keegan enjoyed spells at Scunthorpe United, Liverpool, Hamburg, Southampton and Newcastle during an illustrious playing career.

He later went on to manage Newcastle, Fulham, England and Manchester City.

Keegan revealed he had stage four cancer in June, which is the most advanced stage of cancer and means the disease has spread to other parts of the body.

His family initially disclosed he was battling the disease in January, after he had "further evaluation of ongoing abdominal symptoms" in hospital.

A statement on behalf of the Keegan family said he was "surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments".

"Kevin, a double Ballon d'Or winner, was a much loved husband, father and grandfather," it continued.

"The family would like to thank Kevin's incredible medical team for all their support. This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy."

Newcastle United paid tribute, describing Keegan as "one of the most iconic, influential and deeply loved figures in our club's history".

The club statement added: "Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager. He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters.

"Kevin's impact will not be measured by appearances or results. It will live on in the memories he created with club and country, the dreams he inspired wherever he went, and the generations of supporters around the world who fell in love with football because of him."

Liverpool, for whom Keegan played for between 1971 and 1977, said Keegan's "indomitable spirit and remarkable contribution will be forever etched in our history and his legacy will live on".

Hamburg said football had lost one of its "defining figures" and they would always "cherish" his memory, while Fulham said Keegan "forged a strong connection" with the fans, who would "forever hold wonderful memories" of his short time at the club.

Keegan's first club, Scunthorpe, described him as "one of the best players of his generation", with an "inspirational demeanour" and "brilliant personality".

England and Manchester City both offered their condolences to the Keegan family, with the latter describing him as "one of the most iconic and fondly remembered figures in English football".

The Three Lions will celebrate Keegan's life when they host Spain in a Uefa Nations League match at Wembley on 26 September.

News.title: Ofcom launches investigation into Married at First Sight UK
News.content:
Married at First Sight UK is facing renewed pressure after the broadcast regulator launched an official investigation into the hit Channel 4 reality TV show.

In a statement on Monday, Ofcom said it was investigating "a fairness and privacy complaint" about the prime-time show.

In May, a BBC Panorama investigation revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show - allegations the men involved deny.

An Ofcom fairness or privacy complaint can be lodged by individuals who participated in TV or radio programmes. Complaints like these usually relate to claims of being treated unfairly or having unwarranted infringements of privacy on programmes.

It is understood the watchdog is considering a complaint of unjust or unfair treatment from a cast member of Married at First Sight UK.

At least one other cast member previously complained to Ofcom about their treatment on the show, but the watchdog dismissed their complaint as it found the broadcaster had no case to answer.

An Ofcom spokesperson said such complaints are considered "on a case-by-case basis through a detailed and careful assessment process".

News.title: Fifa opens investigation into Argentina post-final trouble
News.content:
Argentina will face an investigation into the ugly scenes at the end of the World Cup final, Fifa has confirmed.

Fifa's disciplinary committee has appointed a disciplinary and ethics prosecutor to assess what happened after the final whistle at MetLife stadium.

Any player or coach involved in the fracas could face suspension, while the Argentine Football Association (AFA) may also be fined.

Following their 1-0 defeat on Sunday, members of the Argentina team and backroom staff were involved in altercations with Spain players as they began to celebrate their World Cup success.

Nahuel Molina, Leandro Paredes, Thiago Almada and assistant coach Roberto Ayala all appeared to be involved.

It was initially reported by Fifa that Paredes had been sent off by referee Slavko Vincic after he pushed Spain's Eric Garcia by the throat.

Paredes' red card was removed from the record shortly afterwards and Fifa has confirmed to BBC Sport that no disciplinary action was taken at the time.

Argentina had already had one player dismissed, with Enzo Fernandez receiving a second yellow card in second-half stoppage time.

Fifa had already begun the process of potential disciplinary action against Argentina after their players held a banner in support of their country's claims to the Falkland Islands following the 2-1 semi-final win against England.

News.title: Watch: 'My flat was turned into a brothel,' landlord tells BBC Panorama
News.content:
A BBC Panorama investigation has uncovered how organised crime gangs are exploiting the UK's private rental market - targeting properties to take over and use for their operations.

Among those featured in a new documentary is landlord and property developer Craig Shepheard, who discovered his flat was being used by a prostitution ring, run by a network in Brazil.

BBC Panorama reporter Hazel Martin also found that criminals are using fake IDs to get rental agreements.

News.title: Russian warship carried out firing exercise off Plymouth coast
News.content:
A Russian warship, shadowed by a Royal Navy vessel, carried out a live-fire artillery exercise just 40 nautical miles south of Plymouth on Monday.

The Royal Navy monitored the exercise and is continuing to "track the vessel's activity closely", a Ministry of Defence (MoD) spokesperson said.

The Russian frigate, Neustrashimy, was also being monitored by a French military aircraft which made radio contact with the warship asking it to clarify its intentions, the BBC has been told.

Prior to opening fire, the BBC was also told that the Russian warship informed the Royal Navy Offshore Patrol Vessel, HMS Tyne, of its intention to conduct gunnery activity.

The Russian warship requested that that HMS Tyne reposition to a safer distance, which it did. The Russian live-fire exercise took place in international waters and lasted for 30 minutes.

The incident will be a reminder for the new prime minister of increased Russian naval activity near UK waters in recent months. UK defence sources would not comment on whether the incident might have been timed to coincide with the start of Andy Burnham's premiership.

Last month, Royal Marine Commandos boarded a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel in a six-hour operation which was the first of its kind by UK armed forces.

Also in June, a British couple in international waters in the English Channel came across a Russian warship - Admiral Grigorovich - 23 miles (37km) off the Isle of Wight.

The frigate fired warning shots as Jane and Alan Kelvey sailed their yacht on what Russia's defence ministry said had been a "dangerous approach". However, the couple said they were "not on a collision course".

Russian warships regularly pass through international waters in the Channel, which are separate from UK and French territorial waters.

Additional reporting by Ella Kipling

News.title: Canadian wildfires rage as Trump warns Carney again over 'poisoning' US air
News.content:
Trump's remarks to Carney when they attended the game on Sunday came after he threatened last week to impose new tariffs on Canada to pay for what Trump described as the "incalculable" cost of the smoke's impact on the US.

The US president posted the threat on social media on Friday as thick smoke shrouded Washington DC and New York City as it drifted across a large swathe of the eastern US.

Ford told reporters on Monday that the neighbourly squabbles can be maddening.

"I get frustrated just listening to a bunch of rubbish," he told reporters at a press conference. Canada has helped during natural disasters in the US, he noted, such as Hurricane Helene and wildfires in California.

"Maybe one day you're going to need our help," Ford said.

In Ontario, some 1,800 people have been evacuated due to the wildfires, according to Ford.

Whitewater Lake First Nation in Ontario, which consists largely of seasonal camps and has no full-time residents, was burned over the weekend. Infrastructure, community homes, and personal property were all destroyed, Chief Pauline Drake told CBC News on Sunday.

"It was full of beaches, sand beaches, good fishing, good hunting - the wildlife was beautiful. We had eagles that were always there," she said. "I don't know how the wildlife is now. That's very concerning, because they were part of our upbringing there."

Over the weekend, Ford visited Thunder Bay, Ontario, and promised to "do and spend whatever it takes to protect people from these devastating wildfires".

In the western Canadian province of British Columbia, the entire city of Kimberley has been placed under an evacuation alert, affecting some 9,000 people.

Carney said in a statement on Sunday that he had mobilized more than 5,000 firefighters and nearly 300 waterbombers, helicopters, and evacuation aircraft "to contain, control, and mitigate the fires".

"It's an enormous, complex effort that ultimately depends on dedicated and brave individuals who work relentlessly to keep Canadians safe," he added.

News.title: South East Water hosepipe ban to affect 2.4 million people
News.content:
A hosepipe ban has been expanded to cover 2.4 million people across the south of England after record-breaking temperatures.

South East Water's ban now includes parts of Sussex, Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire - an extra 1.5m customers. A ban in parts of Kent has been in force since 3 July.

Douglas Whitfield, SEW's water supply director, said it was "deeply sorry" and "incredibly grateful to everyone helping us protect water supplies" after exceptionally hot and dry weather.

Eastbourne MP Josh Babarinde said he was "appalled", calling it "the direct result of years of underinvestment in upgrading infrastructure and building resilience".

Under the restrictions, households in the affected area will be banned from using a hosepipe in their homes for tasks including cleaning, filling ponds, or watering plants.

The ban will officially come in from 00:01 BST on Saturday, but SEW has asked its customers to abide by the restrictions immediately.

The UK record for the hottest day in June was broken for a third day in a row last month, with temperatures reaching 37.3C, the Met Office said.

News.title: Sara Sharif killer wants inquest with jury
News.content:
The woman who murdered her stepdaughter Sara Sharif has asked for the inquest into her death to be held in front of a jury.

Beinash Batool and Sara's father Urfan Sharif were jailed for life in 2024 after the 10-year-old was found dead at the family home in Woking.

She had been violently abused in a "campaign of torture" lasting two years.

Bite marks, an iron burn and scalding from hot water were among dozens of injuries found on her body in a post-mortem examination.

On Monday, Batool's lawyer Dr Anton van Dellen said jurors would help determine if Sara was failed by people who were scared of being accused of racism.

"This is just the type of judgement where a diverse local jury would provide a helpful perspective," he added.

A review into the 10-year-old's death found that services in Surrey failed to properly investigate why Sara started wearing a hijab - that covered her bruising - for "fear of causing offence".

Neighbours also said they were worried about "being branded as being racist" if they reported concerns.

News.title: Ryanair profits drop as Iran war puts off passengers and lifts fuel costs
News.content:
Ryanair's profits have fallen sharply as war in the Middle East sent jet fuel prices soaring and customers reluctant to book flights.

The Irish airline's pre-tax profits dropped 34% to â¬593m (Â£503m) between April and June while sales were flat as the company was forced to cut fares to stimulate demand.

Ryanair also said it expects summer fares to be slightly lower than last year due to "consumer hesitancy" around air travel.

The price of fuelling a plane has jumped since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February and while Ryanair said it had "hedged" or struck deals for the most future fuel costs, those not included in these arrangements had more than doubled.

Crude oil prices hit $90 (Â£67) a barrel for the first time in a month on Monday, before falling back slightly, after a weekend of intense exchanges of fire between the US and Iran.

Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz â an essential route for global oil and gas supplies â has ground to a halt.

An interim peace deal last month brought some respite to oil and energy prices, but they spiked again as negotiations broke down and fighting resumed.

The airline warned that its results for the year will be "highly sensitive" to external factors such as conflict escalation in the Middle East and Ukraine as well as the price of unhedged jet fuel.

Fares for for the key summer period between July and September are on track to be "modestly" lower than last year, with many passengers booking closer to departure than normal.

The firm's finance chief, Neil Sorahan, said flights on its popular Mediterranean routes were still full. "People [are] as keen to get away as ever, albeit booking just a little bit later," he said.

Between April and June, Ryanair's revenue ticked up 1% to â¬4.4bn.

While passenger numbers rose 6% to 6.1 million- helped by the Easter holiday in April - fares fell by 6% as the airline reduced fares to entice flyers concerned about the Iran war.

Ryanair's share price fell 5% on Monday.

Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, said Ryanair was in a better position than many of its rivals, but nonetheless "visibility is worse than San Francisco airport when the fog sets in".

"The renewed escalation in hostilities in the Middle East is unhelpful and without a lasting resolution, challenging times for the airline and travel space look set to continue."

News.title: Ofcom unable to take further legal action against suicide forum
News.content:
Ofcom said it is unable to take further legal action against a pro-suicide forum which campaigners say has been linked to over 130 UK deaths.

The regulator said, external the site had blocked access for the "vast majority" of UK users, and it had "no further legal routes available" under the Online Safety Act.

But it accepted people would still be able to access the forum by using a VPN, which hides your location online.

Andy Burrows, chief executive of the Molly Rose Foundation, said the decision to take no further legal action would "result in more lost lives" and that announcing it on the day a new prime minister was named showed "an utter lack of moral courage".

In response, an Ofcom spokesperson said it had made the decision a "matter of days ago" following "months of work to exhaust all possible legal routes".

They said bereaved families were informed of the decision this morning after being contacted last week.

"In that context, we do not consider it appropriate to delay the announcement further to accommodate today's political developments," they said.

Meanwhile, Ofcom enforcement director Suzanne Cater said the regulator had used its powers "to the fullest extent possible".

"We'll continue to monitor the forum closely to check the geoblock remains in place," she said.

The geoblock means people based in the UK are unable to access the site, unless they mask their location through a VPN or similar means.

Ofcom said it was working with the government to explore whether its enforcement powers should be strengthened.

In particular, this concerns its ability to get a website blocking order through the courts, which would legally mandate internet service providers in the UK to block the website.

The regulator says it has reached the limit of what it can legally do under the Online Safety Act because the forum has implemented the geoblock.

The BBC has approached the government for comment.

News.title: 'Scrutiny' needed over baby's death, court hears
News.content:
Preston had been taken to Blackpool Victoria Hospital three times before his death and seen by a "battery of professionals" including medical staff, social workers and welfare officers from various bodies.

Wilson told the hearing an inquest had initially been opened shortly after Preston's death but was then suspended while police investigated, culminating in the trial and conviction of his adoptive parents.

Wilson said he had to consider whether an inquest should continue, given "relevant issues" had already been heard during the eight-week criminal trial.

However, while he said he would not make a final decision on Monday, subject to submissions from lawyers for other public bodies, it was "highly likely" one would take place, probably in the autumn of next year.

He said: "I feel there's sufficient reason to resume. There are acts and omissions of public authorities that need to be scrutinised in a public hearing in which Preston's family can participate.

"It's clearly going to be a wide-ranging inquiry."

The coroner said he was aware there had been calls for a public inquiry, but his role meant that was not a matter for himself to consider, but to proceed on the basis of whether or not to hold an inquest.

The court heard Oldham Safeguarding Children's Partnership, had resumed a review into Preston's death, following its suspension for the criminal trial to take place.

This review was likely only to be completed by January 2027, and the inquest cannot be held before then, the court heard.

Much of the hearing dealt with which people or public bodies should be legally represented at any inquest.

They included Preston's biological mother and grandmother, Sara and Debbie Davey, neither of whom were present for the hearing but were represented by lawyers in court.

Preston was born while his mother was in custody and a place in a mother and baby unit in prison was refused, the court heard.

Instead, he was taken from her by a court order from Oldham Council and placed with temporary adoptive parents before being adopted by Varley and McGowan.

News.title: Fire crews to remain at Arthur's Seat for days after blaze
News.content:
Firefighters are expected to remain at Arthur's Seat in Edinburgh "for a couple of days" following a large blaze on Sunday evening.

Small plumes of smoke could still be seen on Monday morning along Salisbury Crags and large swathes of vegetation below the cliff face had been burned black.

Six fire engines were sent to tackle the the grassfire on the slope between the Scottish Parliament and St Leonard's, with crews working overnight to douse the flames and dampen hotspots.

The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) said there were "no reported casualties" but Police Scotland said Queen's Drive, the road that encircles the Holyrood Park hills, remained closed to all vehicles.

It is the second fire in the last three months at the landmark, an ancient extinct volcano that offers panoramic views of the Scottish capital.

A Very High risk of wildfire warning for the central Highlands, southern and eastern Scotland has been extended to Friday as warm weather is forecast to continue.

The warning was extended by the SFRS, in conjunction with the Scottish Wildfire Forum (SWF).

News.title: Prisons minister Lord Timpson quits government
News.content:
The prisons minister has resigned from the government, the BBC has been told.

Lord James Timpson was appointed to the role in July 2024 after leaving his job as CEO of the Timpson group, a business which provides key cutting and shoe repair services and employs hundreds of former prisoners.

His arrival in government was greeted with much fanfare by some in the Labour Party and described as "radical" and "innovative".

But in a departing statement on Monday, seen exclusively by the BBC, Lord Timpson said he was stepping down and it was an "honour" to serve in the post.

His statement did not give a specific reason for resigning, but it is understood he feels he has done as much as he can in the role.

Prisons in England and Wales were at crisis point, reaching almost full capacity, when he first entered Sir Keir Starmer's government.

He oversaw the controversial early release scheme which saw tens of thousands of inmates let out to create more space in jails.

His critics will argue prisons continue to be violent, drug infused and overcrowded, while probation officers still report being overworked and unable to cope.

But figures do show assaults against staff and self-harm in prisons are falling.

Lord Timpson said in his resignation statement that he had left "our prisons and probation service in a much healthier and happier state than two years ago".

He added: "I'm proud to have become the longest-serving minister in this role for 15 years. I'm also proud that 75% of prisons and 90% of probation teams are now performing better than when I started.

"Self-harm, violence and assaults on staff are all down, and fewer people are leaving prison without a home to go to, a measure of dignity I care about deeply."

He also pointed to the Women's Justice Board he established, saying he "believe[s] most women should not be in prison at all" and "diverting them away from custody, helping them with often chaotic, damaged, and addicted lives, is one of the changes I'm proud to have achieved".

His critics may question why he is leaving before the Sentencing Act 2026 is enacted in September, when more people are expected to be released early and further criminals will serve their sentences in the community.

A source in the Ministry of Justice told the BBC: "We're gutted he's going but the new person is going to have their work cut out to get their head round what's round the corner."

News.title: Pupil not guilty of trying to murder history teacher after stabbing her in the head
News.content:
A pupil has been found not guilty of attempted murder after stabbing his teacher in the head with a kitchen knife.

The boy, 16, followed Vicki Williams into her empty classroom at Milford Haven Comprehensive School in Pembrokeshire, after asking for help with his history work on 5 February.

He pulled a knife from his bag and lunged at her. Williams told a jury at Swansea Crown Court she feared she would die.

On Monday, he was found not guilty of attempted murder but guilty of wounding with intent, and unlawful wounding. He will be sentenced on 3 September.

The boy had previously pleaded guilty to possessing a kitchen knife on the school grounds.

Judge Paul Thomas KC accepted a majority verdict on the charge of wounding with intent, which meant at least 10 jurors agreed following four hours deliberation.

During the attack, Williams grabbed the knife, pushed the boy back with her legs, and screamed.

She received injuries to her head, back and hands after the attack.

She said the look on the teenager's face was one of "pure hatred".

During a police interview, Williams said how the boy, who was 15 at the time and who cannot be named due to his age, came to her classroom "cool and collected" at the end of the school day to ask if his "work was correct".

She said that "got [her] confused" because he had "never seemed bothered before".

It was when he shut the door to the classroom, saying it was cold, that "alarm bells" began to ring in her head.

Williams said he was trying to "keep her talking" while he was "trying to find something in his bag".

"I ask him again, 'are you sure you're alright?' And then he pulls [the knife] out of the bag and lunges at me," she said.

The boy told the court Williams had seen him with the knife and "tried to grab it" from him. He said he "accidentally assaulted her" during the struggle.

She told the court she believed she was about to die, thinking: "I'm fearful that I am dying, I've seen the knife, I know I've been stabbed, all I'm thinking at that point is, 'I need help'."

Williams said the attack "came out of nowhere".

Five people drowned in an Ohio river on Sunday after multiple members of a group attempted to rescue a struggling swimmer, an emergency that was discovered after a passing motorist spotted a distressed young child running on a nearby road.

According to Delaware County Sheriff Jeffrey Balzer, the child’s presence on the road prompted a 911 call from the motorist, alerting law enforcement to the unfolding tragedy along the Scioto River in Powell, a suburb of Columbus, the Associated Press reported.

The incident began when one member of the group entered the water to swim and quickly began to experience distress. Several other individuals then entered the river in an effort to assist, but they also began to struggle in the water, Balzer said during a Monday news conference.

A search and rescue operation was launched Sunday, during which crews recovered two women from the water. Both were transported to a local hospital, where they were pronounced dead, Balzer said.

The search continued into the following day. Tracy Whited, a spokesperson for the Delaware County Sheriff’s Department, confirmed that the bodies of three men were recovered from the river on Monday.

open image in gallery Five people drowned in an Ohio river after multiple members of a group attempted to rescue a struggling swimmer, according to police ( WSYX )

At the scene, law enforcement agents staged their operations at a grassy area along Riverside Drive, a largely residential route running north and south along the river. About a dozen people stood by waiting to speak with authorities at the staging area, which sits less than a mile from a designated public fishing area on the O'Shaughnessy Reservoir.

Though officials did not confirm exactly where the victims were recovered, representatives from the Ohio Department of Natural Resources noted that water depths in that area of the reservoir can reach a maximum of 40 feet, though it is mostly 20 feet deep or less, according to the Associated Press. The reservoir was originally built by the city of Columbus in 1925 to provide drinking water to local residents.

open image in gallery Officials stand at a staging area after an operation to recover multiple people who died while trying to save someone from the Scioto River in the Columbus suburb of Powell, Ohio, ( AP )

Following the incident, Balzer urged those gathering near water to take strict safety precautions before entering the water.

“Know your skill level before you get in the water. Are you a confident swimmer?” Balzer said. “Make sure you have other people around in case something goes wrong to notify someone. Wear a life preserver. Wear a life jacket. I get it. People think that somehow those are just for kids. But I tell you, they save everybody’s lives.”

open image in gallery A section of the Scioto River's shore is seen in the Columbus suburb of Powell, Ohio ( AP )

The Scioto River stretches for approximately 230 miles through Ohio, flowing southeast through Columbus before meeting the Ohio River in Portsmouth.

The incident follows another recent water-related tragedy in southern Utah, in which five family members were killed two days prior after being caught in a flash flood during a canyon hiking excursion.

Five family members who had set out for a day of hiking were killed after a flash flood swept through canyons of southern Utah on Friday, law enforcement officials said.

The victims were a captain in the Provo, Utah, fire department, his wife and their sons, according to fire officials. A daughter who was not on the trip survived.

The family arrived Friday at Sunglow Campground in a scenic red rock canyon near Bicknell, Utah for their day excursion, the Wayne County Sheriff’s Office said.

“It is believed the family fell victim to flooding caused by heavy rains,” the sheriff's office said in a news release.

Although the sheriff's office did not identify the victims, the Provo Fire Department confirmed in a social media post that a fire captain, Spencer Long, and his family members were killed.

“We are absolutely heartbroken by the death of Captain Spencer Long and his family. Our thoughts are with his family, friends, and colleagues during this difficult time,” officials with the fire department wrote.

Later Friday night, deputies were called to the campground after the body of a young male was found in the flood wash. The bodies of the other family members were recovered late Friday and Saturday.

Meanwhile, tributes poured into the family.

Long, his wife Katrina and their sons Reid, Thayne and Gage died in the devastating floods, according to a GoFundMe site set up by a family friend to support the Longs' daughter as she navigates the loss of her family.

“Spencer and Katrina were loving, devoted parents whose greatest joy was their family. They touched the lives of so many with their kindness, generosity, and unwavering love,” Bree Nielson wrote on the page.

Katrina Long was the cofounder of a medical spa. "Our hearts are with all of their loved ones as we grieve the unimaginable loss of Katrina, her husband, and their three beautiful boys," Summit Medical Spa posted on Facebook.

Robbie Williams has jokingly addressed a "deeply unprofessional" on-screen gaffe during the World Cup final in which he accidentally spat a small white object onto his microphone.

The 52-year-old singer, who had performed alongside Nicole Scherzinger and Laura Pausini at the closing ceremony on Sunday, drew attention during an appearance on German TV channel Magenta Sport.

While speaking to pundits, the object emerged, which he then picked up, held, and subsequently rubbed onto his head, where it stuck to his forehead.

open image in gallery Robbie Williams performed alongside Nicole Scherzinger and Laura Pausini at the World Cup closing ceremony ( Bradley Collyer/PA Wire )

The incident quickly garnered attention. Williams later took to social media to share a video explaining the mysterious item, clarifying the nature of the unexpected moment.

Filming himself lying in bed, the performer says: “I’d just like to apologise for the object that fell on to the microphone yesterday.

“I was deeply unprofessional, and people worried about me.”

“But it’s OK. Because I had several more,” he continues, before sticking his tongue out and revealing two circular mints.

open image in gallery Williams stuck the object on his forehead after it dropped onto his microphone ( Magenta Sport )

Williams breaks out laughing before the video cuts off.

Captioning the Instagram post, he wrote: “Just woke up and feeling…. Mint x.”

On Sunday night, the first World Cup half-time show was also held.

The final between Argentina and Spain featured an 11-minute spectacle with stars from around the world including Madonna, Shakira, BTS and Justin Bieber.

The show at the New York New Jersey Stadium also featured an appearance from Muppets characters Kermit the Frog and Miss Piggy.

Fifa extended the half-time interval of the match from the customary 15 minutes to more than 27 minutes.

Former England forward Wayne Rooney, who was at the New York New Jersey Stadium working as a BBC pundit alongside Joe Hart and Micah Richards, did not hold back when asked for his highlights of the show by presenter Gabby Logan

“I’ll be honest, mine was when it finished. I like a lot of them artists but I thought it was crap,” he said.

“It just didn’t get me going and I wanted the football to come back on. I like Burna Boy, I like Bieber, I like Shakira, but that was too flat.”

Richards called Rooney “miserable” for his assessment, while Logan added: “I’ll tell you what else you get on the BBC: honest reviews.”

President Donald Trump has imposed steep 50 percent tariffs on a range of Canadian imports, citing “continued discrimination” against American industries, including autos, alcohol and dairy products.

This aggressive move threatens to unleash significant economic instability, potentially driving up inflation and further straining the relationship between two historically close allies.

An administration official, speaking anonymously to reporters, justified the action by stating that Canada, alongside China, was among the few nations to retaliate against previous tariffs imposed by Trump, necessitating accountability.

The tariffs were enacted through three proclamations under Section 338 of the 1930 Trade Act. This particular section has drawn criticism, with several Democratic lawmakers last year advocating for its repeal due to concerns that Trump could wield it to destabilize the national economy.

The tariffs also pose a threat to other US trading partners, not just Canada ( Evelyn Hockstein/Getty Images )

The new 50 percent tariffs would exclude energy products, potash, fish and critical minerals, but they would include goods that had previously been protected from import taxes by the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA. That 2020 trade pact was not renewed by the U.S., triggering a new set of negotiations that could run until 2036.

The White House said in a fact sheet that the tariffs would go into effect in 30 days, meaning there is time for negotiations, as Trump has not always followed through on his announced tax hikes on imports.

Canada faces the risk of a broader trade war

Still, the tariffs could escalate into a wider trade war as Canada seeks to defend its economy.

The Canadian federal government did not immediately comment on the tariff, but Ontario Premier Doug Ford saw a possible showdown ahead.

“If these tariffs proceed, Canada should respond tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar,” Ford posted on social media.

Candace Laing, CEO of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, said the Trump administration's moves were “regrettable” but the two countries need to use the 30-day window before the tariffs start "to make meaningful progress in advancing formal talks.”

The tariffs also pose a threat to other U.S. trading partners, not just Canada, and inject “massive uncertainty” into the global economy, said Scott Lincicome, vice president of general economics at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank.

“We crossed the Rubicon,” Lincicome said. “The invocation of 338 is the nuclear option for Trump tariffs.”

Tariffs are also a political challenge for Trump

The new tariffs carry serious political and economic risks for Trump ahead of the November midterm elections for control of Congress. His “Liberation Day” tariffs last year in April provoked a financial market meltdown over concerns about inflation and a recession, prompting him to walk back the rates for a period of negotiation.

The Supreme Court ruled this February that Trump had lacked the legal authority to impose the tariffs by declaring an economic emergency, causing the administration to find alternative ways to raise import taxes based on a series of legal authorities.

Tariffs are taxes on imports, which companies can then pass along to consumers in the form of higher prices. The president maintains that the costs created by tariffs will cause manufacturing to relocate to the U.S., though there is little evidence of that in the economic data.

The latest import taxes could worsen Trump's weak ratings on the economy. He promised voters when running for the presidency that he would bring prices down, but the annual inflation rate has risen since he became president because the tariffs and the war in Iran are pushing up oil prices.

Trump has repeatedly targeted Canada on trade issues

The Trump administration official said the president had also requested that his aides look into additional tariffs on Canada because its wildfires hurt air quality in the U.S. He had publicly threatened to do so in social media posts.

At the World Cup final on Sunday, Trump watched the game with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has openly challenged the U.S. president and has sought to expand Canada's trade relations with other nations. The Trump administration official said their time together at the game was not a working visit to discuss trade and tariffs.

Trump claims in the proclamations that Canada discriminates against American autos, alcohol and cheese relative to other nations, but his argument rests in large part on retaliatory actions taken by Canada after the U.S. president imposed tariffs on Canada under the pretext that it should do more to stop fentanyl smuggling.

Trump noted in his autos proclamation that Canada maintained, starting in April 2025, a 25 percent tariff on the imports of U.S. motor vehicles that did not qualify for preferential treatment under the USMCA.

The White House said that, regarding alcohol, all but two Canadian provinces and territories halted the purchase and retailing of American alcoholic beverages beginning last year, which was also a response to Trump's tariffs and taunts of making Canada the 51st state.

But Trump has long objected to Canada's treatment of U.S. cheese, saying in his proclamation that Canada discriminates against the U.S. compared to Europe on dairy products.

Trump and Carney have had a frosty relationship, with Carney, a former central banker, who pledged to stand up for Canada during his election campaign last year.

At the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January, Carney called out Trump — without naming him — by saying that the “most powerful” countries are using the economy to coerce less powerful nations.

Trump responded at the time by saying: “Canada lives because of the United States."

The Government-owned British Business Bank has revealed its annual profits have tripled after benefiting from a jump in the valuation of its investments.

The UK’s economic development bank, which lends money to and buys stakes in smaller UK businesses to help them start and grow, is also set to be boosted by supporting the Government’s industrial strategy.

It recorded a pre-tax profit of £426 million for the year to March, almost three times the £144 million generated the previous year and the largest profit in four years.

This was driven by an increase in the valuation of its investments in funds and businesses.

The bank generated around £115 million worth of realised gains from the sale of equity in companies it has invested in, up from £84 million the prior year.

The British Business Bank, which gets funding from the Government’s Department for Business and Trade (DBT), said the increase points to its ability to generate returns for UK taxpayers.

But it acknowledged that the wider economic environment was “uncertain with a number of factors both locally and internationally which may impact on valuations in the short term” including from conflict in the Middle East.

“The bank is ultimately focused on delivering realised returns at the end of multi-year investment cycles, therefore, year-on-year fluctuations are to be expected,” it insisted.

The bank’s annual report showed that it deployed £1.5 billion during the latest financial year into a mixture of new and existing investments.

open image in gallery The bank has been allocated extra funding to support the Government’s industrial strategy and invest in priority sectors such as clean energy (PA) ( PA Archive )

Some 87% of newly funded businesses were based outside of London, a higher proportion than the business population more widely, according to the firm.

Furthermore, costs in relation to the Covid-19 loan schemes reduced last year as they continue to wind down.

The bank administered the Government’s loan schemes to businesses during the pandemic, and landed in hot water over the loss of an estimated £1.1 billion to fraud and error.

Meanwhile, the bank has been allocated extra funding to support the Government’s industrial strategy and invest in priority sectors such as clean energy, defence, life sciences and financial services.

It said this will help it to step up activities and encourage investment into firms to grow in the UK rather than move overseas.

News.title: David Dimbleby ‘appalled’ by BBC plans to cut 2,000 jobs: ‘Why on earth have they done that?’

Veteran broadcaster David Dimbleby has expressed his profound dismay over impending job cuts at the BBC which could see up to 2,000 employees lose their positions.

Speaking to Radio Times, the 87-year-old said he was "appalled" by the national broadcaster's decision.

The BBC is aiming to achieve £500 million in savings over two years, with the announced redundancies expected to be implemented over the next three years.

“Why on earth have they done that? The best analysis of politics, both national and international… I’m appalled. Very bad, bad, bad, bad, bad call,” he said.

The Independent understands morale among some staff at the corporation is low as news of the cuts comes amid the release of a number of presenters’ salaries who were found to earn six-figure salaries.

One staff member, speaking anonymously, said there was “an obvious disconnect in the organisation” and staff want senior leadership to “be more transparent and self-aware”.

Dimbleby, who previously hosted Question Time, also criticised cuts made to BBC Studios Events.

The team responsible for coverage of national occasions like Remembrance Day and state funerals was told all but one of them will be axed to cut costs.

David Dimbleby also criticised cuts made to BBC Studios Events ( BBC/The Garden TV )

“And my God, BBC Events being closed!” Dimbleby said.

“It takes months of connections to make friends with the people at the Palace, with Westminster Abbey, with the police, to know what’s going on with Downing Street, so that when the day comes, everybody helps you.

“It’s a BBC gold standard to cover big national events. It’s at the heart of the BBC, and I cannot understand what they’re up to. But I have no power in the BBC.”

In a statement, the BBC said: “The BBC has to make at least £500m of savings and BBC News, like all of the BBC, needs to play its part.

“We have tried to mitigate the impact on audiences as much as possible, so The World Tonight will be replaced by BBC World Service’s Newshour, another high-quality news analysis programme made by the same production team, preceded by a domestic news bulletin.”

It was previously announced BBC Radio 4’s The World Tonight will be axed after more than 50 years, one of the first victims of the broadcaster’s savings drive.

Dimbleby joined the BBC as a news reporter in Bristol in the 1960s.

He presented Question Time from 1994 to 2018.

In other changes, the Sunday morning edition of BBC Breakfast will be cut from September and the production teams for Newsnight and Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg will be merged.

BBC director-general Matt Brittin said in a note to staff that the corporation will “review our broadcast TV channels and radio network portfolio as audiences move online”.

He also said up to 10% of “senior leaders” will be cut from the organisation.

England’s 32 motorways and major A roads have been ranked from best to worst following polling of more than 9,500 drivers in March.

The survey conducted by the watchdog Transport Focus revealed 71 per cent of drivers were satisfied with their journeys on motorways and major A roads nationwide, up from 69 per cent last year, with improvements noted in journey times, road surfaces, and roadworks management.

However, the M27 in Hampshire was branded the least satisfactory, plagued by persistent roadworks and subsequent delays. Only 56 per cent of drivers who used the 28-mile stretch were satisfied with their journey.

One frustrated respondent described the roadworks as "terrible," citing reduced speeds and narrowed lanes, despite "very rarely" witnessing any actual work taking place. The M27 has been subject to extensive ongoing projects, including resurfacing and junction modifications.

In contrast, Kent’s M20 emerged as the nation’s favourite motorway, with a satisfaction rating of 79 per cent.

England’s network of motorways and major A roads is entering one of its largest maintenance periods since much of it was first built in the 1960s.

National Highways is embarking on a five-year renewals programme as part of the third Road Investment Strategy, which is likely to involve more roadworks.

Transport Focus director Louise Collins said the survey results demonstrate that “positive improvements to the road user experience are possible”.

She went on: “Overall satisfaction has increased and there are encouraging signs that drivers are noticing improvements in key areas, however, drivers continue to tell us that roadworks can make or break a journey.

“By applying the positive lessons from recent schemes, National Highways has an opportunity to ensure roadworks are well planned, clearly communicated and minimise disruption wherever possible.”

Satisfaction with journeys on smart motorways rose from 60 per cent last year to 66 per cent.

Transport Focus attributed this to the completion of work to retrofit 150 additional emergency refuge areas, which involved widespread roadworks causing delays.

Kent’s M20 was ranked the country’s favourite motorway ( PA )

Drivers on sections of smart motorway continued to feel less safe than those on conventional motorways, at 78 per cent and 82 per cent respectively.

The A30, which runs between west London and Cornwall, was ranked the best A road, with a 79 per cent satisfaction score.

At the other end of the scale, the A12 between the east of the capital and Suffolk had the lowest rating, at 64 per cent.

A National Highways spokesperson said: “We manage our roads to ensure the highest levels of safety while minimising disruption to drivers.

“The survey results show our work to improve road conditions and incident response times have had a positive impact on drivers.

“When roads are well maintained, businesses and communities feel the benefit, and we are committed to tackling an ageing network head-on to keep the country moving and give drivers better experiences.”

The survey of more than 9,500 drivers was conducted in the 12 months to the end of March.
