Sports.title: Martin Keown names three transfers Arsenal need – but rejects Marcus Rashford calls
Sports.content:
Martin Keown believes that Arsenal have three positions they need to fill this summer, but Marcus Rashford shouldn't be one of them.

The Manchester United winger has been linked with a move to the Emirates Stadium in the past, but nothing so far this summer as the England international's future remains in limbo.



3 Rashford wanted to join Barcelona permanently, but the LaLiga giants signed Anthony Gordon instead Credit: Getty

However, Keown does believe that the Gunners need a new left winger with Leandro Trossard departing north London to join Besiktas.

This leaves just Gabriel Martinelli as Arsenal's only natural left forward, though Eberechi Eze can play there having done so regularly at former club Crystal Palace.

The former centre-back would also like to see a central midfielder added and possibly a striker.



Newcastle United's captain Bruno Guimaraes has informed the club that he would like to join the Gunners.

However, talkSPORT understands the Magpies are looking for £100million to part ways with the Brazilian.



The Gunners are also interested in Julian Alvarez, who is seeing a potential move to Barcelona being blocked by Atletico Madrid.

Speaking with Alex Crook on talkSPORT, Keown said: "I think Arsenal need another midfield player, someone who can control things.



"I think they need a left winger. You could say, they might go into the transfer market for a striker - I wouldn't put it past them.

"Most players will want to sign for Arsenal, but the most important thing is to get the people who are successful to re-sign their contracts.

"Keep them on board, build what you have got, and then, add real quality to it. It has to be quality because we are talking about the champions."

3 Trossard leaves an Arsenal cult hero, but he needs replacing Credit: AFP



Crook then read out some messages from people who suggested Rashford, but it was put to bed by Keown.

"I don't see that. I'd be surprised if that happened," Keown said when asked about Rashford potentially joining Arsenal.

"I thought Rashford did well for Aston Villa. They didn't have the money to buy him."

When asked if he didn't want Rashford because of attitude, Keown responded: "I just think he went off the rails. Lots of talk behind the scenes of potential issues.



"I think he's back on track now, and it is an interesting one when he goes back to Manchester United with Carrick.

"Does he welcome him back in? There is talk of him living in the city again. Is that a problem?

3 Rashford is an option on the left but Keown doesn't see him in an Arsenal jersey Credit: Getty

"But I think he's back on keel, and you really want to see these players play at their best. It is a short career, so get out there and play."



No go

It is increasingly likely that Rashford will start the season as a Manchester United player.

The £40m clause in his deal has expired, with Barcelona choosing not to activate the option to buy in the loan.

Instead, they signed Anthony Gordon from Newcastle as well as Karim Adeyemi.

Rashford not going back to the Camp Nou leaves a potentially awkward reunion with the Man United fans on the cards.

Sports.title: ‘Thank you’ – Lionel Messi gives emotional statement one day after World Cup heartbreak
Sports.content:
Lionel Messi has penned a message of thanks to Argentina fans in an emotional statement after their World Cup final defeat to Spain.

The 2022 winners were beaten 1-0 on Sunday as Ferran Torres scored in extra time following a rather dull 90 minutes of football.



3 Messi missed out on winning a second World Cup Credit: AFP

Argentina went down to ten men late on when Enzo Fernandez was sent off for two yellow card offences.

Messi, who captained his country, appears to have made his last ever appearance at the World Cup at the age of 39.

And less than 24 hours after defeat at the MetLife Stadium, he wrote down his emotions in a statement posted on Instagram.



'Thank you'

"The pain is immense, and it will take time for this wound to heal. But I also hold on to all the good," he said.

"The matches we turned around, giving our all, matches that will forever remain in our memories, the support of an entire country that, together with the hard work and effort of this group, led us to be, once again, among the best in the world.



"Today it's hard to fully appreciate what we accomplished, but this group reached two consecutive World Cup finals.

"Thank you from the bottom of my heart for every greeting and every message. Once again, we managed to unite as a country and be together, sharing the immense pride of being Argentinian.



"I also want to congratulate Spain on winning the championship."

Messi scored eight goals and assisted another four for Argentina in their World Cup run.

The defeat to Spain was the only match in which he didn't produce a goal contribution.

3 Messi had to settle for a silver medal this time round Credit: Getty

He hinted at possible retirement before kick-off as his boots for the final had 'El Ultimo Tango', which is 'The Last Tango', written on them.



However, he is under contract at Inter Miami until December 2028, and there is nothing concrete in regards to him calling it quits.

Argentina were way off the pace against Spain as they had just two shots compared to their opponents' 20 throughout the match.

Fernandez was dismissed just moments before the start of extra time and therefore left the holders with a mountain to climb.

He also posted on Instagram on Monday, saying: "As time goes by, you realize there is something much bigger than just a result.



"For years, this group has represented the team in the best possible way. It teaches that competing isn't just about winning; it’s about giving your all for the jersey and never giving up.

3 Ugly scenes marred the end of Spain's World Cup win Credit: Getty

"It has been a privilege to be part of a group that always stepped up, competed at the highest level, and defended these colors with pride, humility, and commitment.

"I want to thank all the Argentine fans. Thank you for always being there, for supporting us in every match, for the affection, for the unconditional support, and for making us feel at home anywhere in the world.



"Wearing my country's jersey is the greatest honor of my career, and I will continue to give my all every time I get to defend it."

Some Argentina players let their emotions get the better of them at full-time, with Nahuel Molina throwing a punch at Rodri.

Leandro Paredes also attacked two Spain players, and FIFA are set to investigate the post-match scenes.

Sports.title: 2034 World Cup could be played in 2035 with FIFA boxed into ‘unprecedented scheduling dilemma’
Sports.content:
FIFA has a logistical nightmare on its hands with the 2030 and 2034 World Cups posing different challenges.

2034 World Cup could be played in 2035 with FIFA boxed into ‘unprecedented scheduling dilemma’

The 2034 World Cup in Saudi Arabia could pose a nightmare for FIFA.

As happened with Qatar 2022, the tournament is expected to be moved to winter due to the oppressive heat of Middle Eastern summer.

3 Champions Spain will defend the World Cup on home soil Credit: Getty



However, a report from American outlet Politico has revealed several major scheduling conflicts in an 'unprecedented scheduling dilemma.'

The Qatar edition was held from November 20 to December 18, which will clash with Ramadan in 2034.

Dictated by the Islamic lunar calendar, the holiday is expected to run from November 12 through December 12.

In Muslim countries including Saudi Arabia, Ramadan has a major impact on public life and matches would potentially have to be played at night to fit in with local customs.



The tournament could be hosted earlier in the year, but the Winter Olympics is slated for January and February.

March sees around two million pilgrims head to Mecca for Hajj -- another event which cannot be moved.



With temperatures then set to rise, FIFA could be stuck between a rock and a hard place and that is before taking into account the need to accommodate the schedule of worldwide leagues and continental competitions.

FIFA's 2034 World Cup scheduling conundrum

Politico suggests that between Christmas 2034 and Hajj -- set for mid-February in 2035 -- could be the most logical window.



If FIFA wants to avoid Christmas, that doesn't leave very long for a tournament which has already ballooned to 48 teams and could be 64 by 2030.

President Gianni Infantino is clearly not afraid of a logistical challenge.

3 Infantino's relationship with Trump has been questioned pre-tournament and during the tournament Credit: Getty

After the 2026 tournament was hosted across the United States, Canada and Mexico, 2030 is a six-country affair spread over three continents with Morocco and Spain fighting for the right to host the final.



The FIFA president is likely to be re-elected unopposed for another four-year term in 2027, although there is mounting opposition to his rule, especially in Europe.

UEFA chief Aleksander Ceferin refused to attend Sunday's final in protest at a number of controversies, with the final straw being Folarin Balogun's overturned suspension.

That could see more pressure from European clubs over any schedule changes in 2034.

There are also concerns over Saudi Arabia's human rights record, as was the case for Qatar and Russia in 2018.



FIFA insists it is opening up the game and becoming truly global.

3 Saudi Arabia is home to the holiest site in Islam -- Mecca's Masjid al-Haram (The Sacred Mosque) Credit: AFP

Maintaining that stance will put bosses in an awkward situation should any conflicts arise with Muslim holidays.

Searing heat has been an issue at the current tournament thanks to a heatwave and Infantino spoke about the potential need to be flexible over football's traditional June-July schedule.

“We are already into the nitty-gritty, we are discussing all the time,” he said in 2025. “It’s not just about one World Cup, it’s a general reflection.



"Even to play in some European countries in July it is very, very hot. The best month to play football, which is June, is not used very much in Europe.

“Maybe there are ways we can optimise the calendar, but we are discussing it and we will see when we come to some conclusions. We just have to keep an open mind."

Sports.title: 2026 World Cup team of the tournament: Harry Kane omitted and six Spain stars named in Gabby Agbonlahor’s XI
Sports.content:
2026 World Cup team of the tournament: Harry Kane omitted and six Spain stars named in Gabby Agbonlahor’s XI

The 2026 World Cup is officially over after an incredible five weeks of action, with Spain lifting the trophy for a second time.

But now the tournament is complete, it's a popular time for fans and pundits alike to put together their standout XIs.



5 Spain became world champions for a second time Credit: Getty

There were many starring performances, ranging from the world's best players to complete unknowns becoming legends.

Kylian Mbappe won the Golden Boot, while Rodri won the Golden Ball and Pau Cubarsi was handed Young Player of the Tournament.

Those three stars got the accolades, but do they all make the World Cup Team of the Tournament? And if so, who joins them?



Here's who Gabby Agbonlahor and Troy Deeney think deserve to be among the best 11 players of the summer:

Instagram star and Spain's defence

Agbonlahor, of course, started off with his defence, making a simple choice for his back four after selecting a star goalkeeper.



"There have been some good goalkeeping performances, but I have to give it to Vozinha," the ex-England striker began.

"Two clean sheets, five goals conceded, clean sheet against Spain, who went on to win the tournament.



"That just shows how good of a performance it was...a fantastic tournament and he got a load of Instagram followers."

He then moved on to his back four and simply selected the entire Spain defence, picking Pedro Porro, Pau Cubarsi, Aymeric Laporte and Marc Cucurella.

"Porro, I think he was fantastic, passion, determination...Cucurella is one of the best in the world, and Cubarsi and Laporte, how they played was incredible," Agbonlahor explained.

5 Cape Verde's Vozinha was one of the heroes of the 2026 World Cup Credit: Getty



'A credit to the nation'

He then moved on to his midfield, including Player of the Tournament, Rodri, and picking England's main man.

"Rodri went through a terrible knee injury...that was Ballon d'Or Rodri; those were the performances we've seen," he said.

"He's not been the same player since his injury, but any talk we were having of him going from City, now fans and Enzo Maresca will be saying no, Rodri will be starting with Elliot Anderson."

Agbonlahor then selected: "Alongside him I want Dani Olmo...Spain play to his strengths, behind the striker, receiving the ball, finding passes, I thought he was fantastic.



"And also in midfield, Jude Bellingham. Words can't describe how good he is, seven goals, one assist, the most goals by an English player at a World Cup.

"What he's proved to everyone is that he's a leader, a future captain, and he did everything in the tournament to get us over the line...the manager cost us...I thought he was a credit to the nation"

5 Bellingham made Agbonlahor's XI for his showing, but Kane was omitted Credit: Getty

Kane left out

Bellingham is the only England player in Agbonlahor's World Cup XI, as he opted against including Harry Kane in the team.



Kane scored six goals at the tournament and became the country's all-time top scorer there, but he didn't claim a place.

The Three Lions captain was snubbed amid some criticism for his performances, with three stars picked over him.

Agbonlahor explained: "The front three speak for themselves: Mbappe, 10 goals, four assists, Lionel Messi, eight goals, four assists, Erling Haaland, seven goals, zero assists.

"They were fantastic and it was a pleasure to see a World Cup where the top, top players turned up."



Agbonlahor's World Cup TOTT: Vozinha; Porro, Cubarsi, Laporte, Cucurella; Rodri, Olmo, Bellingham; Messi, Mbappé, Haaland.

5

Troy Deeney's Team of the Tournament

Similarly to Agbonlahor, Deeney couldn't help but have Spain dominate the defence in his best XI of the World Cup.

He also picked Cubarsi and Cucurella, adding in goalkeeper Unai Simon over Cape Verde's hero Vozinha.



On Simon and the Spanish defence, Deeney said: "He's been unreal... when you only let in one goal, that's frightening."

The former Premier League striker went on to select what he called a 'wildcard', with Lisandro Martinez being picked.

Martinez starred for Argentina ahead of the final, but he was unfortunately substituted with an injury in the showpiece.

In midfield, Deeney, of course, picked Golden Ball winner Rodri, but then selected a surprise name next to him.



He chose France's Manu Kone to slot into his team, as the 25-year-old impressed despite starting just half of Les Bleus' eight games.

Bellingham was also included in Deeney's team, like Agbonlahor's.

However, Kane wasn't snubbed for a second time, as the ex-Watford man picked the England captain for his line-up.

He was selected alongside Messi and Mbappe in the front line.

"Harry, Messi on the right, Mbappe on the left, Jude in the 10," he explained when picking his star-studded forwards.

Deeney’s World Cup TOTT: Simon; Porro, Cubarsi, Martinez, Cucurella; Kone, Rodri; Messi, Bellingham, Mbappe; Kane

Sports.title: England icon Kevin Keegan was a football romantic who loved Scotland and loved beating them too
Sports.content:
England icon Kevin Keegan was a football romantic who loved Scotland and loved beating them too

For all that he was an icon of English football, Kevin Keegan also left his mark north of the Border. Not just as a player and manager who often broke the Tartan Army’s hearts, but as a passionate, open-hearted dreamer who later in life fell so in love with Scotland that he moved there.

Not for him the narrow-minded ill-feeling that continues to divide the two countries, although it would be fair to say he lapped up those sepia-tinted days half a century back when his perm bounced around Wembley, often at the expense of travelling Scots.

Who can forget that goal in 1979 when Keegan, England’s captain no less, collected the ball on the halfway line, exchanged passes with Trevor Brooking and slipped it under goalkeeper George Wood to secure a 3-1 victory and, with it, the British Home Championship?

Or indeed the European Championship playoff in 1999 when, as England manager, he followed a 2-0 win at Hampden with a 1-0 defeat at Wembley. ‘I've never been as glad to hear a final whistle in all my life,’ said Keegan who later admitted that he would have resigned had Scotland overturned the deficit.

And yet Keegan, who has died at the age of 75, had nothing against Scotland. If he had, he wouldn’t have agreed to play for Hearts in Alex MacDonald’s testimonial match against Rangers in 1984. His appearance at Tynecastle in the home side’s Skol-sponsored shirt helped to attract a crowd of around 18,000.

Nor would he have been a regular visitor to Scotland during his playing days, enjoying holidays in some of its remotest locations. He would take in the views, the atmosphere and become so enamoured with it that he and his wife decided in 2005, when his football career was all but over, to set up home on the Inverclyde coast.

Kevin Keegan celebrates after scoring one of his most famous goals against Scotland in 1979

Keegan poses with Alex MacDonald at the latter's testimonial match against Rangers in 1984

Keegan promotes the Soccer Circus business he launched in Glasgow while living in Scotland

At that time, he told the Largs and Millport Weekly News: ‘I’m living in Inverkip just now with my wife, Jean, and every morning I look at the scenery around the Clyde and think to myself, ‘This is magic’.

‘Ever since the early 1980s I have been coming here, going round the Highlands and Islands, going to Inverlochy Castle, Skibo, St Andrews, and there is always something different in the landscapes and the weather, which sends a shiver up my spine.’

This correspondent was lucky enough to spend some time with Keegan around then. After declaring his retirement from football in 2005, he set up something called Soccer Circus in Braehead and was keen to do an interview on condition that the project was publicised.

Even in those pre-TikTok days, his interactive football centre didn’t seem especially modern and it only lasted a few years, but who cared?

It was the product of everything that was good about Keegan. Yes, he was a little naive at times, but he was a born entertainer, a passionate, pied piper of a man, full of ambition and ideas. And if they didn’t work, he would admit it and move on, as he did when it became clear that the England job was too big for him.

If Keegan wasn't transcending his sport as a tragic cyclist on Superstars, he was releasing a single - Head Over Heels in Love reached number 10 in the German charts - or unleashing his notorious ‘I would love it’ rant against Manchester United boss Alex Ferguson as his Newcastle team’s title challenge disintegrated. There was no filter, no safety net, and Keegan was all the better for it.

He was honest (often to his own detriment), emotional and he always wore his heart on his sleeve.

He embraced life and football without fear of failure, which is how he ignited the Geordie nation during those mythical spells as a manager and player at St James’ Park.

On Tyneside right now, they are mourning the loss of a legend who was the very soul of their club and their people.

North of the Border, he will be missed too. For Keegan was a football romantic who showed it was possible to love Scotland and love beating them too.

Sports.title: Tennis brings in sex tests: Martina Navratilova praises 'step in the right direction' as WTA launches new policy forcing stars to prove eligibility
Sports.content:
The Women's Tennis Association (WTA) has become the latest sporting organization to implement genetic testing in a bid to establish players' eligibility to compete as a female.

The governing body's previous policy permitted biological males to compete in the women's category if they maintained testosterone levels below a certain level.

But now a tweak to the rules - which will be implemented from Tuesday - states that WTA players must undergo a sex screening for the SRY gene, which is found on the Y chromosome and is typically involved in male sex development.

Only once they have passed the test - which is completed through a simple cheek swab, blood test or saliva sample - will players be eligible to compete on the female-only WTA Tour.

A positive test, meanwhile, will spark further medical assessment before a player is cleared to play against their female rivals. Players must also sign documentation acknowledging that refusal to be tested could result in disciplinary action.

Tennis icon Martina Navratilova, who has been strong in her views on keeping trans athletes out of women's sport, was quick to praise the WTA for making the move.

Barbora Krejcikova celebrates after winning the latest WTA tournament in Athens on Sunday

Martina Navratilova (right, with the Princess of Wales at Wimbleon) has praised the new policy

World No 1 Aryna Sabalenka reacts during her last match, against Naomi Osaka at Wimbledon

Writing on X, she said it was a 'step in the right direction', adding: 'I played no part in this particular policy, but am very happy that we at the WTA are clear that we are a women's association and only women, as in females, can compete at the highest level of women's tennis.'

In the policy itself, the WTA states: 'The WTA's women's eligibility policy is designed to promote equal athletic opportunities in women's professional tennis and maintain fair competition for all players participating in WTA tournaments.

'The WTA recognises that this is a sensitive and complex issue and is committed to treating all players with dignity and implementing the policy in a respectful and thoughtful way.'

Other organizations, such as World Boxing and World Athletics, have already implemented similar testing for its athletes seeking to compete in the women's category.

The IOC has also confirmed it will sex test athletes ahead of the next Olympic Games, which will be held in Los Angeles in 2028.

Sports.title: Spain's World Cup heroes touch down in Madrid for triumphant parade after enjoying £1K bottle of red wine and cigars in their New York hotel before late-night dash to airport
Sports.content:
See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Spain have landed in Madrid after wasting no time in jetting out of New York in the immediate aftermath of winning the World Cup with the victory over Argentina on Sunday night.

Luis de La Fuente's side secured a second star for their nation with a dogged victory against a difficult Albiceleste at the MetLife Stadium just across the river from Manhattan.

But after lifting the trophy in front of a full house of their adoring fans, La Roja opted not to ring in their victory with a night of partying in the city that never sleeps.

Instead, Golden Ball winner Rodri got the party started in transit, leading a round of singing on the team bus as the jubilant players sped back to their hotel for a team meal, before moving on to Newark Airport.

Back at the hotel, noted oenophile Marcos Llorente enjoyed a bottle of Chateau Rayas Chateauneuf-du-Pape Reserve 2014 - which costs a festive £1,009 to uncork - in his room with team-mates Ferran Torres and Marc Pubil.

The stars then boarded the Airbus A350-941 waiting for them - clad in their team's livery - and took off shortly after 2am local time.

Captain Rodri lifted the World Cup as Spain touched down in Madrid on Monday afternoon

The country's most-likely weary players will now have a little downtime before their parade

Before leaving the tarmac however, the team posed for a group photo with their manager Luis de la Fuente

Join the discussion Should Spain have celebrated more publicly in New York, or was rushing home for a trophy parade the right move?

Spain's players landed at Madrid's Barajas Airport at 2.30pm local time, and stepped out onto the tarmac with the World Cup trophy held aloft.

The reasoning behind flying out immediately after winning the World Cup is thought to be that the team will be welcomed with a trophy parade in Madrid's Plaza de Cibeles - where Real Madrid often host their own celebrations.

The players are now believed to be set for just a little downtime, before heading to the picturesque square to kick-off the party on home soil.

According to Spanish outlet La Razon, officials from Madrid have organised a secure welcome for the players that is set to attract thousands of fans as the team travels to Plaza de Cibeles in an open-top bus.

Once on board the flight, Aymeric Laporte was among the players to pose with the World Cup trophy, giving it a tender kiss in his seat as he soaked up the once-in-a-generation feeling.

Spain had previously celebrated on the pitch with their friends and family, with crossover superstars including seven-time Grand Slam champion Carlos Alcaraz also joining in on the fun.

Players were draped in flags from their regions in the country as they posed for photos and celebrated with loved ones.

But the show was thoroughly stolen by Spain's unofficial talisman Keyne Yamal - the little brother of teen starlet Lamine.

Dressed in a replica Spain jersey with his brother's No 19 and his own first name emblazoned on the back, Keyne darted onto the pitch at MetLife Stadium, where he then ran straight into his older brother's arms.

Lamine Yamal carried his bags - including an oversized Hermes Birkin bag - off the plane

Spain were in high spirits as they celebrated winning the World Cup on their bus home to Madrid in the early hours of Monday morning

Festivities in the hotel were limited to a bottle of £1,000 red wine drunk by Marcos Llorente, goalscorer Ferran Torres and Marc Pubill

Marc Cucurella and Gavi posed in front of the team's Airbus as they prepared to go home

The airplane arrived hours later as the city of Madrid readied a welcome home fit for heroes

Aymeric Laporte and Alex Baena both posed with the World Cup trophy onboard their plane

Rodri led a bus full of Spanish players in rounds of singing as they headed for Newark airport

Yamal had previously enjoyed a cigar in the lift as he began his journey back to Spain

The prodigal Barcelona star had celebrated earlier on the pitch with his girlfriend Ines Garcia

Yamal was all too happy to accept a hug from Keyne and quickly lifted his younger brother into the air before gently placing him back down on the field and putting a red 'Lamine' baseball hat on the toddler's head.

And that wasn't the only hat Keyne tried on while roaming around the MetLife pitch on Sunday.

A New Jersey State Trooper couldn't help but remove his cap to briefly share with Keyne, who tried it on before politely returning it to the officer.

Yamal also posed with his girlfriend Ines Garcia in a sweet photo on the pitch, with the influencer sharing it with the caption: 'You did it. Congratulations, my love - you're a world champion'.

Later, Yamal was snapped lighting a large cigar as he waited in a lift at the hotel on his journey home.

Then, hours later, the Spain players enjoyed a celebratory night as their players embarked on a parade in the capital, showing off their World Cup trophy to their fans.

The highlight, despite the celebrations on stage, was arguably Yamal holding up a sign that read: 'Event of the year: Paredes vs Gavi.'

As high-spirited as Spain's celebrations were, they came in stark contrast to the ugly scenes on the pitch after the final whistle, when Argentina stars including Leandro Paredes attacked Spanish players Eric Garcia and Rodri.

Yamal held up a sign during the celebrations that read: 'Event of the year: Paredes vs. Gavi'

Spain's players had a night of celebration upon landing in Madrid as they were greeted by their supporters

They also embarked on a parade around the city as they displayed their World Cup trophy

Paredes throttled Garcia and pushed Barcelona star Gavi to the ground, while Nahuel Molina also punched Rodri in the torso as he was running by.

Argentina defender Nicolas Otamendi later complained to DAZN Spain that rival players had been complaining to the media in the build-up to the final.

Argentina players later turned their backs on Spain's trophy lift in their last bitter act following a blue-and-white campaign as noted for its thuggishness as its strong tournament play.

Sports.title: 'He showed how to lead by example and was a huge influence on me - I took so much from how he went about things': BRYAN ROBSON on KEVIN KEEGAN
Sports.content:
'He showed how to lead by example and was a huge influence on me - I took so much from how he went about things': BRYAN ROBSON on KEVIN KEEGAN

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

I'll never forget when I first walked into the England dressing room, it was Kevin Keegan who came over, gave me a hug and said 'enjoy this, son'.

He was the captain, the superstar and reigning European footballer of the year but there were no airs or graces, no front, just this fantastic footballer and man who was genuine in his support.

It was my debut against the Republic of Ireland at Wembley. We won 2-0 and Kevin scored both goals.

How to lead by example. This great No 7. That was Kevin all over. He was a huge influence on me.

He didn't have to go out of his way to make a fuss of me but he was really welcoming. This big star recognised I just needed a bit of encouragement and him adding normality by saying 'just enjoy it'. Playing for England.

I took so much from how he went about things. He had loads of energy and worked so hard. That always stood out. You didn't get to be European footballer of the year twice on talent alone.

Kevin Keegan led by example when Bryan Robson joined the England team. From left: Robson, Ray Wilkins, Keegan and Trevor Brooking at the England hotel for the 1982 Spain World Cup

He gave everything in training, not just the games.

I maintain to this day that if Kevin had been fit for the 1982 World Cup, we would have had a great chance of winning it. Instead, a back injury meant he could only play a small part as a substitute. But he was that good. He would have made the difference.

He retired at international level after that and I've always thought it would have been the most fitting way for him to end his England career to have won that World Cup.

Even when he went into management, his teams had his style. Always attacking, always wanting to entertain, reflecting his great enthusiasm for how to play the game.

As we got older, he moved round the corner from me in Hale and we used to meet up for a coffee. Reminiscing about the old days, mainly those with England, laughing about the characters we knew, the experiences we'd had. I used to see him on the after-dinner circuit and his stories were always so funny, a great raconteur. A genuine star, a terrific player but he could back it up as a terrific man.

To lose him is such a shock. It's a sad, sad day.

My condolences go to Jean and his daughters.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi breaks his silence on Argentina's World Cup heartbreak with emotional statement - after snubbing interviews in the wake of brutal loss to Spain
Sports.content:
Lionel Messi has taken to social media to speak following Argentina's World Cup final defeat by Spain that left the forward crying on the pitch.

Messi was bidding to lead his country to World Cup glory for the second time in as many tournaments on Sunday, but Argentina came up short on the night.

It was a game of intense controversy and drama, with an investigation underway into Argentina's conduct after the game, which saw the likes of Leandro Paredes lose their cool and get violent at the full-time whistle.

Messi himself drew attention too, as he tried to get Spain's Marc Cucurella sent off for covering his mouth in the second-half.

But his attempts failed and the star, who finished second behind France's Kylian Mbappe in the Golden Boot rankings, has now spoken on the ordeal.

'The pain is immense, and this wound will take time to heal,' he wrote on Instagram. 'But I also hold onto all the good things... The matches we turned around by giving it our all—moments that will remain in our memories forever—and the support of an entire country which, combined with this group's hard work and effort, brought us back among the world's elite once again.

Lionel Messi has broken his silence following Argentina's World Cup defeat against Spain

Messi was inconsolable shortly after receiving his runners-up medal from Donald Trump

'It is hard to fully appreciate our achievement right now, but this group reached two consecutive World Cup finals. Thank you from the bottom of my heart for every greeting and message.

'Once again, we managed to unite as a country and stand together, sharing the immense pride of being Argentine.

'I also want to congratulate Spain on winning the championship.'

The Argentina squad has also been slammed for standing with their backs to the winning team at MetLife Stadium as Spain lifted the World Cup trophy.

Instead, the Argentina players, coaching team and staff walked over to the end where the majority of their fans were sat and turned their backs as their rivals celebrated.

Footage shows Spain players holding the World Cup trophy aloft as gold confetti explodes behind them, with the Argentina team facing the other way.

Messi and his team also refused to face the music and speak to the media following their defeat.

Argentina only had two shots in the entire match, with the first coming in the 117th minute.

Sports.title: Football world mourns Kevin Keegan: Heartbroken Alan Shearer pays tribute to his 'hero', Jamie Carragher hails 'one of the greatest players this country has ever produced', while Prince William says he 'inspired generations'
Sports.content:
See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Alan Shearer has led the tributes to football legend Kevin Keegan after he passed away at the age of 75 following a short battle with illness.

Keegan was diagnosed with stage four stomach cancer in January, having been admitted to hospital with abdominal problems.

In a statement, his family said: 'It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75. The former England player and manager had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments.

'Kevin, a double Ballon d'Or winner, was a much loved husband, father and grandfather. The family would like to thank Kevin's incredible medical team for all their support. This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy.'

And following the tragic news, figures from across the footballing world were quick to pay their respects to Keegan, who represented Scunthorpe, Liverpool, Hamburg, Southampton and Newcastle and later managed the Magpies (twice), Fulham, England and Manchester City.

Newcastle legend Shearer said: 'My Hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy Boss.'

Alan Shearer and Jamie Carragher led the tributes to football legend Kevin Keegan (pictured after winning the European Cup with Liverpool in 1977) after he passed away

Keegan is one of the best ever English players and enjoyed a successful managerial career

Former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher added: 'RIP Kevin Keegan. One of the greatest players this country has ever produced, trophies & goals galore, double Ballon d'Or winner shows he was an absolute giant of the English game.

'One of the most important men in making @LFC what it is today.'

Prince William, the official patron of The FA, said: 'Incredibly saddened to hear of the passing of Kevin Keegan.

'A truly remarkable footballer and manager who inspired generations with his talent, passion and love of the game.

'Above all, he will be remembered as a kind and generous man. Our thoughts are with his family and all who knew him. W.'

Shearer pictured with then Newcastle boss Kevin Keegan after signing for the club in 1996

Trevor Brooking said: 'I am so very sad to hear the devastating news today about my friend and former team-mate Kevin Keegan.

'My friendship with Kevin goes back many decades, to our playing days for England. We were lucky enough to develop a real understanding on the field of play and know what each other was thinking.

'Kevin liked to run and find space on the pitch and I’d try to time my passes to give him the best chance to use his world-class skills to score.

'We roomed together on England duty and Kevin, with his bubbly character, was never shy of making jokes, often at my expense!

'I recently met up for lunch with Kevin and Jean when they were visiting London. Although it had been a while since we’d last seen each other, we picked up our conversation as if it had been yesterday.

'That afternoon, reminiscing about our footballing days, is one I will always treasure.'

Former England captain David Beckham posted: 'Such a sad day to hear the passing of Kevin Keegan.

'A man that was very kind to me and my family xx. Sending lots of love and thoughts to his family and friends.'

Several of Keegan's former clubs also shared their own tribute, including Newcastle.

Taking to social media, they said: 'We are devastated to learn of the passing of Kevin Keegan, one of the most iconic, influential and deeply loved figures in our club’s history.

'Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager. He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters.'

Liverpool shared their own heartfelt post which read: 'We are deeply saddened by the passing of the legendary Kevin Keegan and mourn his loss.

'His indomitable spirit and remarkable contribution will be forever etched in our history and his legacy will live on. Rest in peace, Kevin. 1951-2026.'

Former Reds star John Aldridge said: 'I've just been passed the really sad news.

'The great Kevin Keegan has passed away! He gave me great joy in my teens as a huge LFC fan, and the saying says never meet your heroes?

'Well I did!! Roger Hunt and KK and they surpassed everything I thought they were as people. Our thoughts are with all his family. God bless Kevin YNWA.'

Keegan, a forward in his playing days, won 63 caps for England before he later managed the Three Lions.

And they also posted a tribute which said: 'We are incredibly saddened by the news that Kevin Keegan OBE has passed away.

'Kevin earned 63 international caps and scored 21 goals between 1972 and 1982, before managing the #ThreeLions from 1999 to 2000.

'Our thoughts and condolences are with Kevin's family, friends and former clubs.'

Heartfelt tributes poured in for Keegan from figures and clubs across the footballing world

Former Newcastle owner Mehrdad Ghodoussi added: 'Devastated to hear about Kevin Keegan. Growing up watching football, he was one of the names that defined an era, a double Ballon d’Or winner, European Cup champion, England captain, and one of the most exciting players the game has seen.

'But what he did at Newcastle was different. He turned belief into something you could feel in the stadium.

'King Kev wasn’t just admired, he was loved, because everything he did came from the heart. Rest in peace, Kevin. Thank you for everything you gave the game.'

During his managerial career, Keegan also took Fulham from the Second Division (now League One) to the First Division (now Championship).

And the Cottagers shared some words for the footballing legend as they said: 'We're incredibly sad to hear the news that our former manager Kevin Keegan has passed away.

'A legend of the game, Keegan led Fulham to the Football League Second Division title in 1999. He left Craven Cottage at the end of that season to focus on his duties as England manager.

'Our thoughts are with his friends and family at this difficult time.'

Manchester City, another of the teams Keegan managed, added: 'Everyone at Manchester City is devastated to learn our former manager Kevin Keegan has passed away, aged 75.

'Kevin was a transformative manager who brought optimism and vibrancy to City during his four-year spell in charge.

'The promotion campaign in 2001-02 will never be forgotten, and Kevin then established us once again as a top Premier League side in the years that followed. Our thoughts are with Kevin’s family and friends at this very difficult time.'

Sports.title: Farewell to 'Mighty Mouse' Kevin Keegan - the diminutive pioneer who let his emotions run wild and was a riot of colour and flame in a grey world, writes OLIVER HOLT
Sports.content:
Kevin Keegan, a kid from mining stock in South Yorkshire, a kid who started out at Scunthorpe United and went on to conquer Europe, was one of the greatest players English football has ever produced but it was the unquenchable passion that burned within him that won him such a prominent place in the hearts of the public.

Mighty Mouse, he was called as a player and it suited him. He was the little man who would never give up. He was the small guy who punched way above his weight. He was the lad who never bowed to anyone. He may have been slight of stature but he had the biggest heart that ever beat in the chest of an English footballer.

Sometimes, it feels as if time has dimmed the memory of quite what an outstanding footballer Keegan was and how he became a pioneer and a pathfinder, the first Englishman to play in a European Cup final with both English and foreign clubs, in his case Liverpool and Hamburger SV.

Sometimes it feels as if England’s mediocrity when he was at the peak of his playing career and the fame and affection he garnered in his managerial career, particularly at Newcastle United, have obscured the fact that he remains the only Englishman to have won the Ballon d’Or, the prize bestowed on the greatest player in the world each year, more than once.

Keegan won it in successive years during his time in Germany, in 1978 and 1979. For context, that puts him level with Franz Beckenbauer, Alfredo Di Stefano, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge and the Brazilian Ronaldo in the pantheon of the greats of the game. ‘I’m probably the most ordinary player to have won it twice,’ Keegan said in a recent interview.

But there was nothing ordinary about Kevin Keegan. Anybody who ever met him or ever watched him play or ever heard him giving a manager’s post-match press conference or ever saw him spending hours with fans desperate for a word or an autograph, knew that.

Liverpool, Newcastle and England legend Kevin Keegan has died at the age of 75 after a short battle with illness

Keegan (pictured in 1977 after winning the European Cup with Liverpool) is one of the greatest players English football has ever produced

Once, after his playing career was over, I sat opposite him on a stage at Westminster Central Hall, asking him questions in an interview organised by the newspaper I worked for then. I don’t remember the questions I asked, or the answers he gave.

What I do remember is how Keegan held the audience in the palm of his hand. They were rapt. After it was over, Keegan stayed until he had fulfilled every autograph request and spoken to every man and woman who wanted a word, who wanted to say that they had talked to one of the legends of the English game.

Keegan was an extraordinary man. He was a riot of colour and flame in a grey world. In a sport where players are told to keep their mouths shut and their emotions in check, he let his emotions run wild and people loved him for it.

His public profile rose even more when he competed in the BBC programme Superstars, which aired in the 1970s and 80s, and featured sportsmen battling it out against each other in series of different disciplines.

‘Superstar’ has become an overused term now but if ever a man fitted that description, it was Keegan. He was box office, from head to toe. The combination of the reach of television and the dynamism of his personality made him one of football’s first new age icons.

Even in the midst of everything he achieved on the pitch, what endeared him to people, and a huge part of the gift he leaves behind for us, was his heart and soul. His passion lit up his life. He could not contain it and we loved him for it.

His passion gave us some of the landmarks we remember him for. The fight with Leeds United captain Billy Bremner at the 1974 Charity Shield that got both men sent off and saw Keegan ripping off his shirt as he left the pitch.

What a different world it was then. ‘That looked very much like a right hook by Johnny Giles,’ commentator Barry Davies said when Keegan was flattened by a sweet right hand. Keegan pleaded for leniency for Giles. A few moments later, he was trading punches with Bremner. ‘This is a side of English football we do not want to see,’ Davies opined.

Keegan was beloved in Germany after moving to Hamburger SV in 1977. He won the Ballon d'Or twice on the continent

Keegan was an extraordinary man. He was a riot of colour and flame in a grey world

Keegan, who was born in Doncaster, had begun his career with Scunthorpe United before he was spotted and scouted by Liverpool manager Bill Shankly and established himself as the star player of the team that went on to win the European Cup, under Bob Paisley, in 1977.

That team was one of the great sides in the history of the English game. Let the names roll off your tongue: Ray Clemence, Phil Neal, Joey Jones, Tommy Smith, Ray Kennedy, Emlyn Hughes, Kevin Keegan, Jimmy Case, Steve Heighway, Ian Callaghan, Terry McDermott.

Keegan tormented the Borussia Monchengladbach captain Berti Vogts in that final in Rome and won the penalty in the 83rd minute that sealed a 3-1 victory for Liverpool and was the start of the club’s rise to being the most successful club in European competition in this country.

When Keegan moved to Hamburger SV that summer, many thought it would mark the end of Liverpool’s hegemony but they signed a player called Kenny Dalglish, who went on to emulate Keegan’s successes and more.

Then there was his bike crash in Superstars when he pedalled furiously down the main straight of an athletics track at the start of a race against Belgian footballer, Gilbert Van Binst, wobbling from side to side as he desperately tried to keep up, before crashing to the tarmac on the first bend.

It was a nasty accident. Keegan, who was close to the height of his powers as a footballer at that point, sustained cuts and grazes but he still refused to give up. The race was re-started and Keegan won. It was the show’s greatest moment.

Keegan became a hugely successful manager and is particularly adored by Newcastle fans

Keegan pictured in 1995 with famous entertainers Ant McPartlin (L) and Declan Donnelly (R)

Then there was the most famous diatribe in English football history when, feeling the hot despair of Sir Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United closing in on the league title after they had overhauled his wonderful Newcastle United team, he snapped as he spoke to Sky Sports after an away win over Leeds United at Elland Road at the end of April 1996.

‘We’re still fighting for this title,’ Keegan almost shouted into the camera, his voice shaking with anger and his finger pointing and jabbing, ‘and he (Sir Alex Ferguson) has got to go to Middlesbrough and get something and I’ll tell you honestly, I will love it if we beat them. Love it.’

David Beckham has said since that when the United players watched Keegan’s rant, they knew they had won the league. They knew that Ferguson’s mind games had exploded in Keegan’s head and that the title was theirs.

But that only added to Keegan’s legend. There was something magnificently untameable about him, something beautifully unpredictable, something free and untrammelled. He was still Mighty Mouse.

And he is still adored in Newcastle. It may be, in fact, that he is adored there more than anywhere else. He is adored for the pride he brought to the city and the way he resurrected the club and for the thrill of the beautiful football the Geordies played under his management.

That team was made in his image and so it was brilliant and it was entertaining and it was breathtaking but it was also fragile. And it could not quite cope with the relentlessness of Manchester United. But every neutral was desperate for Newcastle to win the title that season. And that was mostly down to Keegan.

Keegan's 'I will love it' rant was a sign that he was cracking under the pressure of a title race with Manchester United - but it only added to his legend

In a sport where players are told to keep their mouths shut and their emotions in check, he let his emotions run wild

There was no artifice about Keegan. He did not bother to try to hide what he was feeling. Or what he was. It was all out there, everything worn on his sleeve. He would have been the world’s worst poker player. He was not a man for keeping his counsel. Or for keeping his cool. Again, we loved him all the more for that.

Keegan always burned hot. At his unveiling as England manager in 1999, Daily Mirror journalist Nigel Clarke, who was sitting on the front row of the press conference, coughed while Keegan was speaking. Keegan became convinced that Clarke was mocking him and demanded to know why he was coughing. A long stand-off ensued.

Before a game against Sweden the same year, Keegan told Paul Scholes to ‘go out there and drop a few hand grenades’. Scholes promptly became the first England player to be sent off at Wembley after two horrendous challenges on opponents.

At the end of his short reign as England boss, Keegan was preparing his team for the final game at the old Wembley on October 7, 2000, a World Cup qualifier against Germany, and he decided he was going to play Gareth Southgate, a central defender in midfield.

On the Friday night before the game on the Saturday, the news began to leak out. I was on a Sky programme called Hold the Back Page, hosted by Brian Woolnough and Jimmy Hill, and we began the show by discussing the Southgate plan with varying degrees of scepticism.

Keegan was incandescent. He asked the FA to phone Sky to demand that the programme be taken off the air. Sky, obviously, could not accede to that request and the show continued as normal. To no one’s great surprise, the Southgate experiment did not go well.

Keegan managed England from February 1999 to October 2000 but resigned from his post

Keegan scored 40 goals in 113 games for Hamburg, between 1977 and 1980

England lost the game 1-0 and Keegan was booed by a section of England fans as he walked off the pitch. He stopped to remonstrate with some of them at the entrance to the tunnel. When he reached the dressing rooms, he summoned FA officials, retreated to the quiet of the toilets, and promptly resigned. The FA tried to talk him out of it but he would not reconsider.

Keegan had been a sublime player at Liverpool and Hamburger SV and then, in the late summer of his career with Southampton and Newcastle. I say late summer deliberately. There was never anything autumn about Keegan. His football did not yellow and fade. After his last game for Newcastle, a testimonial against Liverpool, he was lifted from the St James’s Park pitch in a helicopter.

‘Auf Wiedersehen, Kev,’ a message on the scoreboard at the Gallowgate End read that day in May 1984. And now, it is time to bid him farewell once more. Auf Wiedersehen, Kev, and thank you.

Sports.title: Josh Kerr's coach says there's more to come after world record
Sports.content:
Josh Kerr's coach says there's more to come after world record

Josh Kerr's stunning mile world record may not even represent his full potential, with coach Danny Mackey insisting the British star still has another second to find after his historic run in London.

View Image Josh Kerr celebrates after breaking the men's mile world record with a time of 3:42.66 at the Wanda Diamond League in London.

Josh Kerr broke a world record that had held for more than a quarter of a century but the scary part is that his coach is adamant he can go even quicker. In erasing Hicham El Guerrouj’s mile world record from the history books, Kerr cemented his place as one of the all-time greats of British middle-distance running.

‌



His time of 3:42.66 was 0.47 seconds quicker than Moroccan great El Guerrouj had managed in Rome 27 years ago and completed his Project 222 – the number of seconds required to break the record.

‌



But for Danny Mackey, who has coached Kerr to Olympic medals, world titles and now this world record, he is capable of going even faster. He said: “Based on a couple of his workouts, I think if the weather had been better he probably could have run 3:41. I think there was another second there. That's scary.

‌



“That's probably the most emotional I've been. When he won the world title, he wasn't the favourite. The year before hadn't gone the way he wanted, and we knew he could do it, but there wasn't this huge expectation on him.

“He's really unusual. We're in the tunnel right now, and most people, even if they're not racing, find this overwhelming. But he's different. He likes that kind of pressure.”

Kerr’s world record puts him in the same stratosphere as the British middle-distance legends of the 1980s, two of whom were in attendance in London on Saturday – World Athletics president Lord Coe and BBC commentator Steve Cram.

‌



And Lord Coe, who held this record three times, backed Kerr to flourish after continuing the legacy that dates all the way back to Sir Roger Bannister’s iconic sub four-minute mile.

He said: “I think this will have blown the wall away, he will go on to do incredible things. It’s just nice to see it back in the hands of a Brit. We’ve had a few but he’s as good as they get.”

Kerr planned to have a beer, or maybe two, to celebrate with his family and team, who have sacrificed a lot in this world record attempt. But there will be no time off, with a home Commonwealth Games in Glasgow just around the corner and redemption to be had.

‌



Mackey added: “We'll have to switch gears quickly for the Commonwealth Games. We'll go back to what we're used to, which is championship racing and tactics. We haven't really been training specifically for that, so hopefully he's fit enough to handle it.

It's important to him.

“At the last Commonwealth Games he'd had COVID after Worlds and struggled there as well, so doing well this time matters a lot, especially in front of a home crowd.”

Sports.title: Matt Richardson returns in England colours at Glasgow 2026
Sports.content:
Matt Richardson returns in England colours at Glasgow 2026

Four years after winning Commonwealth gold for Australia, Matt Richardson returns to the Games wearing England colours, with the former champion targeting another sprint title in Glasgow after his high-profile switch of allegiance.

View Image Matt Richardson.

Four years after winning Commonwealth gold for Australia, Matt Richardson will return to the Games wearing England colours – and sharing the athletes' village with a girlfriend representing Wales. The arrangement certainly gives a new meaning to the 'Friendly Games'.

‌



Richardson, whose partner is Olympic champion Emma Finucane, is one of Team England's leading medal hopes after a high-profile switch of allegiance that surprised many in the sport. The move came after an Olympic campaign in Paris that yielded two silver medals and a bronze.

‌



Born in England and raised in Australia after his family relocated from Kent when he was nine, the now 27-year-old watched the 2018 Commonwealth Games as a junior rider, having recently abandoned a promising gymnastics career because of an elbow injury. Four years later, he emerged as one of the stars of Birmingham 2022, winning gold in both the individual and team sprint.

‌



“At Birmingham 2022, I was racing for Australia but in the UK,” he said. “I had more friends and family come and watch me than at any other race that I had ever had.

“It was a great atmosphere in that velodrome. The last Commonwealth Games almost didn't feel like an away Commonwealth Games. It almost felt like home to me.”

Richardson dominated the sprint programme in Birmingham, beating all British opposition before cementing his reputation as one of the world's leading track cyclists with three medals at the Paris Olympics two years later.

‌



Soon afterwards, he stunned the sport by announcing a switch to Great Britain, for whom he qualified through his birth in Maidstone.

Yet Richardson's greatest inspiration is neither an Australian nor an Englishman, but the Scot whose name graces Glasgow's velodrome.

“Chris Hoy has always been my idol on and off the bike," he added. "My first memory of the Olympics is watching Chris win the keirin in Beijing in 2008 so he's always been at the forefront of my mind when it came to track cycling.

‌



“I love racing in the Chris Hoy Velodrome. The track itself has its little differences. It makes it a slightly different style of racing. The straights are very long for starters so that can change the dynamic of racing because opponents have more time to pass from behind. That can catch you out sometimes if you're not careful.

“The 200-metre timing line is quite late in the corner so the line you would take in a flying 200 needs to be slightly different to maximise it.”

At a British Cycling event in Konya, Turkey, Richardson set a world record of 8.857 seconds for the flying 200m, becoming the first rider to break the nine-second barrier.

‌



He said: “My favourite moment with Team England has to be the world record for the amount of work and effort that I put into it. To go there and do exactly what I wanted to do was really, really special.

“Whether it was here riding for GB or for Australia, that would always be one of the absolute top-tier highlights of my career. To make history and still be the only rider to go sub-nine seconds is really special to me.”

He has continued to build on that success, winning two silver medals at the World Track Cycling Championships in Santiago last year and becoming the first British man to win a European sprint title in Konya earlier this year.

‌



Beyond Glasgow, however, lies the ultimate objective: the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.

He said: “The Commonwealth Games are so special because it's the only time that I get to represent England once every four years.

“The form that I've been carrying recently puts me in a good place for this year and also the year after and the year after. It's all about the momentum I'm trying to carry going into the Los Angeles Olympics.”

‌



Talk of the Olympics is rife in the Richardson/Finucane household, as the Welshwoman is equally fixated on adding to her medal tally from Paris.

Alongside Sophie Capewell and Katy Marchant, she broke the world record three times on the way to gold in the team sprint, before adding bronze medals in the keirin and the sprint to become the first British woman to win three medals at a single Games since Mary Rand in 1964.

She told Cyclist: "I feel like I grew so much off the bike that now, going into 2026, I have more of a focus. I was asked recently why I don’t feel like I do during the Olympics year every year.

‌



“It’s such a magical thing that happens every four years, and protecting this to appreciate the lead up to the Olympics more. I go into a routine then I won’t go home as much. If I want to be here for ten years, I need to have this balance.

“Cycling consumes you. It’s your life. I love it, I wouldn’t do it otherwise, but it’s finding that balance – a time and a place for everything.”

But despite her achievements, the 23-year-old will still feel she has unfinished business at the Commonwealth Games. Four years ago in Birmingham, she clinched two bronzes in the sprint and team sprint, and came away delighted to have exceeded her expectations and delivered two of Wales’ impressive six-medal haul in the velodrome.

‌



She said: “It’s so unique. It’s a nice environment and we’re such a small country. Last time I was 19 years old and I was so young; it was overwhelming. I think this time around I’ll be able to soak it up more.

“We go back to Glasgow and I love that velodrome. It’s different not racing for Great Britain because then you’re lining up against your teammates, but that’s what I love about it.”

In the time since Birmingham, Finucane has grown into one of the world’s most feared riders, to the extent that she struggled to manage the expectations laid on her shoulders at the Paris Olympics in 2024, resorting to crying before each race to release her emotions.

‌



She told the Guardian: “I wouldn’t say I need to push it to one side but I need to learn from it. At the next Olympics in LA [in 2028] I don’t want to be the same person. I want to learn why did I feel like that? Why did I need to let that emotion out? Who did I speak to who made me feel better?

“It’s emotionally exhausting when you’re racing for seven days and, as I look at Olympic champions who win multiple Olympic medals, that needs to be addressed.”

The story of a medal-laden match-making in the velodrome is a well-told one in the UK, but Richardson and Finucane are not simply Gen Z’s Jason and Laura Kenny, nor do they want to be, despite Laura’s glowing endorsements of the pair in her new role as President of the Commonwealth Games England.

Article continues below

Between Finucane’s emotional burden and Richardson’s peppering of abuse on social media after he switched nationality, the internet age has carved them into a more vulnerable, yet more grounded form in the public eye.

Time will tell if that ground yields more gold.

Sports.title: Dame Laura Kenny hails National Lottery's sporting legacy
Sports.content:
Dame Laura Kenny hails National Lottery's sporting legacy

Dame Laura Kenny has thanked National Lottery players for transforming British sport, saying the investment has supported every stage of her career and continues to help athletes reach the Commonwealth Games.

View Image Dame Laura Kenny.

Dame Laura Kenny has hailed the investment of The National Lottery and the backing its players give to every corner of sport, from grassroots clubs to elite programmes.

‌



Without The National Lottery backing, Dame Laura believes coaches, the science, the facilities, and athlete development pathways would not exist and the much-needed cash injection is the reason home nation teams have got to the start line for the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games.

‌



“The National Lottery has obviously funded pretty much my whole career,” she said. “I was part of a National Governing Body that is funded by the National Lottery.

‌



“But that's just one small part of it; it funds so many amazing projects. I mean, it raises over £32million and that is just huge because that means the younger generation can benefit just like I have.

“I just want to say a huge thank you to everyone that goes and buys a National Lottery ticket because you do not understand how much that money is used across so many different projects. I'm so grateful for everyone that plays the National Lottery.”

In the last three decades, National Lottery players have invested more than £1 billion into Glasgow - supporting thousands of arts, heritage and community projects that help the city, every single day.

‌



The first National Lottery grant in Glasgow went to a touring theatre company in Govan on 11 January 1995. Thirty-one years later, that investment is still flowing through every part of the city.

Since 1994, the funding has reached people across Glasgow through more than 14,000 grants and the investment has not been about grand gestures.

And now, as Glasgow prepares to host the Commonwealth Games, the impact of that long‑term support is everywhere. National Lottery players have helped fund three of the four Games venues, supported many of the city’s museums and galleries that visitors will experience, and made possible a new small‑grants programme helping communities celebrate the Games in their own way.

‌



For Dame Laura, meanwhile, this summer’s Games will be a family affair.

Having spent her career on the track alongside her husband Sir Jason Kenny, the two will now hold different roles in Glasgow, with Dame Laura in place as Team England President and Sir Jason part of the coaching staff within the Team England Cycling set up.

And it provides a great opportunity to let her two eldest children, Albie and Monty, finally watch their parents at work.

‌



"The thing for me is that the kids will see Jason in his actual role," she said. "There are so many times that, you know, I say, "Daddy's at work," because obviously, the job Jason's in, it does take him away loads, but I don't think they truly understand it.

"And it's not like you can show old videos of us racing because that's not the role that we're in now.

"So, for me, I'm quite excited for them to actually see him pushing the lads up onto the track and really understand what it is that we do."

‌



On the track, Dame Laura believes Glasgow 2026 will usher in a changing of the guard. Britain's most decorated female Olympian retired in 2024 and with the likes of Scotland's Katie Archibald having stepped away from the sport as well, Kenny is excited to see fresh faces step up.

"You’ve had lots of people step away and then you've got a really strong group of youngsters coming through, especially in women's endurance," she said.

"This is actually going to be the first time that we don't see Katie Archibald compete and obviously, she has been a huge part of the Scottish women's endurance squad for years now.

Article continues below

"It is almost out with the old, in with the new and I feel like this could be the first time that we sort of get a glimpse of what the Olympic team might look like, albeit split into three different nations."

Sports.title: Sarah Adlington back where her Commonwealth story began
Sports.content:
Sarah Adlington back where her Commonwealth story began

Sarah Adlington believes Glasgow 2026 is the perfect way to bring the curtain down on her remarkable career, with the double Commonwealth champion targeting one final gold medal where her multi-sport journey began.

View Image Sarah Adlington.

Sarah Adlington is hoping to embrace her full circle moment as she prepares for a ‘bonus’ Commonwealth Games. As the first judoka to win two Commonwealth Games gold medals, Adlington remains an enduring presence at the heart of Scottish sport and will leave an astonishing legacy in combat sports north of the border upon her retirement.

‌



This will be the 39-year-old’s last hurrah on the world stage, 12 years after debuting at another home Games in Glasgow.

‌



She said: “Glasgow was my first multi-sport event, so I was like a kid at Disneyland. Everything about Glasgow in 2014 was just so exciting.

‌



“It feels ages ago. This is really a bonus Games, because if the Commonwealths were going to be in Australia, then judo wouldn't have been in.

“I wasn't 100% sure if I would end my career before, then this seemed like the fitting end. It's a full circle moment.”

Shrewsbury-born Adlington endured near-misses for London 2012 and Rio 2016 but made her Olympic bow at the third attempt at Tokyo 2020.

‌



Adlington had been weighing up her future in the sport ahead of the 2028 Olympic cycle, but after Glasgow replaced the bid from Victoria in Australia, the target of a home Games was irresistible.

Among the 13 Scottish judokas heading to the Games is 30-year-old Scott Cusack, son of Billy and Loretta, both of whom competed at the Commonwealth Games in their career.

Adlington said: “Billy's been my coach my whole senior career, for 22 years, and his son fights the day before me, so that’ll be exciting.

‌



“You’ve got to aim for the top. That would be the fairytale end of my career. I'm doing everything I can to be in the best possible shape when I step on the mat and then give the best performance I can on that day. Hopefully that ends up to the top of the podium - that's the dream.”

At Glasgow 2026, Adlington is among 43 Team Scotland athletes across eight sports benefiting from the sportscotland Athlete Personal Award programme (SAPA).

The programme, which has been funded by a £210,000 grant from The National Lottery, is designed to ease financial pressures and allow athletes to dedicate more time to training, recovery and competitions as they build towards representing Team Scotland on home soil.

‌



“Balancing other commitments with training and competitions is always difficult,” Adlington said.

"In a Commonwealth Games year, we know we have to do everything we possibly can in terms of our preparation. The SAPA funding from sportscotland and The National Lottery is a huge help with that and has allowed me to attend more international competitions and camps leading up to the Games."

Adlington competes in the +78kg weight division and earned Commonwealth golds in 2014 and 2022.

‌



But after the last Games in Birmingham, she had a more unusual problem when moths in her loft ate her official Team Scotland kilt, rendering it unwearable.

She has keenly followed Scotland’s first men’s FIFA World Cup campaign in 28 yeara and believes there are still positives to be taken despite a disappointing group stage exit.

She said: “I've had a long career, and I've learned there's no ‘shoulda woulda coulda’, because sometimes it just doesn't go your way.

Article continues below

“There are a few big teams in the World Cup for whom it’s not gone their way and you realise it's sport. Anything can happen and that's what makes it so exciting. That's why people want to watch it, and that's why people will watch the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

“It's hopefully the start of the buzz of people getting back behind Scotland and it's great that they'll get plenty of Scottish people in here in a few weeks’ time.”

Sports.title: Georgia Hunter Bell eyes Glasgow redemption in the 800m
Sports.content:
Georgia Hunter Bell eyes Glasgow redemption in the 800m

Georgia Hunter Bell returns to Glasgow with unfinished business this summer, as the world indoor champion looks to add a Commonwealth Games medal in the city where she made the decision that transformed her career.

View Image Georgia Hunter Bell.

Glasgow will bring a sense of familiarity for Georgia Hunter Bell as she looks to mark another career milestone in the city. The 32-year-old was a frequent commuter to the Commonwealth Games host city in her job in tech sales before the 2024 World Indoor Championships provided her breakthrough.

‌



And this summer she will return for an 800m rematch with Kenyan Lilian Odira, who came from nowhere to pip Hunter Bell to the World Championship title in Tokyo last year.

‌



“It’s a really special city for me. I have a lot of good memories there,” said Hunter Bell, whose National Lottery funding has helped ensure access to full-time training, access to the world's best coaches, and pioneering technology, science and medical support.

‌



“I used to go there quite a lot for work with clients so it’s funny seeing my two lives collide when I go back and drive past companies I use to work with.

“But now I head to the stadium to run around in circles. I’ve got nothing but good memories from there now.

“The 2024 World Indoor Championships was the opportunity when I really made the decision to go for running and change my life and that led me to the amazing path I’m on now.

‌



“I’m so grateful for the opportunity that Glasgow gave me and very excited to come back and compete.”

Hunter Bell’s career away from sport saw her take five years away as a result of injuries, before making an unlikely return in 2023. Since then, she has become one of the world ’s leading track stars across the 800m and 1500m, with the former her pick for Glasgow 2026.

But it was in the latter in 2024 that she became British Indoor champion to earn selection for the worlds, where she would go on to not just qualify for the final but finish just off the podium in fourth.

‌



It was the result that marked her capabilities on the world stage, before she went on to claim Olympic bronze and European silver in the same year. Hunter Bell already has one gold to her name this year – winning her first global title in the World Indoor Championships’ 1500m – and has been in fine form in the Diamond League.

She will now hope to add two more medals to that growing honours list as she prepares to compete at both the Commonwealth Games and the Birmingham 2026 European Championships.

“I want to take advantage of every opportunity and the fact both are on home soil in Glasgow and in Birmingham means I absolutely want to run in front of a home crowd,” she said.

‌



“Any opportunity to win a medal, I want to be there. I feel like I’m in really good shape so it would be such an exciting opportunity to do that.

“I feel very lucky that it's crossed over into my career because athletes' careers can be 10 to 15 years and you may never race on home soil. To have two in one summer is so special. I was absolutely going to always take advantage of that.”

It was the decision between the 800m, in which she won her World Championships silver, and the mile where the real contention lay.

Article continues below

But with training partner Keely Hodgkinson not competing in Glasgow, and honour to restore against Odira, who beat her by just 0.28 seconds in Tokyo, it was two laps that came out on top and she will now go for glory at Scotstoun, one of three competition venues which has benefited from National Lottery funding.

England Athletics, meanwhile, has received 32 National Lottery grants totalling around £22 million for athletics and para athletics since 2006.

Sports.title: Kevin Keegan was real-life Roy of the Rovers star who lived and breathed football
Sports.content:
Kevin Keegan was real-life Roy of the Rovers star who lived and breathed football

Kevin Keegan was one of English football's all-time greats and the sport will never be the same after the desperately sad news of his death at the age of 75

View 3 Images Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75 (Image: Owen Humphreys/PA Wire)

After such a memorable England World Cup campaign, the news about Kevin Keegan feels particularly sad.

‌



King Kev will go down as one of the greatest players England has ever produced and his international career - both as player and manager - was unforgettable.

‌



Keegan was a two-time Ballon D’Or winner, a trailblazer after he joined Hamburg, hugely successful with Liverpool and Newcastle. He was a real Roy of the Rovers player who gave absolutely everything on the pitch and a household name thanks to his starring role on the 1970s TV show Superstars.

‌



He was an icon who was back page gold because of his huge ability, his personality and he was never short of opinion which is another reason we loved him quite apart from his football ability.

Kevin Keegan dies aged 75 as family, fans and former players pay tribute to Liverpool and Newcastle icon READ MORE :

Alan Shearer sends emotional goodbye to 'hero' Kevin Keegan as tributes pour in READ MORE :

There was the often forgotten bust-up with the late Sir Bobby Robson which ended his England career prematurely - and also saw him quit as a player at Newcastle aged 33.

Keegan quit as England manager in the toilets at Wembley in October 2000 after losing to Germany as he admitted he fell short of what was needed to manage his beloved country. That hurt him so much and, realistically, it scarred him because he scored 21 goals in 63 appearances for England in an international career which lasted ten years from 1972 until 1982.

‌



Keegan deserved a better platform than England gave him. They did not qualify for the 1974 or 1978 World Cups when Keegan was among the best players in the world.

By 1982, Keegan was in his 30s but went to the World Cup even though he had a bad back. He drove from Spain to Germany in secret to get treatment with a trusted specialist. As England were chasing a game - they needed a result against Spain - they threw on Keegan and Trevor Brooking to search for a late winner. Keegan missed a header and little did he know then that would signal the end.

View 3 Images Keegan represented England over 60 times (Image: Peter Robinson/EMPICS Sport/PA Wire)

‌



Keegan was dropped by Robson after he took charge - but was furious after finding out second hand from then Newcastle boss Arthur Cox who heard it on the radio. “I’m finished with England. I’ll never kick a ball for my country again,” Keegan ranted after hearing the news. And his retirement from England duty hastened the end of his playing career.

It is a crying shame we never saw Keegan at his peak on the biggest stage because he deserved it. England will always be a source of regret.

Let’s not forget here that, after his amazing stint in charge at Newcastle and working wonders at Fulham, there was huge public clamour for him to be England boss. So the revisionism about his shortcomings - he was a motivator but a limited tactician - must be put into context. We all wanted him because we loved King Kev.

‌



Keegan’s relationship with the press was tested particularly with England. He hated criticism. I remember seeing him for an interview during that ill-fated reign and it quickly turned into an interrogation. Him questioning me rather than the other way round.

View 3 Images Keegan managed England for almost two years (Image: PA)

He was angry, bitter and upset at the criticism. What did I think? Was it fair? Over the top? Say the wrong thing and the interview was not going to happen. It did go ahead because fundamentally he was a nice man. But he really cared and was so sensitive.

‌



I remember seeing him in Doha years later. We’d watched some football. He was still wary. He’d had enough of us press lot. But we started chatting football - and he just forgot what I did.

He couldn’t help himself. If anyone shared his passion and love of the game then he’d just get carried away and lose himself all over again. We talked and talked.

That was the thing with Keegan. His love of football was pure. He was one of the most passionate people I’ve ever met. And that mix made him King Kev.
