Dividend Breakdown: What Was Paid

Ternium’s board of directors initially proposed a fiscal year 2025 dividend of $2.70 per ADS. However, on April 15, 2026, the company revised that proposal downward to $2.20 per ADS, equivalent to $0.22 per share. The final net portion of this distribution, $1.30 per ADS ($0.13 per share), was paid out on May 15, 2026, effectively closing the book on the 2025 dividend cycle. No new dividend announcements for 2026 have been made as of mid-July.

At the time of the revision, Ternium‘s share price hovered around $43.27, giving the reduced $2.20 annual dividend a yield of approximately 5.1%. While earlier drafts based on the original $2.70 proposal had suggested a yield closer to 6%, the final figure remains notable for income-focused investors. The stock was trading near $43.57 during intraday activity on February 18, 2026, though updated share prices for July 2026 are not available in recent disclosures.

2025 Earnings: The Write-Down That Shaped the Payout

The dividend revision cannot be separated from Ternium’s full-year 2025 financial performance, reported on February 18, 2026. The company posted a net income of $303 million for the year, a figure deeply impacted by a $405 million write-down of deferred tax assets at Usiminas, its Brazilian steelmaking affiliate. This non-cash accounting charge significantly eroded bottom-line results, prompting a more conservative capital-return strategy.

In the fourth quarter alone, Ternium generated $171 million in net income, which included a $94 million gain from deferred taxes. Quarterly revenue reached $3.78 billion, representing a 2.6% decline compared to the same period in 2024. Earnings per ADS came in at $0.62, missing analyst consensus estimates by $0.15. The mixed results underscored the challenges in a global steel market still navigating uneven demand and pricing pressures.

2026 Outlook: Mexico and Brazil Drive Optimism

Despite the cautious dividend action, Ternium’s forward guidance strikes a more optimistic tone. The company expects Adjusted EBITDA to increase in the first quarter of 2026 compared to the fourth quarter of 2025. This anticipated improvement is pinned on higher shipment volumes, primarily in Mexico, and better Adjusted EBITDA margins in both Mexico and Brazil. Management attributes the margin recovery to rising revenue per ton, though it notes this will be partially offset by higher costs per ton.

For the full year 2026, analysts project earnings per ADS of $6.05. If Ternium maintains an expected annual dividend of $1.80 per ADS, the implied payout ratio would sit at a comfortable 29.8%, suggesting ample room for the company to fund its distribution from profits. The strategic focus on Mexico and Brazil as operational drivers is clear, though the company’s public disclosures do not provide detailed mid-2026 data on market conditions in Argentina or the specific impact of Chinese steel import pressure on the region.

What Foreign Investors Should Watch

For expats, tourists-turned-investors, and global market watchers following Latin America, Ternium offers a window into the region’s industrial health. The company’s ADR structure makes it easily accessible on the NYSE, but its fortunes are tied to construction, automotive, and infrastructure cycles in Mexico and Brazil – two of the area’s largest economies. The 5.1% dividend yield, based on the revised $2.20 payout, remains competitive in a global context, but it comes with the volatility typical of commodity-linked equities.

Key signposts for the months ahead include any updates on Usiminas’ tax-asset recovery, quarterly shipment data out of Mexico, and broader trade policy shifts that could affect steel flows into the Americas. While the 2025 dividend chapter is closed, the 2026 story will hinge on whether Ternium can convert its guided margin improvements into the earnings growth that analysts are penciling in.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was Ternium’s final 2025 dividend per ADS?

Ternium’s board revised the 2025 dividend to $2.20 per ADS, down from an initial $2.70 proposal. The final net payment of $1.30 per ADS was distributed on May 15, 2026.

Why did Ternium cut its 2025 dividend?

The reduction followed full-year 2025 net income of $303 million, which was heavily impacted by a $405 million write-down of deferred tax assets at its Brazilian unit Usiminas, prompting a more conservative payout.

What is Ternium’s business outlook for 2026?

Ternium expects higher shipments and improved EBITDA margins in Mexico and Brazil during Q1 2026. Analysts forecast full-year 2026 earnings of $6.05 per ADS, which would comfortably cover an expected $1.80 annual dividend.

World.title: Peru Economy May 2026: Fishing Crash Hits Growth
World.content:
Peru · Economy

Key Facts —GDP growth. Peru’s economy grew 1.80% year-on-year in May 2026, down from 3.73% in April and the slowest expansion in 2026. —Fishing collapse. The fishing sector contracted 73.10%, driven by El Niño conditions that warmed Pacific waters and drove away anchovy stocks. —Manufacturing drag. Manufacturing fell 10.67%, weighed down by a 41.70% drop in fishmeal and oil processing and a weak textile production cycle. —Trade leads. The trade sector grew 6.91%, accounting alongside other services and mining for roughly 95% of the month’s overall expansion. —Year-to-date. Cumulative growth for January through May 2026 stood at 3.20%, with annualized growth reaching 3.54%.

Peru’s Peru economy May 2026 expanded just 1.80% compared to the same month a year earlier, decelerating sharply from April’s 3.73% pace and marking the weakest monthly performance of the year, the national statistics agency INEI reported on Wednesday.

For readers unfamiliar with the region, INEI is Peru’s official body responsible for collecting and publishing economic and demographic data. Its monthly GDP reports are the primary gauge of the country’s economic health, much like the Bureau of Economic Analysis releases in the United States.

El Niño slams fishing and manufacturing

The dramatic slowdown was driven overwhelmingly by climate. El Niño conditions warmed the Pacific Ocean off Peru’s coast, drastically reducing the availability of anchovy and other hydrobiological resources.

As a result, the fishing sector collapsed by 73.10% year-on-year, the single worst-performing segment of the economy in May.

That collapse spilled directly into primary manufacturing, where fishmeal and fish-oil processing plummeted 41.70%. Combined with a downswing in the textile industry’s production cycle, overall manufacturing contracted 10.67% compared to May 2025, acting as the heaviest drag on the headline GDP figure.

To understand why this matters so much, it helps to know that Peru is the world’s leading producer of fishmeal, a high-protein feed ingredient used in aquaculture and livestock farming globally. The anchovy fishery off its coast is among the richest on the planet, but it is also among the most sensitive to ocean temperature shifts.

When El Niño arrives, warmer waters push the nutrient-rich cold currents deeper or farther offshore, scattering the anchovy schools and making them far harder to catch.

Trade, mining, and construction provide support

While fishing and manufacturing cratered, several large sectors kept the economy in positive territory. The trade sector – which spans wholesale, retail, and automotive sales – surged 6.91% year-on-year.

Alongside other services and mining, it accounted for roughly 95% of the month’s total growth.

Mining and hydrocarbons returned to expansion after three consecutive months of decline, growing 2.60%. Construction also posted a solid 4.66% increase, while electricity, gas, and water output rose 5.21%.

Accommodation and restaurants grew 5.05%, and government services added 3.69%, rounding out a picture of an economy where domestic demand and services largely offset the climate-driven supply shock in primary industries.

On a month-on-month basis, however, economic activity fell 1.11% from April, underscoring the abruptness of the May deceleration.

The resilience in trade and services tells an important story about Peru’s economic structure. While the country is famous for its commodity exports, a large and growing portion of its workforce earns a living in commerce, tourism, and public services.

When these sectors hold up, they act as a shock absorber, preventing a climate-driven downturn in one industry from turning into a broad recession.

Broader trends and the 2026 outlook

Despite the weak May print, Peru’s cumulative growth for the first five months of 2026 stands at 3.20%. The annualized rate – measured from June 2025 through May 2026 – reached 3.54%, indicating that the economy entered this soft patch from a position of relative strength.

The agriculture and livestock sector barely moved the needle, growing just 0.10%, as a 1.99% increase in livestock output was largely canceled out by weakness elsewhere. Telecommunications expanded a modest 0.65%, while finance and insurance rose 1.79% and transport, storage, and courier services grew 2.42%.

Analysts caution that El Niño‘s intensity in the coming months will be critical for the fishing sector’s recovery and, by extension, for manufacturing. A prolonged warm-water event could continue to weigh on primary industries, though robust trade and services activity may keep overall growth in positive territory.

What to watch next is whether the central bank adjusts its monetary policy stance in response to this slowdown. A single weak month does not usually trigger a rate change, but if the fishing and manufacturing weakness persists into the third quarter, policymakers may face pressure to support domestic demand.

Another open question is how global fishmeal prices will react to the supply disruption from Peru, and whether competing producers in other parts of the world can fill the gap without pushing up costs for the aquaculture industry.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Peru’s economy slow so sharply in May 2026?

The slowdown was primarily caused by El Niño, which warmed Pacific waters and devastated the fishing sector. Fishing output fell 73.10%, and the shock spilled into manufacturing – especially fishmeal processing – which contracted 10.67% overall.

Which sectors performed well in Peru in May 2026?

Trade grew 6.91%, construction rose 4.66%, and electricity, gas, and water expanded 5.21%. Mining and hydrocarbons returned to growth at 2.60%, and accommodation and restaurants increased 5.05%.

What is Peru’s cumulative growth so far in 2026?

For January through May 2026, Peru‘s economy has grown a cumulative 3.20%. The annualized rate from June 2025 to May 2026 is 3.54%, reflecting solid momentum before the May slowdown.

World.title: EU Charges Mexican Giant Cemex with Price-Fixing Cartel
World.content:
Latin America · Companies

Key Facts —Charges filed. The European Commission issued formal cartel charges against Cemex on July 20, 2026, for alleged price-fixing of construction chemicals. —Product in focus. The investigation targets additives for cement, concrete, and mortar, not cement itself. —Markets affected. The alleged collusion took place in France, Germany, and Spain between 2021 and 2022. —Potential penalty. If found guilty, Cemex could face fines of up to 10% of its global annual revenue. —Prior probe closed. A separate seven-year EU investigation into the cement sector involving Cemex was dropped in July 2019 due to insufficient evidence.

The European Commission has formally charged Mexican cement giant Cemex in a Cemex EU cartel charges case, alleging the company conspired with rivals to fix prices of construction chemicals across three major European economies. The charges, announced July 20, 2026, follow dawn raids conducted in October 2023 and mark a significant escalation in Brussels’ scrutiny of the building-materials supply chain.

What the EU is Alleging

The European Commission’s statement of objections accuses Cemex and several other companies of colluding between 2021 and 2022 to artificially raise prices of chemical additives used in cement, concrete, and mortar. The alleged coordination took place in France, Germany, and Spain, three of the European Union’s largest construction markets.

According to the Commission, the firms exploited cost spikes triggered by the Covid-19 pandemic and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Investigators claim the companies used press releases distributed through trade associations to signal and coordinate price increases, rather than competing fairly during a period of genuine supply-chain disruption.

The charges target construction chemicals specifically, not cement. This is an important distinction: Cemex, the world’s third-largest cement producer, is not accused of fixing cement prices in this case.

Other companies charged include Swiss specialty-chemicals group Sika, Germany’s MC Bauchemie, Italy’s Mapei, France’s Chryso, and Master Builders Solutions, along with several trade bodies.

Potential Fines and Next Steps

If the Commission ultimately finds Cemex and its co-accused guilty of breaching EU antitrust rules, each company could be fined up to 10% of its global annual turnover. For Cemex, a multinational with operations spanning the Americas, Europe, Africa, and Asia, that represents a potentially substantial financial hit.

Cemex has confirmed it is cooperating with authorities and providing requested information and testimonies. The company now has the right to examine the Commission’s evidence and submit a formal reply to the statement of objections.

There is no fixed deadline for the EU to conclude its investigation, and companies can challenge any final decision before European courts.

The charges stem from dawn raids – surprise inspections – conducted by Commission officials in October 2023. Such raids are a common preliminary step in EU cartel probes, allowing investigators to gather documents and digital evidence before companies have time to alter or destroy them.

A Look Back: The Closed Cement Probe

For international readers following Cemex‘s regulatory history in Europe, the new charges may sound familiar. The company was previously caught up in a much broader EU investigation into alleged price-fixing and import-export restrictions in the cement sector itself. That probe, which also involved France’s Lafarge, Germany’s HeidelbergCement, and Switzerland’s Holcim, lasted seven years.

In July 2019, the Commission scrapped the entire cement-sector case, concluding there was insufficient evidence to substantiate the claims. The investigation had begun with dawn raids back in November 2007, underscoring how long such antitrust inquiries can drag on without yielding penalties.

The contrast between the two cases highlights the EU’s shifting focus. While cement-price collusion proved difficult to prove, regulators are now targeting adjacent markets like construction chemicals, particularly where they suspect companies exploited pandemic and war-related cost volatility to coordinate price hikes.

Why This Matters for Latin America’s Multinationals

Cemex is one of Latin America’s most internationally exposed industrial companies, with a deep footprint across Europe. The case serves as a reminder that Brussels remains one of the world’s most aggressive antitrust enforcers, willing to pursue complex, cross-border cartel investigations that can take years to resolve.

The EU has a long track record of scrutinizing the cement and construction-materials sector. Previous merger reviews include the 2014 approval of Cemex’s acquisition of Holcim’s Spanish operations and the 2015 decision to block HeidelbergCement and Schwenk’s attempt to buy Cemex’s Croatian assets, citing concerns the deal would control 45% to 50% of the market and push prices higher.

For investors and expats watching Latin American companies navigate European regulations, the July 2026 charges signal that even when one probe closes – as the cement case did in 2019 – regulatory risk can resurface in related markets. The construction-chemicals case is now one of the most significant antitrust actions facing a major Latin American multinational in Europe.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Cemex being charged for fixing cement prices?

No. The July 2026 charges relate to construction chemicals – additives for cement, concrete, and mortar – not cement itself. A previous EU cement-sector probe involving Cemex was closed in 2019 without charges.

What is the maximum fine Cemex could face?

Under EU cartel rules, the Commission can impose fines of up to 10% of a company’s global annual turnover if it finds a breach. The final amount depends on the gravity and duration of the infringement.

Which countries are involved in the alleged cartel?

The European Commission says the alleged price-fixing took place in France, Germany, and Spain between 2021 and 2022.

World.title: Brazil’s Pix Payment System Eyes Global Expansion at $660B
World.content:
Brazil · Markets

Key Facts —Massive user base. Pix has 200 million monthly active users, including 25 million businesses, as of early 2026. —Staggering volume. The system processes roughly 8.6 billion transactions per month, totaling R$3.4 trillion (approximately US$660 billion). —Financial inclusion engine. Over 70 million Brazilians entered the formal financial system for the first time thanks to Pix since its 2020 launch. —Global ambitions. Brazil’s central bank has explicit plans to take Pix cross-border, with fintechs already enabling its use for international payments. —US trade scrutiny. In July 2025, the US Trade Representative opened an investigation into Pix, labeling it a potential discriminatory ‘national payment standard’.

Brazil’s ubiquitous instant payment system, Pix, is no longer just a domestic powerhouse processing a staggering US$660 billion each month. With its Pix global expansion plans now firmly underway, the central bank-backed network is stepping onto the international stage, challenging traditional card networks and drawing a mix of admiration and trade friction from abroad, including a formal investigation by the United States.

A Domestic Giant with Global Dreams

To understand why Pix’s international move matters, you first have to grasp its jaw-dropping scale at home. Launched by Brazil’s central bank in late 2020, the system has achieved near-total saturation in record time.

By the first quarter of 2026, Pix counted 200 million monthly active users – a figure that includes 175 million individuals and 25 million businesses. That represents well over 80% of the country’s entire population, with 93% of Brazilian adults actively using the platform.

The transaction volumes are equally staggering. Brazilians make about 8.6 billion Pix transfers every month, moving R$3.4 trillion (roughly US$660 billion). To put that in context, Pix now moves 8.6 times more value than all credit and debit card transactions in Brazil combined. In 2024 alone, the system processed 68.7 billion transactions worth around US$5 trillion, accounting for a full 14% of all instant payments made globally that year.

How Pix is Going Cross-Border

Brazil’s central bank has not hidden its ambition to take this homegrown success story global. As early as late 2024, officials outlined a concrete strategy to enable cross-border payments via Pix, allowing the system to be used for international transfers, travel spending, and e-commerce with foreign merchants.

Fintech companies like PagBrasil have already begun rolling out Pix-based solutions for international travelers and cross-border shoppers.

The appeal for foreigners is straightforward: Pix transactions clear instantly, 24/7, often at zero cost for individuals. For a tourist visiting Rio de Janeiro, paying a street vendor by scanning a QR code with a Pix-enabled app is faster and cheaper than using a credit card. For an expat sending money home, Pix promises to slash the high fees and multi-day waits typical of traditional international wire transfers. The system’s domestic dominance also suggests a ready-made user base of millions who would eagerly use Pix abroad if given the chance.

Financial Inclusion and E-Commerce Dominance

Pix’s global push is built on a foundation of radical financial inclusion. Since its debut, the system has brought more than 70 million Brazilians into the formal financial system – people who had never before made an electronic transfer.

By eliminating fees for individuals and requiring only a smartphone, Pix turned bank accounts from a luxury into a utility.

This inclusion engine is now reshaping commerce. Analysts project that Pix will capture 50% of Brazil’s entire e-commerce market by 2028, surpassing credit cards as the preferred online payment method.

For foreign investors and companies looking at Latin America’s largest economy, ignoring Pix is no longer an option. Any business selling to Brazilian consumers – whether a global e-commerce platform or a local restaurant – must integrate Pix or risk losing access to the vast majority of the country’s purchasing power.

US Scrutiny and Trade Tensions

Pix’s rise has not gone unnoticed in Washington. In July 2025, the Office of the United States Trade Representative opened a formal investigation into Brazil’s digital trade and electronic payment services.

The probe specifically flagged Pix as a potential ‘national payment standard’ that could discriminate against US-based payment companies like Visa and Mastercard.

The investigation highlights a growing tension: Pix’s state-backed, fee-free model is difficult for private-sector competitors to match. While the US has not yet imposed any measures, the probe signals that Pix’s global expansion could face regulatory headwinds.

For now, Brazil’s central bank continues to promote Pix as an open, inclusive system that benefits consumers and merchants alike. For international readers, the key takeaway is that Pix is a financial force that is here to stay – and it is increasingly a factor in trade relations between the Americas.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly is Pix?

Pix is an instant payment system created by Brazil’s central bank. It allows individuals and businesses to send and receive money in seconds, 24/7, using just a phone number, QR code, or key.

For individuals, transactions are typically free.

Can foreigners use Pix?

Yes, but currently you generally need a Brazilian bank account or a digital account with a participating fintech. As Pix expands globally, cross-border options for tourists and international transfers are being developed by companies like PagBrasil.

Why is the US investigating Pix?

The US Trade Representative opened an investigation in July 2025 to determine whether Pix acts as a discriminatory ‘national payment standard’ that unfairly disadvantages US-based payment companies operating in Brazil.

World.title: Brazilian Author Felipe Cattapan Brings Apocalyptic Love Story to London
World.content:
Brazil · Culture

Key Facts —Author. Felipe Cattapan is a Brazilian writer, conductor, and lecturer at the University of the Arts Bern in Switzerland. —Book. ‘Um Espaço além do Tempo, um Tempo além do Espaço’ combines a theater play and a novella centered on unconditional love during an apocalypse. —Venue. The presentation takes place at the Biblioteca Brasileira Casa do Livro, a Brazilian cultural library in London. —Date. The event is scheduled for July 26, 2024, from 2 PM to 4 PM local time. —Publisher. The book is published by Kotter Editorial, which operates in both Brazil and Portugal.

Brazilian author and conductor Felipe Cattapan London readers will get a rare chance to meet the Rio de Janeiro-born writer this July, as he presents his latest book, a genre-blending work that fuses a theater play with a novella, at a Brazilian cultural hub in the UK capital.

A Book That Defies Genres

The work, titled “Um Espaço além do Tempo, um Tempo além do Espaço” (which translates to “A Space Beyond Time, A Time Beyond Space”), is not a straightforward novel. Published by Kotter Editorial, a house with a presence in both Brazil and Portugal, the book contains two distinct yet thematically linked unpublished pieces: the theater play “X Minutos” (X Minutes) and the novella “Emulação” (Emulation).

The central thread is unconditional love set against an apocalyptic backdrop. Cattapan uses this extreme setting to explore human relationships across time and space, creating what his announcement describes as a guide to a “different level of consciousness.” His writing style uniquely blends prose and poetry, a technique heavily inspired by his parallel career in classical music.

For a foreign audience, this hybrid format is worth understanding. In Brazilian literary culture, it is not unusual for authors to move fluidly between forms—poetry, theater, and prose—often within a single volume.

Cattapan’s decision to pair a play with a novella reflects a broader Lusophone tradition where the boundaries between literary genres are treated as porous, inviting the reader to experience the same emotional core from different structural angles.

From Piano in Rio to Podium in Europe

For international readers unfamiliar with his work, Felipe Cattapan’s path is deeply interdisciplinary. Born in Rio de Janeiro, he first studied piano in his home city before moving to Europe to pursue orchestral and choir conducting. His credentials include studies at the prestigious Conservatoire National Supérieur de Musique in Paris and the École Normale de Paris, followed by a contemporary music conducting degree in Lugano, Switzerland.

Since 2010, he has worked professionally with literature, writing poems, short stories, and theater plays in his native Brazilian Portuguese. His first edition was published in 2018.

Today, he balances his writing with a role as a lecturer at the University of the Arts Bern in Switzerland, where he also directs interdisciplinary projects that sit at the interface of literature and music.

This dual life as a conductor and writer is central to understanding his literary voice. Musicians who turn to literature often bring a distinct sensitivity to rhythm, silence, and structure.

In Cattapan’s case, the prose-poetry blend he employs is not merely decorative; it mirrors the way a musical score alternates between tension and release, a quality that likely shapes how the apocalyptic love story unfolds on the page.

Event Details for London Attendees

The London presentation is scheduled for July 26, 2024, running from 2 PM to 4 PM local time. The venue is the Biblioteca Brasileira Casa do Livro, a Brazilian library in London that serves as a cultural bridge, often hosting Lusophone authors and artists.

The event follows what was described as a successful launch in Zurich, Switzerland, on May 27, 2024.

The book is written entirely in Portuguese, so the event will be most accessible to Portuguese speakers or those with a deep interest in Brazilian literature in its original language. No entry fee or ticket price was specified in the author’s announcement, suggesting a free, open-door cultural event typical of such library-hosted literary afternoons.

For anyone planning to attend, it helps to know that the Biblioteca Brasileira Casa do Livro occupies a special niche in London’s multicultural landscape. Such libraries function as more than book repositories; they are community living rooms where the Brazilian diaspora and UK-based Lusophiles gather for readings, workshops, and conversations that rarely make it into mainstream British arts listings.

An afternoon event of this kind typically includes a reading by the author, a moderated conversation, and an open question session, all conducted in Portuguese.

The broader significance of this London date lies in what it says about the circulation of contemporary Brazilian literature. While translated Brazilian classics occasionally surface in English-language bookshops, living authors writing in Portuguese often reach international audiences through exactly this kind of grassroots, community-anchored event.

It is a reminder that a book’s journey beyond its home market frequently depends on cultural institutions that operate below the radar of large publishing fairs.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Felipe Cattapan presenting a book in London in 2026?

No. According to the author’s own announcement and available sources, the confirmed London event at the Biblioteca Brasileira Casa do Livro took place on July 26, 2024. There is no evidence of a 2026 London presentation.

What is Felipe Cattapan’s book about?

The book “Um Espaço além do Tempo, um Tempo além do Espaço” combines a theater play and a novella. It explores unconditional love in an apocalyptic setting, crossing themes of time, space, and human relationships in contexts of existential tension.

In what language is the book written?

The book is written in Brazilian Portuguese. The London event was hosted at a Brazilian cultural library, and the presentation was conducted in that linguistic context.

World.title: Zema Privatization Plan Targets Petrobras, Banco do Brasil
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts —The proposal. Romeu Zema pledges to sell Petrobras and Banco do Brasil if elected president in October 2026. —The revenue goal. Sale proceeds would fund roads, railways, waterways, and ports, not pay existing federal debt. —The economic team. The plan is coordinated by Carlos Da Costa, a former secretary in the Bolsonaro administration. —The inspiration. The platform is structurally modeled on Javier Milei's free-market reforms in Argentina. —The legal hurdle. Privatizing Petrobras requires a constitutional amendment passed by Brazil's Congress.

Zema privatization of Brazil’s two largest state-owned enterprises took center stage this month as presidential pre-candidate Romeu Zema formally launched his 2026 economic platform in São Paulo.

Romeu Zema is a Brazilian politician and businessman serving as governor of Minas Gerais.

The Zema Privatization Blueprint

Romeu Zema, the former governor of Minas Gerais state and a member of the Novo party, first floated the idea in an April 26 Instagram video. He formally presented the plan on July 18 at the 10th National Meeting of the Novo party.

The proposal calls for selling Brazilian oil giant Petrobras and lender Banco do Brasil as a starting point. Zema then aims to privatize every federal state-owned enterprise without exception.

Petrobras is the world’s largest oil producer by output and a symbol of Brazilian industrial might. Banco do Brasil, one of the country’s oldest financial institutions, holds a vast network of accounts and credit operations touching millions of citizens and businesses.

For foreign investors, these two firms are pillars of the state’s direct involvement in strategic sectors. Selling them would mark the most radical redefinition of Brazil’s economic model in decades.

Funding Infrastructure, Not Paying Bills

Zema argues that revenue from the sales must build roads, railways, waterways, and ports. He explicitly ruled out using the money to pay Brasília’s bills.

He claims the federal government spends more than it collects, creating a debt near R$9 trillion (US$1.77 trillion). Privatization, he says, would cut corruption and lower interest rates.

The distinction is crucial for his campaign narrative: he wants voters to see the sell-off as a long-term investment in the country’s notoriously bottlenecked logistics network. Brazil’s infrastructure gap has long been cited by exporters and agribusiness as a primary brake on competitiveness.

By ring-fencing the proceeds for ports and highways, Zema hopes to appeal to the powerful farm caucus and industrial sectors that lose billions annually to clogged transport routes. For expats and foreign traders, smoother logistics would directly lower the cost of moving goods from the interior to global markets.

The Exploration and Production segment explores, develops, and produces…

Milei-Style Shock Therapy for Brazil

The economic plan is coordinated by Carlos Da Costa, a former secretary to Paulo Guedes under ex-President Jair Bolsonaro. It is structurally modeled on Argentine President Javier Milei’s aggressive free-market reforms.

Zema wants to eliminate the so-called ‘Custo Brasil,’ an estimated R$1.7 trillion (US$335 billion) annual drag on production. He blames tax complexity and high capital costs for the inefficiency.

The ‘Custo Brasil’ encapsulates the extra expenses businesses face in Brazil that they would not encounter in more efficient economies. For international companies weighing a Brazilian expansion, this cost is often the invisible wall that makes the market uncompetitive.

By invoking Milei’s name, Zema signals to investors that he would pursue a no-compromise deregulation agenda. However, Brazil’s fragmented political system requires constant negotiation with a sprawling Congress, making a pure shock-therapy approach harder to execute.

Steep Political and Legal Hurdles

The proposal has drawn sharp criticism from the left-wing Workers’ Party (PT) and other groups. They view Petrobras and Banco do Brasil as strategic national assets.

Privatizing Petrobras requires a constitutional amendment, a heavy lift without a broad coalition in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies and Senate. The sheer size of the entities would also make any sale a complex multi-year process.

Brazil’s 1988 Constitution grants the state a monopoly over oil exploration and production, a legal shield that cannot be removed by a simple presidential decree. Amending the constitution demands a three-fifths majority in two rounds of voting in both legislative houses.

Beyond the legal text, nationalist sentiment around Petrobras runs deep across the political spectrum. The company was born from a ‘O Petróleo é Nosso’ (The Oil is Ours) campaign in the 1950s, and any attempt to sell it touches a raw cultural nerve.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

For the foreign community eyeing Brazil, a successful Zema privatization push would reshape the investment landscape overnight. A privately run Petrobras could prioritize profitability over political pricing, potentially unlocking higher dividends and attracting fresh foreign capital into the pre-salt oil fields.

A privatized Banco do Brasil might streamline lending and reduce the state’s habit of using the bank for subsidized credit programs that distort markets. For expats managing cross-border finances, a more market-oriented banking sector could simplify access to credit and investment products.

However, the transition period would likely bring volatility. The Brazilian real could swing sharply on election polls, and the timeline from a potential October 2026 victory to an actual asset sale would stretch years, filled with legal challenges and public hearings.

For tourists and short-term visitors, the immediate impact is minimal. A successful infrastructure push funded by privatization could eventually improve the airports, highways, and port terminals that make traveling and doing business in Brazil a famously endurance-testing experience.

What Happens Next

The campaign is still in its early stages, with the first round of the presidential election scheduled for October 4, 2026. Zema must first secure the Novo party’s formal nomination and then build enough national name recognition to challenge better-known figures in a crowded field.

Even if he wins, the privatization timeline would begin only after the January 2027 inauguration. The constitutional amendment process alone could consume the first year of a new government, followed by the technical work of valuing two of Latin America’s largest companies and structuring an international tender.

For now, the Zema privatization plan serves as both a campaign differentiator and a litmus test for how much appetite Brazilian voters have for radical economic change. Foreign capitals and multinational boards will be watching closely to see whether this bold promise gains traction or fades under the weight of political reality.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Zema privatization plan?

It is a campaign pledge by presidential candidate Romeu Zema to sell all federal state-owned enterprises, starting with Petrobras and Banco do Brasil, to fund infrastructure. The plan was first announced in an April 26 Instagram video and formally launched on July 18 at the Novo party's national mee

ting. It is coordinated by Carlos Da Costa and modeled on Javier Milei's free-market reforms in Argentina.

Why does Romeu Zema want to privatize Petrobras?

He argues private management is more efficient and that sale proceeds should build ports and railways rather than cover government operating expenses. Zema contends that state interference links the company to political interests and resource diversion, and that privatization would help eliminate the 'Custo Brasil,' an estimated R$1.7 trillion (US$335 billion) annual drag on production caused by tax complexity and high capital costs.

Can Zema actually privatize Banco do Brasil?

It would require winning the October 2026 election and passing complex legislative changes, including a constitutional amendment for Petrobras, which faces strong political resistance. The constitutional amendment needs a three-fifths majority in both the Chamber of Deputies and Senate, a difficult threshold without a broad coalition.

Even if approved, the sheer size of these entities would make any sale a multi-year process with significant valuation and regulatory challenges.

World.title: Criminal and internal investigations launched after off-duty cop shoots man in San Pedro during domestic disturbance
World.content:
Criminal and internal investigations launched after off-duty cop shoots man in San Pedro during domestic disturbance

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have launched simultaneous criminal and internal investigations after an off-duty police officer, identified as PC Keenan Yearwood shot Maverick Fuentes during an alleged domestic disturbance in San Pedro Town.

The incident occurred on Sunday, July 19, 2026, at an apartment building where the officer reportedly resides. Police said the officer was returning home when he encountered an ongoing domestic altercation in a common area of the building.

Police report that Yearwood reportedly attempted to de-escalate the situation, however, Fuentes’ common-law wife, Delia Martinez, claims that Yearwood entered their house without consent. Martinez claims Yearwood entered the home and attacked Fuentes, however, police report that Yearwood attempted to detain Fuentes but was attacked by both Fuentes and Martinez.

The officer then reportedly drew his personally licensed firearm and discharged one round, striking Fuentes in the leg. Martinez claims it was at this point that Yearwood called in for police backup, though police report that Yearwood had called for police assistance prior to entering the home.

Fuentes was airlifted from the island for further medical treatment. According to Martinez, Fuentes suffered a broken leg due to the gunshot. The officer also sought medical attention, though the extent of his injuries has not been disclosed.

Police have confiscated the Yearwood’s firearm and recovered the expended shell casing. Martinez also told Breaking Belize News that during the scuffle, Yearwood dropped a fully loaded magazine, which she later found and turned in to CIB.

No charges have been brought against anyone at this stage as investigators work to establish the full sequence of events and obtain statements from the woman and other potential witnesses.

World.title: International News: Ortega says Nicaragua will no longer hold elections
World.content:
International News: Ortega says Nicaragua will no longer hold elections

By Zoila Palma: Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega has announced that the country will no longer hold elections, a move that would eliminate the possibility of an electoral challenge when his current term ends and further consolidate the power he shares with his wife, Vice President Rosario Murillo.

Ortega, who has remained in power since 2007 after previously serving as president in the 1980s, said the decision would close the door to any opposition takeover.

However, he did not provide specific details on how the change would be implemented or what political system would replace the electoral process, Reuters report.

The announcement comes amid growing international criticism of Ortega and Murillo’s government.

The United Nations Human Rights Council has accused Nicaragua’s leadership of transforming the country into an authoritarian state and carrying out systematic human rights violations.

World.title: International News: Australian woman gives birth to rare identical quadruplets
World.content:
International News: Australian woman gives birth to rare identical quadruplets

By Zoila Palma: An Australian couple is celebrating the birth of four identical baby girls after an extremely rare, naturally conceived pregnancy that doctors estimate occurs in only one out of every 15 million pregnancies.

The babies were delivered by caesarean section at 28 weeks and four days on July 14 at the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital, BBC reports.

The newborns — Emily, Harriet, Catherine and Alexa — are monozygotic quadruplets, meaning they developed after a single fertilized egg split into four embryos. Doctors described the pregnancy as exceptionally high-risk, with the babies sharing one placenta, a condition specialists said is virtually unheard of.

Doctors closely monitored 34-year-old mother Jenitar Na’amoana after admitting her to the hospital at 25 weeks. Maternal fetal medicine specialist Dr. Alexa Bendall said reaching 28 weeks was a major milestone, adding that both the mother and babies avoided the serious complications often associated with such pregnancies. The fourth baby was named Alexa in honor of the doctor.

The four girls are receiving care in the hospital’s neonatal intensive care unit and are reported to be doing well.

World.title: Gales Point Manatee celebrates first-ever Gales Point Village Cultural Festival
World.content:
Gales Point Manatee celebrates first-ever Gales Point Village Cultural Festival

By Zoila Palma: On July 18, 2026, the community of Gales Point Manatee celebrated its first-ever Gales Point Village Cultural Festival, honoring its rich African heritage and vibrant Kriol identity.

Following the landmark 2025 inscription of the Krimos Bram and Sambai on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, the festival makes an important step in the community’s ongoing commitment to celebrating and safeguarding its treasured traditions.

The day featured vibrant brokdong and bram music performances, and traditional games. Delicious foods like shingding, crab soup, fish sere, and traditional fire-hearth rice-and-beans and powder bun brought the community together in celebration of cultural heritage.

The Institute for Social & Cultural Research (ISCR) extended congratulations to the people of Gales Point Manatee, Chairlady Nadine Moore and all council members, for successfully organizing this memorable celebration.

“We also extend our sincere appreciation to Hon. Francis Fonseca, Minister of Culture, NICH President Mr. Albert Vaughan, and all sponsors for their invaluable support and continued commitment to safeguarding and celebrating Belize’s living cultural traditions,” ISCR said.

World.title: University of Belize takes major step toward International Accreditation
World.content:
University of Belize takes major step toward International Accreditation

The University of Belize (UB) has reached an important milestone in its pursuit of international institutional accreditation with the official submission of its Application for Accreditation Candidacy to the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges (SACSCOC).

“This is a historic day for the University of Belize,” said President Dr. Vincent Palacio. “Our submission represents the culmination of years of work to strengthen our academic and administrative systems and position UB to meet internationally recognized standards of excellence. Today, we have taken a decisive step toward our vision of becoming an internationally accredited university.”

UB’s candidacy application involved strengthening its institutional effectiveness framework, faculty credentialing, the enhancement of academic and administrative policies and quality assurance throughout the institution.

President Palacio expressed appreciation to the University’s Board of Trustees, its Quality Assurance team, its Vice President of Academic Affairs, deans, faculty, professional and administrative staff, whose dedication and collaboration made the submission possible.

He also acknowledged the contributions of the University’s external reviewers, whose positive assessments and endorsements affirmed UB’s readiness to advance to this important stage.

UB now prepares itself for the beginning of the next phase of the accreditation process.

SACSCOC will now undertake a comprehensive review of the application before determining the University’s candidacy status.

World.title: Cayo Central Summer camp inspires next generation of Belizean farmers
World.content:
Cayo Central Summer camp inspires next generation of Belizean farmers

By Zoila Palma: The Cayo Central Youth in Agriculture Summer Camp officially got underway this morning at Central Farm, bringing together young participants for a week of learning and hands-on agricultural activities.

The camp opened with a brief ceremony where Cayo Central Area Representative and Minister of State in the Ministry of Agriculture, Luis Alex Balona, encouraged the youths to explore opportunities in agriculture and highlighted the importance of the sector to Belize’s future.

Following the opening remarks, participants were divided into groups and began the first day of activities.

Throughout the week, the campers will take part in both classroom sessions and practical training in areas including horticulture and aquaculture, gaining valuable knowledge and skills in modern agriculture.

World.title: International News: Teen dies after fountain collapses during Spain’s World Cup celebrations
World.content:
International News: Teen dies after fountain collapses during Spain’s World Cup celebrations

By Zoila Palma: A 13-year-old boy was killed and two other young people were injured after part of a fountain collapsed during Spain’s World Cup victory celebrations in Ciudad Rodrigo, Salamanca province, early this morning, BBC reports.

Emergency services said the incident occurred around 12:30 a.m. local time when several youths climbed onto the Árbol Gordo fountain to celebrate Spain’s 1-0 victory over Argentina in the World Cup final.

Local reports indicated that part of the structure gave way under the weight of the crowd.

The injured included one child who was taken to hospital with a suspected broken leg.

Emergency responders, firefighters, police and medical teams were dispatched to the scene, while authorities later requested psychological support for the victim’s family as an investigation into the incident got underway.

World.title: Belize participates in 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic
World.content:
Belize participates in 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic

By Zoila Palma: On July 18, 2026, athletes and officials representing Team Belize gathered for an important briefing ahead of their departure to the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic.

The session provided key information on travel logistics, accreditation, competition procedures, athlete services, and team expectations, ensuring all delegation members are well prepared for the Games.

The Belize Olympic and Commonwealth Games Association says that with the countdown underway, Team Belize continues its final preparations as athletes get ready to proudly represent Belize on one of the region’s biggest sporting stages.

World.title: 27 dead, 83 missing from capsized Guyana ferry, says PM
World.content:
Handout picture released by NCN Guyana showing President Irfaan Ali (L) attending a meeting with some of the survivors and relatives of those still missing after a ferry carrying more than 100 people capsized off the coast of the country, in Mabaruma, Region One, Guyana, on July 20, 2026. The ageing ferry MV Barima capsized off the coast of Guyana late on July 18 during a trip from the capital Georgetown to Port Kaituma. Rescue teams saved 67 people, officials said, as the search continues into July 20. (Photo by Handout / NCN Guyana / AFP)

GEORGETOWN, Guyana (AFP) — At least 27 people are dead, and 83 more are missing after a ferry capsized off the coast of Guyana over the weekend, Prime Minister Mark Phillips said Monday.

The search for survivors is ongoing after the MV Barima flipped over late Saturday, with Phillips telling a press conference that 69 people had been rescued so far. The previous death toll had stood at 10.
