World.title: WATCH: A colourful goodbye to late revival singer Kukudoo
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica – A vibrant celebration of life unfolded Sunday as scores of mourners gathered at the Ranny Williams Entertainment Centre in St Andrew to bid farewell to late gospel and revival singer David “Kukudoo” McDermott.

McDermott died on May 8 after a battle with cancer. He was 52.

In a fitting farewell on Sunday, his funeral was marked by colourful traditions, spirited dancing and soul-stirring songs.

There were also glowing tributes from members of the gospel music fraternity, friends, family and government officials including Entertainment and Culture Minister Olivia Grange; State Minister in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, Arlando Terrelonge; and State Minister in the Ministry of Health and Wellness, Krystal Lee.

McDermott’s remains were interred at the Dovecot Memorial Park.

(Video by Llewellyn Wynter)

World.title: More traffic headache coming for motorists in Liguanea
World.content:
Sewer upgrade work underway on Retreat Avenue off Old Hope Road on Saturday. The work will shortly be extended on Old Hope Road to its intersection with Wellington Drive. Naphtali Junior

MOTORISTS in the Liguanea area of St Andrew should brace for major traffic disruptions this summer as the National Water Commission (NWC) undertakes the renovation of sewage infrastructure along Old Hope Road

Speaking during a recent meeting of the Jamaica Observer Press Club at the newspaper’s headquarters in St Andrew, Minister of Water Matthew Samuda said the work forms part of the Government’s ongoing programme to strengthen resilience through upgrading the county’s water and sewage network.

He explained that work on Munroe Road and Wellington Drive, which led to traffic snarls in the area for weeks, is now complete, allowing work to begin on the stretch of Old Hope Road that runs through Liguanea, Matilda’s Corner, and Seymour Avenue.

Samuda told Observer editors and reporters that work along that corridor was deliberately postponed to avoid disrupting students travelling to sit their various examinations.

“We didn’t start last month because we didn’t want to run the risk of a child being stuck in traffic trying to get to their PEP [Primary Exit Profile] exams at St Peter and Paul, or a child trying to get to Campion to do their CXC [Caribbean Examination Council] exams along that particular space. We expect to start in the coming week or so,” said the minister.

World.title: APOLOGY AND CORRECTION
World.content:
Dayton Campbell

On Monday, 13 July 2026, the Jamaica Observer published an article entitled ‘Dead girl’s ghost haunts Dayton’.

The Observer acknowledges that the headline was capable of conveying the false impression that Dr Campbell had some association with, or responsibility for, the rape and murder of Diane Smith. The Observer acknowledges that any such implication is entirely false.

Dr Campbell was an infant when Diane Smith was raped and murdered. He has never been implicated, suspected, or connected in any way with that tragic crime.

The Observer further acknowledges that Dr Campbell did not repeat or endorse any allegation connecting any person to the rape and murder of Diane Smith, whether debunked or otherwise.

The Jamaica Observer sincerely apologises to Dr Campbell for the distress, embarrassment, and reputational harm occasioned by the publication and withdraws any defamatory imputations arising therefrom.

World.title: Puzzling double murder in Mandeville
World.content:
An undated photo of murder victim Deneekia Pounall, 24, Knox Community College nursing student and resident of Heartease district in Manchester .

MANDEVILLE, Manchester — Even as police here have launched a manhunt for a gunman who posed as a passenger in a taxi before disembarking the vehicle and killing two passengers on Saturday, detectives are struggling to make sense of the incident as up to press time they had not determined a motive for the attack.

“It is senseless…He paid his fare and got his change and the vehicle drove off and he just fired shots on it. The motive is not clear, because why would you shoot up a vehicle with seven people,” a senior police source told the Jamaica Observer on Sunday.

Police identified those killed as Deneekia Pounall, 24, a nursing student at Knox Community College, a resident of Heartease in the parish, and her neighbour 21-year-old Sadefa Henry.

According to the police, about 7:30 pm on Saturday, Pounall and Henry were seated in a Toyota Voxy operated as a public passenger vehicle on the Mandeville to Royal Flat route when a man, who was a passenger in the vehicle, disembarked at a section of Caledonia Road commonly referred to as Horseshoe Curve.

The man reportedly opened fire on the seven occupants of the taxi, hitting the two who were seated at the back of the vehicle.

They were taken to the Mandeville Regional Hospital where Pounall was pronounced dead on arrival, while Henry later succumbed to his injuries.

Residents of Heartease told the

Observer on Sunday that Pounall and Henry lived in neighbouring apartments at a property in the community.

“She was such a calm girl. She nuh talk, and the guy was quiet and humble, so this incident is quite puzzling,” said a resident who requested anonymity.

The double murder has increased the number of homicides reported in Manchester to 20 since the start of the year.

Just last week acting head of the police’s Area Three, Senior Superintendent Shane McCalla, predicted that fewer than 94 murders will be recorded across Manchester, Clarendon, and St Elizabeth by year end, following the launch of Operation Reset last month.

“We are trending upwards in the murder and aggravated assaults, so Operation Reset was primarily designed to address this…and in terms of the acquisitive crimes, we are trending down by 104. This is our commitment to the High Command that Area Three will deliver in December,” he told the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s High Command last Wednesday at the Mandeville police station.

McCalla gave a breakdown of murders statistics down the years in Area Three. He said in 2023 there were 189 murders, in 2024 there were 150 murders, while 94 murders were recorded last year.

“Year to date we have 58 [murders]. Despite seeing some issues where St Elizabeth is concerned… I am convinced and I am committing to you that we will end under the 94 [in December],” he vowed.

World.title: Sumfest history
World.content:
Mavado (left) and Vybz Kartel share the Sumfest stage. (Garfield Robinson)

For 18 years it remained one of dancehall’s biggest unanswered questions: Could the music that once divided a nation ever become the force that united it?

Shortly after 2:00 am on Sunday that question was answered inside Plantation Cove as a Taste of Reggae Sumfest delivered an experience of history-making proportions.

Vybz Kartel and Mavado stood shoulder to shoulder on the festival’s grand stage, writing a new chapter in one of the most defining narratives in dancehall culture. The showdown was far more than an exhibition of hit songs. It was the closing of a circle that began during the combative Gully/Gaza era — a rivalry that shaped an entire generation of dancehall fans and forever altered the genre’s landscape.

Dressed for battle, but performing in brotherhood, both deejays were ready to give fans exactly what they asked for.

Without hesitation, they reached back into the catalogue that made them icons. Serving up songs such as

The Real McKoy, Real Deal, Send A Hell, the entertainers elicited loud cheers of approval from the sold-out crowd.

The tension that once defined the rivalry had given way to celebration.

“This a history innu,” Mavado declared.

“Memba dat,” Kartel responded before embracing his long-time rival.

“We ago gi unnu supm unnu never see yet,” Kartel continued.

For two hours they spewed hit after hit from their arsenal of songs.

For Professor Donna Hope, one of Jamaica’s foremost authorities on dancehall culture, the significance of the moment extended well beyond nostalgia.

“Eighteen years later… We have been through many things, they’ve been in exile in different ways, they lost things, they gained things, and so the energy was different,” she reflected after the performance. “Gaza/Gully in 2008 was a very combative energy but Reggae Sumfest 2026, it was different. Their performance reminded people that dancehall culture is alive and well and Vybz Kartel and Mavado are powerful artistes that have matured and now understand the mission and are carrying it out.”

Even while revisiting songs born from lyrical warfare, the two men frequently completed each other’s lyrics, laughed together, and embraced the shared legacy they helped create. Records that once encouraged fans to choose sides became reminders of just how deeply both artistes have shaped modern dancehall.

Mavado confidently held his own with crowd favourites, including Weh Dem A Do, Top Shatta Nah Miss, Chat Too Much, Warn Dem, and Amazing Grace.

Kartel answered with equal force, unleashing anthem after anthem through Gaza Army, Broad Daylight, Kill Dem All, Done, Weh Dem A Go, Murder Informa, and Never Scared.

Female fans were delighted with selections including Love Dem, Picture Me & You, Beg You (A Touch), and Come Home, while Mavado countered with Squeeze Breast, Bicycle, Ever Blessed, When You Feel Lonely, and Never Believe You.

The surprises continued as Mavado invited Stacious to recreate their hit Come Into My Room, while Kartel called on Gaza Hindu to perform Spice’s verses on Ramping Shop and Virginity.

“It’s a good feeling to be back on a Sumfest stage,” said Stacious. “Tonight I’m here not just as an artiste, but as a fan of dancehall who lived through the era where Gully/Gaza did a run road… Mavado hasn’t performed in Jamaica for a while so I was happy to witness that return and be a part of it… [I]t’s always fun when we connect…” As they got ready to draw the curtains on their historic set, the clash songs and romance anthems gave way to messages of gratitude and faith as the deejays delivered Hope and Pray, God Is the Greatest, The Messiah, and Thank Yuh Jah. Then came the perfect ending. Their first collaboration, Happiest Days. “This a the first song me and him ever do,” Kartel reminded the audience. “Listen to it good and see how everything come full circle.” Few closing songs could carry greater symbolism — history, legacy secured!

World.title: Rastafari ganja rights review
World.content:
From left: Sancia Bennett Templer, permanent secretary, Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce; Delano Seiveright, minister of state in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce and chairman of the Cannabis Industry Development Taskforce; Delroy Chuck, minister of justice and constitutional affairs; and Olivia “Babsy” Grange, minister of culture, gender, entertainment and sport, engage meeting attendees (out of picture) following Thursday’s high-level ministerial consultation on Jamaica’s sacramental cannabis framework at the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs.

THE Government on Thursday opened consultations on the country’s sacramental cannabis framework during a high-level policy meeting at the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs.

Justice Minister Delroy Chuck; Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Olivia “Babsy” Grange; minister of state in the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs Marisa Dalrymple-Philibert; and minister of state in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce Delano Seiveright led the talks with senior technocrats from the ministries.

The discussions were convened following recommendations of the Cannabis Industry Development Taskforce, chaired by Seiveright, which identified the need for a coordinated consultation on policy and operational issues affecting Jamaica’s sacramental cannabis regime.

The meeting considered the existing legal and administrative framework with the objective of providing greater clarity, consistency, and certainty while safeguarding the religious freedoms provided under Section 7C(2)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act, which makes provision for members of the Rastafarian community to possess ganja.

The meeting discussed matters relating to the recognition and oversight of sacramental organisations, approved cultivation lands and spaces, cultivation and possession limits, transportation arrangements, enforcement protocols, and the need to clearly distinguish sacramental cannabis activities from Jamaica’s regulated, commercial cannabis industry.

Jamaica’s commercial cannabis industry is regulated exclusively by the Cannabis Licensing Authority (CLA) under the Dangerous Drugs Act and its Regulations, with no other entity having legal authority to license or regulate commercial cannabis activities.

There have been growing concerns surrounding the misuse of the sacramental framework to facilitate unlawful activities, as well as persistent confusion about what the law permits.

In recent times there have been repeated allegations from Rastafarians about facing prosecution over their use of ganja, despite the provision in law for its sacramental use.

Recently the

Jamaica Observer reported the case of Westmoreland resident Troy Harrison who had charges of possession of ganja and dealing in ganja against him dropped in the Westmoreland Parish Court.

The Crown offered no evidence on both charges on the basis that Harrison is a member of the Rastafarian community and therefore entitled to possess and use ganja for sacramental purposes.

“Some police continue to want to interpret the law how they want to,” attorney-at-law Marcus Goffe, who represented Harrison, told the

Observer.

“The Rastafari community is fed up with the continual targeting and unfair prosecution of members of the community for ganja, despite the 2015 amendments to the Dangerous Drugs Act intended to recognise and protect the community’s rights. It is clear that the narcotics police are not fully aware of the extent of Rastafari’s ganja rights or how they are to approach, investigate, determine, and resolve the rights of Rastafari in relation to ganja,” charged Goffe, who was then on a mission to have the seized ganja returned to Harrison.

Against charges such as the ones made by Goffe, the high-level meeting led by the Government ministers also explored mechanisms to strengthen coordination among the various ministries, the CLA, and the Jamaica Constabulary Force.

A significant part of the discussions focused on the possible transfer of responsibility for the operational governance and administration of sacramental cannabis matters to the Ministry of Culture, recognising the fundamentally religious and cultural character of the sacramental regime.

Ministers agreed that the proposal should form part of the ongoing consultation process as the Government works to strengthen governance; improve inter-ministerial coordination; and provide a clearer, more effective framework that protects legitimate sacramental rights while preserving public confidence, public safety, and the rule of law.

World.title: Lady Da Flame heats up the summer
World.content:
Lady Da Flame

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Recording artiste Lady Da Flame is setting the tone for the season with the release of her latest single, Summer, now available on all major digital streaming platforms.

Produced by Rawborn Productions, the high-energy track fuses dancehall with island and reggaeton influences, driven by pulsating drums, booming basslines and an infectious rhythm that embodies the carefree spirit of summer.

Crafted with beach parties, festivals, road trips and island celebrations in mind, the song delivers an upbeat soundtrack for the season.

Lady Da Flame said the inspiration behind the record came from a desire to create a fun anthem that people could instantly connect with.

“My inspiration for the track was simple—we wanted a new fun song for the season, which is summer. I want fans to enjoy it and have fun. I think people will relate to the song and also enjoy the sick beat it’s on. Summer songs are important because they capture the mood and the vibes of the season,” she said.

Describing the musical direction of the single, the artiste noted that while the record incorporates island and reggaeton flavours, its foundation remains firmly rooted in dancehall.

“It has a dancehall feel with island and reggaeton vibes that all stem from dancehall,” she added.

She added that the song’s driving percussion and heavy basslines are designed to get listeners moving, while its overall energy evokes images of fast cars, endless sunshine, parties and adventurous island living.

The release comes on the heels of a productive period for the artiste, whose profile has continued to rise across the dancehall and reggae landscape.

Earlier this year, Lady Da Flame performed before thousands at a Mother’s Day concert at UBS Arena, sharing the stage with Beres Hammond, Stephanie Mills and Romain Virgo. The performance further showcased her commanding stage presence while introducing her music to an even wider audience.

She also paid tribute to mothers with the heartfelt single Mama, a release that resonated with fans and highlighted her versatility as both a vocalist and songwriter.

Her momentum continued with The Journey, a spiritually inspired EP produced by Rawborn Productions. The project features the tracks All Praises To The Most High, More Dan Prayer, and No One Like You (Remake), a collaboration with reggae singer Sanchez. Together, the songs reflect her personal growth and spiritual journey while delivering messages of faith, perseverance and hope.

Lady Da Flame also expanded her catalogue with the motivational single Mi Believe Inna Mi and Ropeen, a Lovers Rock collaboration with Richie Stephens. A promotional campaign surrounding The Journey, including an appearance on OnStage, further strengthened her visibility and cemented her place as one of dancehall and reggae’s emerging female talents.

With Summer now available worldwide, Lady Da Flame is hoping listeners will embrace the vibrant energy of the track as they make the most of the season.

“I just want everyone to enjoy themselves, have fun and make great memories every time they hear the song,” she said.

World.title: Wes Streeting named to top UK defense role
World.content:
Wes Streeting arrives at Downing Street on July 20, 2026 before he was named defense secretary in the new Burnham Cabinet. | Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images

The former health secretary had initially intended to challenge Keir Starmer but now joins Burnham’s cabinet.

LONDON — Wes Streeting will become the U.K.’s new defense secretary, Downing Street announced, as Andy Burnham unveiled his new Cabinet after becoming prime minister.

Streeting take over less than six weeks after predecessor Dan Jarvis, who was appointed amid a fierce row within government over defense spending, was named to the job by Burnham's predecessor Keir Starmer.

Jarvis was responsible for delivering the government’s long-awaited Defence Investment Plan, which allocated money to the capabilities needed to deal with the biggest threats to the U.K. over the next four years.

World.title: Britain’s Brexit Minister Nick Thomas-Symonds axed in reshuffle
World.content:
As Cabinet Office minister, Thomas-Symonds also had responsibility for other policy areas including public inquiries and civil service reform.

His departure comes at a key time for negotiations between Britain and the EU.

Before Starmer’s resignation, a U.K.-EU summit had been scheduled for Wednesday July 22 to round off talks on issues like an agri-food agreement, youth mobility scheme, and emissions trading deal.

Starmer had also planned to use the meeting as a launchpad for a closer relationship with the bloc.

The meeting was postponed upon Starmer’s resignation and is now expected to be rescheduled for later this year — with a new minister in charge on the British side.

“I hope that you will continue the negotiations I have started for U.K. participation in the EU's internal electricity market, and implement the key pillars of the Common Understanding: the food and drink agreement; the linking of the U.K. and EU Emissions Trading Systems; and the Youth Experience Scheme that will provide opportunities for young people to travel, work and study across Europe,” Thomas-Symonds wrote in his letter.

World.title: EU bets fossil fuel lobby is crying wolf over supply shock warnings
World.content:
Instead, it has issued new guidelines advising EU countries’ governments to hold off on fining offenders for three years. While that doesn’t officially remove the requirements, it would suspend enforcement to give companies more time to comply. The guidelines, first reported by POLITICO, were made official Monday after months of speculation. Member countries will discuss them Wednesday.

The Commission’s gamble is that companies are raking in so much money from selling to Europe — especially as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz sends energy prices soaring — that they won’t kill a lucrative trade just because of some legal uncertainties.

The executive is also confident that compliance won’t be a problem in the first place, and has reassured diplomats that its three-year “grace period” for penalties will stand up in court if member countries implement it properly. Last week it issued further guidance to help companies prove the emissions intensity of cargoes — a key detail they say has been missing.

“People will come to their senses” over the summer, said one EU official, granted anonymity to speak openly. The guidelines “will make it clearer how and when to comply, and it will become clearer that most importers can comply and will comply rather than lose their sales in a liquid global gas market.”

It’s true that business is booming for companies exporting to Europe. In the first 100 days after the U.S. and Israel’s attack on Iran, the EU paid an additional €62 billion for energy supplies, according to the Jacques Delors Institute. In particular, the bloc massively increased its imports of jet fuel and liquefied natural gas from the U.S., one of the most vocal opponents of the methane rules.

The conviction that companies won’t abandon Europe was illustrated in a meeting of EU ambassadors last week, during which the Commission told member countries that it would be best to wait until 2028 to assess the impact of the rules, instead of tearing them open on the basis of industry speculation, according to two diplomats briefed on the meeting.

World.title: Inquiet des usages de l’IA par les députés, le Parlement européen a une solution
World.content:
“Le Parlement n’a pas été épargné par les erreurs liées à l’IA et les contenus trompeurs générés par IA”, a observé Brando Benifei, député européen du groupe des Socialistes et démocrates qui a dirigé les travaux du Parlement sur l’AI Act, la législation phare de l’UE encadrant cette technologie. “Les députés européens doivent montrer l’exemple à mesure que les règles de transparence prévues par l’AI Act entrent en vigueur.”

Ce projet met en lumière le dilemme auquel est confronté le Parlement à mesure que l’IA générative s’intègre dans son travail. Quelque 2 100 personnes utilisent quotidiennement l’IA, soit environ 20% de l’ensemble des effectifs.

Ses dirigeants souhaitent que les responsables publics cessent de mettre des documents parlementaires sur des plateformes publiques non contrôlées, mais ils craignent également que cette technologie ne nuise à la qualité du travail législatif et n’introduise des erreurs ou des contenus trompeurs dans le processus démocratique. Ils ont soupçonné que les parlementaires et leurs assistants utilisaient déjà l’IA après une recrudescence d’amendements nécessitant une traduction, des styles de rédaction révélateurs et des références parfois fantaisistes à des lois qui n’existent pas.

Les présidents des commissions ont demandé au secrétaire général du Parlement, Alessandro Chiocchetti, d’élaborer des lignes directrices concernant l’utilisation de l’IA par les parlementaires. Celui-ci a répondu que cette question pourrait plutôt relever de la commission des Affaires constitutionnelles, qui devrait alors modifier le règlement intérieur de l’institution afin d’introduire des règles plus strictes.

Aujourd’hui, les députés européens ne sont pas tenus d’indiquer si leurs amendements, questions ou autres travaux parlementaires ont été élaborés à l’aide de l’intelligence artificielle.

Barry Andrews, président Renew de la commission du Développement, a affirmé qu’il était déjà évident que certains députés européens utilisaient l’intelligence artificielle pour rédiger des questions parlementaires, des discours et des amendements.

World.title: EU hits China’s Alibaba with €550M record fine over illegal products
World.content:
The finding that AliExpress failed to check and tackle these risks "is very dangerous for our consumers, but it’s also unfair for those companies that are complying with all our rules," Virkkunen said.

The record fine is the third one imposed under the Digital Services Act so far. It comes two months after Brussels hit rival marketplace Temu with a €200 million bill over similar breaches. “We were looking at the duration and the seriousness of these failures when deciding the size of the fine," Virkkunen said, recalling that Temu had so far only been sanctioned for failing to check its service for illegal products sold in Europe properly.

The Commission opened a probe into AliExpress in March 2024 over suspected breaches of the DSA, including also on the platform's transparency on advertising and recommender systems. Many of these suspected breaches were already settled in a series of commitments in June 2025.

In its new findings, the EU assessed that AliExpress failed to "evaluate whether it had sufficient staff to review potentially illegal products," leading to "overcharged" moderators having "only like 10 or 20 seconds to review the illegal product," a senior Commission official said in a briefing ahead of the announcement. It also failed to assess how its recommender and advertising systems "exacerbate" the spread of illegal products and relied on compliance checks that "could easily be circumvented through mis-categorization."

AliExpress has until Oct. 20 to come up with an "action plan" to address the infringements, which lasted at least until June 2025, or face additional penalties.

A spokesperson for AliExpress said in a statement that the company will appeal the EU's decision, calling it a "disproportionate fine [which] ignores our sound risk management framework and the significant, proactive enhancements we have made." They added: "AliExpress has been and continues to be committed to meeting our obligations to consumers."

This article was updated to include a comment from AliExpress confirming it will appeal the decision.

World.title: America’s reassurance mission at Farnborough
World.content:
Europe’s biggest airshow of the year is set to open this week under the specter of two wars, with the Pentagon facing doubts it can hit a trillion-dollar budget topline and if it will play nice with NATO nations increasingly confident about going it alone.

The show that spans more than five million square feet — enough to fit 78 football pitches or 1,350 Concordes stacked wing to wing — has been running since the end of World War II and will launch tens of billions of dollars worth of deals. But with the U.S. delaying arms sales and hanging onto more weapons, the feeling is in the air that American credibility — especially their ability to clarify what they want from Europe and to meet demand — is on the line here at Farnborough.

“There's no question that the primary subtext to this air show, last year's air show, I'm sure next year's air show, is going to be the geopolitical issues and the transatlantic issue in particular, and a lot of anxiety about what that means on both sides,” said a U.S. industry official. “Europe is far from a monolith. You have European countries that would absolutely like to push full on the gas to build an organic defense industrial base. You have others that are very clear they want to continue to buy American kit.”

“We still argue that we make the best stuff in the world, and everybody wants it,” added the official, who, like others, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “But the Europeans are worried if they can get it.”

Scar tissue: Even as top European officials acknowledge they will need America’s help rearming, some are chafing at the Trump administration’s suggestions that the continent shouldn’t try to replace the U.S. defense industry’s role — even as the Pentagon is signaling that it is removing some U.S. forces from Europe.

“The U.S. is moving the goalpost while demanding Europe take ‘primary responsibility’ for its own defense while opposing the industrial-policy tools to do it,” said Oscar Jonsson, a specialist from the Swedish Defence University. “Most European states figured that buying American won’t reverse the trend of U.S. withdrawal, and it will only prolong an overdependence on the U.S. It’s not unlikely that there will be a compromise with some more buying American, but it’s only a slight delay to the structural shift.”

World.title: Pistorius makes fresh push for Hegseth meeting after spring setback
World.content:
The plans are still being prepared and the individual meetings depend on the minister’s final schedule.

The German defense ministry declined to comment on the plans. However, it would be Pistorius’ second attempt this year to secure a dedicated meeting with Hegseth in Washington.

The German minister abandoned the U.S. leg of a planned North America trip in May after a meeting with Hegseth could not be arranged. Pistorius went ahead with the Canadian portion of the trip, while Hegseth traveled to the Shangri-La Dialogue security conference in Singapore.

The episode was a setback for Berlin as it sought direct access to the Trump administration during a period of growing uncertainty over Washington's military role in Europe.

Pistorius and Hegseth have met before. Most recently, both were at the NATO Summit in Ankara. And during a formal Pentagon visit in July 2025, the two discussed the future of U.S. forces in Europe and Germany's interest in the American Typhon long-range missile system as well as Tomahawk missiles.

Those questions have only become more pressing. Hegseth announced in June a six-month review of U.S. troop deployments in Europe, while Washington has already reduced some of the military capabilities it makes available to NATO. Pistorius has warned that any American withdrawal must be coordinated with European allies to avoid dangerous gaps in the alliance’s defenses.

World.title: More than a million fans fill Madrid’s streets to welcome world champions
World.content:
World Cup champions Spain began their open-top bus parade through the streets of Madrid on Monday evening, as more than one million fans turned out to celebrate.

 

The victory parade is making its way through the Spanish capital, where thousands of supporters are greeting the team with chants of "España, España" and a sea of mobile phones held aloft to capture the moment.

Supporters pack Madrid’s streets

Hundreds of thousands of supporters filled the streets of Madrid on Monday to celebrate Spain’s World Cup victory with the national team.

According to the Government Delegation, more than one million people lined the route of the team’s open-top bus through the city centre cheering the players.

From the bus, the players waved to the crowds, lifted the World Cup trophy and celebrated with supporters lining the streets.

The capital has turned red and white to welcome the Spanish team, with thousands of supporters filling the streets, the Metro stations and the bus route.

Thousands of supporters turn Cibeles Square red as they welcome the world champions after their victory over Argentina. Selección Española Masculina de Fútbol

The tension of the final is now behind them, replaced by emotion and an overwhelming desire to celebrate a new world title.

Pedro Sánchez pays tribute to Spain's world champions

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez welcomed Spain's national team to on Monday to celebrate their World Cup triumph.

The Prime Minister thanked the players and coaching staff for their efforts and the football they produced throughout the tournament, before urging them to dream of another title in 2030.

"Why not believe that, as the saying goes, good things come in threes?" he said.

Official reception with Spain’s royal family

Spain’s national team was received at Zarzuela Palace by King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, accompanied by Princess Leonor and Infanta Sofía, following their World Cup triumph.

During the ceremony, the players broke into the traditional chant of “Campeones, campeones” before posing for the official photograph. The King hailed the victory as an “epic triumph” and thanked the team for returning Spain to the summit of world football.

He also praised the team’s efforts throughout the tournament and dismissed the criticism it had faced, insisting that nothing could overshadow “the joy of bringing the trophy home”.

La Roja in Madrid

Spain’s national team is now back in Madrid. The Iberia flight bringing them home from the United States landed at Adolfo Suárez Madrid-Barajas Airport.

Before the official World Cup celebrations got under way, the players had a few hours’ rest to celebrate the triumph with their families.

This is the first time the team has set foot on Spanish soil since lifting the World Cup, 16 years after their historic triumph at the 2010 tournament in South Africa.

The Spanish capital has turned red to welcome the new champions on a route that will culminate in Cibeles Square, where the main celebrations for Spain's second World Cup title will take place.

FIFA opens disciplinary proceedings against Argentina

FIFA has opened disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over incidents involving several players and a member of the coaching staff during the World Cup final.

The governing body will investigate their conduct and determine whether any sanctions should be imposed.

World.title: Chess legend Judit Polgar rejects offer to become Hungary's president
World.content:
Chess legend Judit Polgar on Monday turned down Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar's offer to become the country's next president.

 

"I do not feel I have the strength to take on the historic responsibility of uniting a divided nation, and so I am unable to accept the invitation," Polgar posted on social media.

"I will do everything in my power to support a new, independent, and respected President of the Republic in achieving these goals," she added.

Polgar issued her response after the Tisza parliamentary group publicly backed her in parliament. However, critics noted that, contrary to earlier promises, her nomination was not preceded by broad public consultation.

Magyar responded to Polgar's decision in a comment.

"Dear Judit, thank you for everything you have done for Hungary. I believe I can say, on behalf of millions of Hungarians, that even if in a different capacity, we will continue to count on you in the future," he wrote.

After ejecting unpopular President Tamas Sulyok by constitutional amendment last week, Magyar backed Polgar late on Sunday as "a president of whom all Hungarians can be proud".

As a result of the constitutional amendment, current President Tamás Sulyok's mandate ended on Monday.

Leaders of the governing Tisza party have repeatedly said they want the president to be elected directly by the public rather than by parliament. As a result, the president elected now could serve only temporarily, until a new constitution is adopted.

World.title: Attacks on Ukrainians in Poland rise, police data show
World.content:
The number of nationality-motivated attacks in Poland is steadily increasing, according to data provided to the Polish press by the National Police Headquarters.

 

This month has already seen widespread coverage of a vulgar attack on teenage girls from Ukraine on a municipal bus in Bielsko-Biała. An adult man verbally abused, threatened and insulted the girls for no other reason than that they were speaking Ukrainian.

And this is just one of 180 incidents that were reported to the police in the first half of 2026.

Alarming figures on attacks

Data shows that the scale of aggression against Ukrainians in Poland has risen sharply.

In 2024, Ukrainians living in Poland filed 267 reports of alleged hate crimes. In 2025, that number rose to 275. The 180 reports filed in the first half of 2026 already represent an increase of more than 30% compared with the same period last year, and nearly 35% compared with 2024.

Political blame game

Politicians are trading accusations over who is to blame for the rise in attacks.

Interior and Administration Minister Marcin Kierwiński wrote on X: "Kaczyński, Braun and Czarnek are doing a great deal to ensure that the brown wave spreads across Poland. The victims are both Poles and foreigners. I have a message for all those who have fallen in love with hatred: the police will always respond firmly. Zero tolerance!".

Opposition Law and Justice (PiS) spokesperson Rafał Bochenek said that "Every form of violence and aggression, both physical and verbal, especially against vulnerable people, including children, should be unequivocally condemned and the perpetrators held to account."

He argued that Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Interior and Administration Minister Marcin Kierwiński bear responsibility for such attacks: "Donald Tusk and Marcin Kierwiński have not only deliberately downplayed the rise in aggression on Polish streets so far, they are directly responsible for the brutalisation of public life in Poland".

Polish-Ukrainian relations deteriorate

Ukrainian activist Natalia Panchenko, from the organisation Stand With Ukraine in Poland, sought to ease tensions between Ukrainians and Poles in a Facebook post following the case in which teenage Ukrainian girls were subjected to abusive comments on a municipal bus in Bielsko-Biała.

"The state is fighting xenophobia. Poland stands for the rule of law. Law enforcement agencies, the courts and the law operate here. That is why we should seek to hold the individual perpetrator to account, rather than projecting his actions onto an entire nation. I know many Poles who have been helping Ukraine for years. (...) Some idiot on a bus is not the whole of Poland. Just as any criminal among Ukrainians is not the whole of Ukraine," she wrote.

World.title: Emergency farming law: reintroduction of two banned pesticides splits political parties
World.content:
French MPs are due to vote on Monday evening on the emergency agriculture bill, whose final version was approved last Thursday by a joint committee (CMP). A piece of legislation whose adoption is far from a foregone conclusion.

 

Of the 78 articles contained in the bill, one in particular is splitting France’s political forces: the reintroduction, by way of derogation, of acetamiprid and flupyradifurone – two pesticides banned in France but authorised in the European Union – for certain struggling sectors.

Last year, the bill put forward by Senator Laurent Duplomb, which already envisaged the return of acetamiprid, ran into strong public opposition, leading to a widely supported petition. The provision was ultimately struck down by the Constitutional Council.

A divisive bill, even within the government

In an effort to rally his troops ahead of the vote, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu convened a meeting at Matignon on Monday with the main representatives of the government coalition (Renaissance, MoDem, Horizons, LR), the centrist Liot group, as well as ministers Annie Genevard, Monique Barbut, Mathieu Lefèvre and Laurent Panifous.

The Minister for Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut, said on Saturday that the reintroduction of banned pesticides remained "the main sticking point".

"To make this bill fail out of ideology, calculation or fear would utterly dash farmers’ hopes", argued Agriculture Minister Annie Genevard.

Renaissance MP Prisca Thevenot says that "it is urgent that [the bill] be passed and implemented" but that "out of 78 articles there is one that raises questions" and puts the legislation "in mortal danger". She is categorical: "Acetamiprid must not appear in this bill."

Prisca Thévenot listens to Emmanuel Macron during a meeting of the Council of Ministers, on Friday 21 July 2023 at the Élysée Palace in Paris AP Photo/Christophe Ena, Pool

Prisca Thevenot had previously recalled that the government could "always table an amendment to delete acetamiprid" before Monday’s final vote.

The secretary-general of Renaissance, Gabriel Attal, had also urged "the government to table a deleting amendment" for the article concerning acetamiprid, according to a Les Républicains (LR) MP speaking to AFP.

Late on Monday afternoon, people close to Sébastien Lecornu nonetheless confirmed that Matignon was not proposing to scrap this derogation, preferring to let Parliament "decide" the matter.

The current version of the bill is backed by the Rassemblement national (RN) as well as many right-wing and centrist MPs.

By contrast, most Horizons MPs "seem to favour removing acetamiprid", according to a source close to the talks. As for MoDem, while one source indicated that "the acetamiprid totem continues to raise questions for some MPs", no common position has yet been made public.

Environmental concerns

A year after the revolt against the Duplomb law, this new bill is once again dividing French society, at a time when the climate context is sharpening anxieties over environmental protection.

For the environmental association Générations Futures, bringing back banned pesticides would mark "the Senate’s deadly U-turn".

Conversely, the president of the Confédération générale des planteurs de betteraves sucrières (CGB), Franck Sander, believes that the reauthorisation "in a targeted and regulated way" of flupyradifurone "is an essential condition for our competitiveness when all the indicators are flashing red".

Related Study links exposure to agricultural pesticides to cancer risk

The reform of water storage for agricultural irrigation, provided for in the emergency agriculture law, is another source of contention. Several protests against this measure are planned this week, including a demonstration on Monday evening at Les Invalides.

Annie Genevard nonetheless considers this reform a "common-sense" measure. "If we give up on this emergency agriculture law, we condemn the French to imported food. I will not accept that", she said on X.

The vote on this bill in the National Assembly, ahead of its passage to the Senate on Tuesday, comes as recent heatwaves have pushed environmental issues back to the forefront of French concerns.

Almost a third of them (32%) now consider environmental protection a priority issue, according to a poll carried out for La Tribune Dimanche, a 12-point increase.

World.title: Brussels proposes easing methane penalties after heavy lobbying from industry
World.content:
The European Commission has proposed waiving penalties linked to the bloc's methane rules for three years.

 

Industry and top liquefied natural gas (LNG) exporters have been pressuring Brussels over its burdensome reporting requirements, which they said could affect exports to the European Union.

EU member states adopted methane rules in May 2024, introducing the bloc’s first framework for measuring, reporting and verifying methane emissions in the energy sector as part of efforts to curb one of the most potent greenhouse gases. Failure to honor such requests would incur penalties, which would start applying in 2027.

But on Monday, the Commission recommended exempting business operators from full compliance.

The much-anticipated recommendations come after months of lobbying from the United States, Qatar, Algeria and Nigeria, who warned the EU executive that its rules would endanger the EU's security of supply at a time when the bloc is struggling to offset losses from the Middle East – a claim hotly contested by environmentalists.

Green organisations warned that broad discretion to waive penalties could weaken one of the world's most ambitious efforts to curb emissions of methane, a greenhouse gas far more potent in the short term than carbon dioxide.

"A three-year sanction holiday, triggered by exaggerated and unsubstantiated security of supply concerns raised by industry, risks giving a free pass to methane-intensive gas imports – notably from the US," said Esther Bollendorff, fossil free program manager at Climate Action Network Europe.

Bollendorff argued that the recommendations "should not deter member states from implementing robust penalty systems", arguing that such actions are "essential to ensuring that companies pay the price for their pollution".

"These recommendations should be reviewed well before the suggested 2028 timeline, to suspend their application as soon as possible," Bollendorff added.

Contractual law for regulatory certainty

In the four-page recommendation, Brussels also instructs importers how to write contracts that will allow them to comply with the rules.

The recommendations don't create new legal obligations, but they provide optional model contract clauses that energy importers can use to comply with the methane rules – a response business operators' calls for regulatory certainty.

"The optional model clauses are intended to promote fair, transparent and sustainable contractual practices, to provide a framework for the adjustment of contractual terms, to support compliance (...) and to foster reliable supply of crude oil, natural gas, LNG or coal to the Union," the Commission's recommendations say.

Industry groups say the Commission has acknowledged flaws in the methane rules that could threaten Europe's energy security, but argue its proposed non-binding guidance falls short.

Related US Democrats urge Brussels to stick to methane rules

"The Commission persists in wanting to fix them through non-binding guidance, which cannot deliver the uniform legal certainty Europe needs. Only targeted amendments, as called for by Member States and industry, can," a spokesperson from the International Association of Oil and Gas Producers told Euronews.

With fewer than six months before key provisions take effect, businesses warn that delays are already affecting commercial decisions and supply contracts. They urge the EU to fast-track targeted amendments that maintain methane reduction goals while safeguarding the EU's security of supply, competitiveness and consumers from higher costs.

Maas Goote, international lawyer and former EU lead negotiator at UN climate talks, welcomed the Commission's "wise approach" by "offering pragmatic solutions for implementation issues and strengthening the EU methane regime step-by-step".

"In doing so, it is important that the integrity of the Regulation remains intact,” Goote noted. "The upward trend of methane emissions worldwide shows that voluntary approaches are not delivering results. We need strong regulatory frameworks to drive down methane emissions, with the EU methane regulation as a strong and critical piece."

World.title: Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended
World.content:
On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

Advertising

On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

A decade ago, factions within the Turkish military, composed of rebellious officers and followers of the Islamic cleric Fethullah Gulen, launched a dramatic attempt to topple President Erdogan.

"I remember, as a soldier, those who started the coup," recalls Murat Aslan, an army officer at the time. "I had no idea that there were members of this organisation (Gulen followers); they were very secretive."

Erdogan tightens his grip

Now a security analyst at SETA, a pro-government think tank, Aslan describes the failed coup as a turning point that reshaped the course of Turkish democracy.

"The message was very clear. Turkish society collectively rejected it," said Aslan. "Thousands took to the streets; that's more than challenging, because you see tanks rolling and people trying to stop them, trying to capture the soldiers with their rifles. It takes more than courage." More than 250 people died resisting the coup.

In the aftermath, Erdogan imposed emergency rule and expanded his presidential authority through a sharply contested national referendum. "This military intervention actually consolidated the Erdogan-led government," Aslan added.

Turkey's military, relations with US to survive failed coup, ruling party vice-president

Hundreds of soldiers and officers faced prosecution as the government declared an end to the army's long history of political interference. Since 1960, the military had orchestrated three coups, the most recent in 1980.

A decade of purges and closures

In the wake of the failed takeover, tens of thousands were purged from state institutions, many never returning even after being cleared.

More than a thousand NGOs were shut down during two years of emergency rule. Milena Buyum, senior Turkey campaigner for Amnesty International, acknowledges the grave threat to democracy posed by the attempted coup: "The state has a responsibility to ensure the safety and security of its citizens and to investigate criminal acts like the ones carried out that night," said Buyum.

Turkey's Erdogan warms to Russia after West coup response

However, Buyum warns that many of the measures introduced under the state of emergency have since been written into ordinary law, permanently curtailing fundamental freedoms: "The right to freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and association: the impact on civil society was felt very sharply and starkly in the immediate aftermath of the coup, but that impact continues," said Buyum.

Ankara's alliances

The failed coup also drove a wedge into Turkey's long-standing alliance with the United States. "Ankara saw the hand of the United States behind the failed coup attempt," claims Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, who leads the Ankara office of the German Marshall Fund.

Even before the attempted coup, Erdogan's relations with President Barack Obama had been tense. Obama's belated support, offered only after the coup had failed, fuelled Ankara's suspicions of US complicity, particularly as Washington refused to extradite Fethullah Gulen, whom Erdogan blamed for orchestrating the plot. Gulen denied the accusation until his death in 2024.

Turks in France divided on failed coup

Unluhisarcikli observes that US-Turkish relations remained strained for years, while Erdogan gravitated towards Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose rapid show of support stood in sharp contrast to Washington's hesitation.

"Putin was among the first leaders, I believe even the first, to extend political support to the elected government in Ankara, and in those days I believe that support mattered greatly to President Erdogan," Unluhisarcikli said.

Rumours still persist in Turkey today that Moscow warned Erdogan on the day of the failed coup. Unluhisarcikli says it was only with the election of President Donald Trump, who shared Erdogan's animosity towards Obama and Joe Biden, that US-Turkish relations began to thaw, a shift highlighted at this month's NATO summit in Ankara. Yet the wave of mass arrests during the summit, enabled by post-coup emergency powers, served as a stark reminder that the shadow of the failed takeover still looms over Turkey.

World.title: US imposes new 50% tariff on many Canadian goods
World.content:
The tariffs will cover products including wine and hockey sticks, but not energy or fish. The move is the latest trade escalation between the US and its northern neighbor under the Trump administration.

US President Donald Trump's administration on Monday announced it was imposing 50% tariffs on a wide range of Canadian goods.

The White House said the tariffs would take effect in 30 days and cover "products ranging from wine to hockey sticks to cement."

Trump signed the three proclamations under Section 338 of the Tariff Act ​of 1930 — a nearly century-old trade law that allows for tariffs of up to 50% on imports from ​specific countries.

However, the new tariffs will not apply to energy, potash (used in agricultural fertilizer), fish, critical minerals and goods already covered by existing tariffs under Section 232 of the law which relates to national security.

Trump threatens new Canada tariffs as wildfire smoke spreads To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

White House accuses Canada of 'discriminatory treatment'

The White House said the move was a response to Canada's "discriminatory treatment" of American goods.

Specifically, it said Canada imposed tariffs and quotas on US-manufactured cars that it did not apply to cars from other countries, and it said all but two Canadian states and territories have restricted the distribution of American alcohol.

"Over the past year and a half, only two countries have chosen to retaliate against President Trump’s tariffs rather than negotiate a deal with the United States: the People’s Republic of China and Canada," the White House said.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

World.title: Iran war: US launches fresh strikes as Trump vows revenge
World.content:
07/20/2026 July 20, 2026 US launches fresh strikes on Iran

The US has launched strikes on Iran for the 10th night in a row.

"The strikes are designed to further degrade Iranian military capabilities used to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz," the US military's Central Command said on social media.

Iran's semi-official Mehr News Agency reported that air defenses were activated near the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant on the southern coast. The complex has been hit by previous waves of US strikes.

Strikes between the US and Iran have escalated in an attempt to control the Strait of Hormuz.

On Friday, Iranian strike on an air base in Jordan killed two US service members and left a third unaccounted for. Another US soldier was reported dead in Iraq on Saturday due to a "controlled detonation" of a downed Iranian drone.

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that whenever Iran killed an American soldier, they would "pay for that killing many times over."

World.title: Mexican drug lord ‘El Mayo’ sentenced to life without parole in US prison
World.content:
Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada, a co-founder of the Sinaloa cartel and one of the world's most notorious drug traffickers, was sentenced to life in a US prison.

Mexican drug trafficker Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole on Tuesday for co-founding and leading the notorious Sinaloa cartel.

Zambada was one of the most prominent Mexican drug traffickers to face sentencing in a United States court since Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman was sentenced to life in prison in 2019.

"The almost unimaginable amount of drugs attributable to him and the number of murders that we can document is enough to justify Congress's decision to make this a mandatory life sentence," US District Judge Brian Cogan said.

The 76-year-old Zambada apologized "for the harm I caused and for the example I set," urging future generations to "choose a different path."

Zambada apologizes before sentencing

He was arrested in July 2024 after he said he was kidnapped in Mexico and flown to Texas.

Zambada helped found and lead the Sinaloa cartel, becoming one of the most wanted figures for US intelligence and law enforcement agencies for decades.

According to prosecutors, he ordered torture and plotted murders, including the killing of his own nephew, as the cartel flooded the US with tons of cocaine, fentanyl, methamphetamine and other drugs.

U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said Zambada had spent nearly four decades 'poisoning American communities' for profit and ordering the murders of anyone who stood in his way, and that all ended with his sentencing Image: Leonardo Munoz/AFP

He pleaded guilty to charges that included engaging in a continuing criminal enterprise and racketeering conspiracy, acknowledging culpability for 85 underlying crimes. In exchange, prosecutors did not seek the death penalty.

"I grew up in an environment where violence and crime seemed normal, but now I know that's no excuse," Zambada said in court on Monday. "There comes a time when every person must take responsibility for their decisions. I didn't, and many people paid the price."

"El Chapo" partner joins cartel leaders serving life terms

Zambada's former partner "El Chapo" is already serving a life sentence in the United States.

He was convicted in 2019 and is serving a life sentence at the federal Supermax prison in Florence, Colorado.

Together they built the Sinaloa cartel into one of the world's most powerful drug trafficking organizations.

Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman was sentenced to ​life in prisonin 2019 Image: Paul Ratje/REUTERS

The Sinaloa cartel is one of six Mexican drug gangs that US President Donald Trump has designated as Foreign Terrorist Organizations.

Zambada was arrested with El Chapo's son, Joaquin Guzman Lopez, one of El Chapo's sons, who has pleaded guilty to federal drug charges. He has yet to be sentenced.

Zambada's arrest led to a splintering of the Sinaloa cartel, pitting his loyalists against backers of Guzman's sons, dubbed the Chapitos, or "little Chapos."

World.title: AliExpress hit with record EU fine
World.content:
The Chinese retailer has become the latest major online marketplace to face penalties under the EU’s Digital Services Act.

AliExpress said it plans to appeal a penalty imposed by European Union (EU) regulators, who found shortcomings in the firm's efforts to curb illegal, unsafe and counterfeit goods.

The largest Chinese e-commerce platform in the EU, AliExpress, has been fined €550 million ($629 million) for failing to tackle sales of illegal, unsafe and counterfeit products.

"The spread of counterfeit clothing, unsafe toys, dangerous cosmetics and other illegal and harmful products is not an unavoidable cost of shopping online - it is a failure by AliExpress to comply with its obligations under the Digital Services Act," European Commission Vice President Henna Virkkunen said on Monday.

It is the largest fine ever imposed under the Digital Services Act (DSA), which sets out clear rules for online services in the EU, targeting especially very large online platforms.

AliExpress said it will appeal the "disproportionate" fine, saying it considers the penalty excessive.

AliExpress faces October 20 deadline

The online retail giant, which belongs to the Alibaba Group, must pay the fine and has until October 20, to submit a plan to address the breaches. EU regulators will then review the plan, after which the company could face further penalties.

A year ago, AliExpress agreed to tighten controls on illegal and potentially dangerous goods, such as medicines and supplements. But the European Commission said the measures did not fully resolve its broader concerns.

The commission said AliExpress:

Failed in some cases to penalize traders selling illegal products, allowing them to continue operating on the platform.

Lacked sufficient staff to effectively review potentially illegal listings.

Inspectors faced excessive workloads, hampering oversight efforts.

Some illegal products were recommended or promoted before being removed from the platform.

But AliExpress said the EU's decision "ignores our sound risk management framework and the significant, proactive enhancements we have made."

The company also said it has worked with the Commission to meet its "evolving expectations."

DSA used to rein in Big Tech

According to the EU, AliExpress has 193 million users in the bloc, ahead of online fashion giant Shein and retailer Temu, which have 156 million and 130 million users, respectively.

"One in five Europeans say they shop once a month from Shein, Temu and AliExpress," Virkkunen said.

Temu was fined €200 million in May, while Elon Musk's social media platform X was fined in December last year, both for DSA violations.

World.title: England and Liverpool foortball legend Kevin Keegan dies aged 75
World.content:
English former striker and manager Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75 after a battle with cancer. He was a two-time European footballer of the year with Hamburg.

The death of Kevin Keegan, regarded as one of the greatest football players of his generation, was announced in a statement released by his family on Monday.

"It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75," the statement read.

"Kevin had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments. A double Ballon d'Or winner, Kevin was a much-loved husband, father and grandfather."

Born in Doncaster, South Yorkshire on February 14, 1951, Keegan got his big break when he was signed by Liverpool's legendary manager Bill Shankly in 1971.

At Anfield, Keegan struck up a striking partnership with Welshman John Toshack, going on to win the First Division title three times as well as the FA Cup, the UEFA Cup twice and the 1977 European Cup. He made 323 appearances, scoring 100 goals for Liverpool.

Success in the Bundesliga

From Merseyside, Keegan moved on to the Bundesliga's Hamburg, where he was twice named European Footballer of the Year, which is now called the Ballon d'Or, in 1978 and 1979. With Hamburg, he won the Bundesliga in 1978-79 and played in another European Cup final, a 1980 loss to Nottingham Forest. He left the club having scored 32 goals in 90 appearances.

Hamburg were among the former teams to pay tribute to Keegan in a statement on their website on Monday.

"In Kevin Keegan, world football loses one of its most defining figures. Hamburger SV will always cherish the memory of its former title-winning player and two-time Ballon d'Or winner," the statement said.

Our thoughts are with his family, his friends, and all those who shared his journey. Rest in peace, "Mighty Mouse."

Return to England

Following his stint in West Germany, Keegan returned to England with Southampton in the summer of 1980 before moving to Second Division Newcastle, helping the club win promotion back to the top flight – before retiring as a player.

He won 63 England caps, scoring 21 goals, playing at the 1982 World Cup and was also later captain of the national team.

Stepping into management

In 1992, Keegan moved into management at Newcastle, leading them into the Premier League and to within touching distance of the 1995-96 title, but they missed out to Manchester United.

The club also paid tribute to Keegan in a statement issued on Monday afternoon, describing him as "the beating heart of Newcastle for generations of supporters."

After leaving St James' Park in January 1997, a brief stint at Fulham followed before he became England manager in 1999. After overseeing a disappointing Euro 2000 campaign, Keegan resigned minutes after a 1-0 defeat by Germany in World Cup qualifying, the last match played at the original Wembley Stadium.

He later managed Manchester City, before returning to Newcastle.

Keegan's family had revealed in January that he had been diagnosed with cancer, which later spread to stage four.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

World.title: Russia says bus strike kills 5 in border region with Ukraine
World.content:
The strike comes as Ukraine launched more than hundreds of drones at Moscow after a Russian missile barrage on Kyiv, as President Zelenskyy sought to calm growing tensions over Ukraine’s military leadership.

Russia said Monday that a Ukrainian strike on a bus in the border region of Belgorod killed five civilians, including a minor, and left three others critically injured.

The attack came after a Ukrainian retaliatory strike on Moscow, with city officials reporting that more than 400 drones targeted the Russian capital.

The latest escalation followed Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities over the weekend.

Russian strikes targeted the eastern cities of Pavlograd and Kramatorsk in Ukraine Image: REUTERS

In eastern Ukraine, Russian attacks on Pavlograd and Kramatorsk killed two people in each city, according to local authorities.

Officials also reported one person killed in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia during Russian bombardment.

Both sides have previously denied targeting civilians.

Ukraine launches large-scale drone attack on Moscow

Ukraine targeted the Russian capital with more than 400 drones from Sunday into Monday, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said.

He added that most of the drones were intercepted, but Moscow region Gov. Andrei Vorobyov said at least 10 people were wounded by Ukrainian drones.

Several residential buildings and civilian infrastructure facilities were also damaged.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces were targeting Russian logistics facilities and an oil depot in the region.

"We are responding, justly, to every Russian strike against our cities and communities," Zelenskyy said in a post on X.

Ukraine rejects rumors of military leadership shake-up

Meanwhile, Ukraine's military publicly denied rumors that Zelenskyy was firing the chief of Ukraine's armed forces, Oleksandr Syrskyi.

Zelenskyy has faced criticism over the dismissal of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov last week.

There have been days of protests in Ukraine following Fedorov's removal, as a long-running dispute between the reform-minded minister and Syrskyi spilled into the open.

Zelenskyy appointed Yevhenii Khmara, the acting head of Ukraine's Security Service (SBU), as acting defense minister and asked parliament to approve him for the position.

On Monday, he posted several messages on social media showing him meeting with Ukraine's top military commanders to discuss the latest developments in the war, which has dragged on for more than four years.
