World.title: Tiny 'desert' fish found only in Australia narrowly avoids extinction
World.content:
Using scoops made from milk bottles, Sarah Butler has been working tirelessly to save a tiny fish found nowhere else in the world.

"Every red-fin blue-eye we've caught has had some damage from gambusia," the volunteer said.

Found only in a hidden network of artesian springs near Aramac in western Queensland, the blue-eyes' survival is critical, Ms Butler said.

"Sometimes, [the damage] presents as fungus from scales missing, [and] the fish get sick. Otherwise, there can be big chunks of the tail missing," she said.

Using plastic scoops, Sarah Butler is rescuing a rare species of desert fish. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

"Their fry, or their babies, are just immediately getting eaten. Eggs are laid, [then] they're eaten."

Flood brings predator onslaught

Earlier this year, metre-high floodwaters washed through Edgbaston Reserve, bringing in the larger, invasive mosquitofish known as gambusia.

All but three of the reserve's springs have been compromised, with some of the rare fish populations already totally wiped out.

Loading...

Bush Heritage fish ecologist Dean Gilligan said the return of the invasive predators required an "emergency response" to save the native fish.

"Once gambusia get into a spring that's occupied by blue-eyes, the blue-eyes have six to 18 months [at] most before the population goes extinct," Mr Gilligan said.

This spring has been compromised. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

After they were introduced from North America in the 1920s to control mosquitoes, the gambusia have long since spread out of control.

Survival under threat, again

The red-fin blue-eye is a critically endangered freshwater species that was first formally recorded in 1990 after being discovered in seven springs on the former Edgbaston Station.

The cattle property was then purchased in 2008 by Bush Heritage for its ecological significance; the livestock was removed and the property converted into a reserve.

Only a few hundred red-fin blue-eye have survived the gambusia onslaught. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

Mr Gilligan said the tiny fish had to fight to survive.

"Not long after the discovery, the pest fish gambusia turned up on the reserve," he said.

" Within a couple of years, those seven sites had dropped back to six and five and four. "

Gambusia do not lay eggs and instead store male sperm to give birth at a "ridiculous" rate, Mr Gilligan said: up to 60 young per female every three weeks.

This dry country is an important habitat for the rare native fish, the red-fin blue-eye. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

Only one Edgbaston spring survived the initial onslaught.

Race to survive

Affectionately nicknamed a "puddle in the desert", the only surviving spring now contains all the species' remaining genetic diversity.

Over two decades, breeding programs slowly restored the red-fin blue-eye populations and returned the fish to springs where it had previously become extinct.

Mr Gilligan said the gambusia-infested waters got "scarily" close to inundating the reserve's most important spring this year but did not spill over.

"If the flood had been another 15 or 20 centimetres higher, we would have lost this spring as well," Mr Gilligan said.

A fence managed to keep the last remnant spring safe, but only just. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

Volunteer Steve Baines said elsewhere, the fish were not so lucky.

"Unfortunately, the water level of the flood exceeded the fence that we've got [here], so, as everyone's pointed out, invasive species are now in this spring," Mr Baines said.

"I can see a massive drop in [red-fin blue-eye] numbers."

Ecologists had hoped the knee-high steel mesh perimeter fence would be enough to keep the isolated artesian springs separate from the surrounding ecosystems.

The fence's mesh was designed to be small enough to keep out the smallest invasive gambusia while still allowing water to pass through.

But this year, the issue was the height. The fences were too short.

Mr Gilligan said the floodwaters were unexpectedly high and a record for the 15 years Bush Heritage had owned Edgbaston Reserve.

Another consideration was that the springs were growing in size following a multi-decade bore-capping program that allowed Great Artesian Basin aquifers to recover.

Volunteers have saved the last known population of red-fin blue-eyes. (ABC Western QLD: Crispian Yeomans)

He said he was working with the National Recovery Team for red-fin blue-eye to find a solution, including seeking help from the Queensland and Australian governments.

"We know that our old strategy of 50cm-high fences isn't going to work in the long term," Mr Gilligan said.

"We've got to come up with something more secure. [We] really don't know what that is yet, but that's what we have to figure out and move on with."

For volunteer Ms Butler, the emergency call-out meant dropping everything to come out.

"It was last-minute," she said.

" I just felt that I needed to help. "

World.title: Fake photos of PNG celebrity being used in Facebook scams
World.content:
Jennifer Baing was scrolling through Facebook when she came across a photo of herself wearing revealing lingerie.

The image was fake.

Scammers had used artificial intelligence (AI) to manipulate photos taken from the former PNG television host's social media accounts, where she has built a large following promoting traditional food and agriculture.

They then used her likeness to promote fake giveaways, asking people to send money for the chance to win.

"It's happening to everybody," Ms Baing said.

"Our photos are being abused, and our public standing is being abused by these scammers, these impersonators."

Her experience comes as Papua New Guinea prepares new laws to criminalise the malicious use of AI, including deepfakes, voice cloning and digital impersonation.

Experts say the reforms are needed, but warn legislation alone will not protect people unless communities understand how AI is being used to deceive.

AI-manipulated images of Jennifer Baing are being used to tout Facebook scams offering big payouts. (Supplied)

Fake accounts and real-world consequences

Ms Baing said she had identified almost 100 Facebook accounts using her name and photos.

Some cloned her social media profile to impersonate her. Others used AI-generated images of her handing out cash to promote fake giveaways.

She said the harm went beyond damage to her reputation.

"I'm concerned about my safety as well because if that person's really scammed someone out of a lot of money, they're going to come after me," she said.

"So my personal safety is also at risk."

Ms Baing said she had repeatedly reported fake Facebook accounts using her name and photos, but they remain online.

The ABC has approached Meta for comment.

Ms Baing, the daughter of former Markham MP Andrew Baing, plans to contest her father's former seat at PNG's 2028 national election.

A composite image showing a real photo and the version manipulated using AI. (Supplied)

She fears AI-generated images, videos and misinformation could also be used to deceive voters, particularly in rural communities where awareness of the technology remains limited.

"We have to run awareness [campaigns] in communities where people aren't educated enough to understand exactly what AI is," she said.

"Don't believe everything that somebody shows you online.

"They could do this to your daughter. They could do this to one of your family members as well."

Jennifer Baing says the damage done by the AI-generated images goes beyond her reputation. (Supplied)

Pacific countries reviewing cybercrime laws

PNG is not alone in trying to strengthen protections against evolving online crime.

Across the Pacific, governments are updating cybercrime laws and improving digital security responses as scams, impersonation and online exploitation become more common.

Several countries, including Fiji, Tonga, PNG and Vanuatu, have signed up to the Budapest Convention on Cybercrime; an international treaty that helps members investigate cyber offences across borders and obtain digital evidence.

West Papuan activists raise alarm over AI-generated videos AI-generated deepfake videos of prominent West Papuan rights campaigners spark concerns about how disinformation is being used as a form of "digital colonisation".

Samoa launched a dedicated cybercrime police unit last year, but its legal framework is still catching up.

The country has no standalone cybercrime law, with offences prosecuted under the Crimes Act. The government has acknowledged gaps in the legislation and lists updating it as a long-term priority in its 2026 National Cybersecurity Strategy.

In Vanuatu, the government amended its Harmful Digital Communications Act last year, introducing tougher penalties for online abuse, digital impersonation and the sharing of intimate images.

PNG's proposed reforms would go a step further by specifically targeting the malicious use of AI.

The government plans to introduce amendments to the Cybercrime Code Act when parliament returns in November. The proposed laws would criminalise AI-generated sexually explicit material, child exploitation content, fraudulent voice cloning, online scams and digital impersonation.

Police struggling to keep pace

PNG Assistant Commissioner of Police Hodges Ette said cybercrime complaints have risen sharply over the past five years.

"It's a daily complaint," he said.

"Not only are complaints lodged at the cybercrime unit, they're also lodged at police headquarters, in the provinces and at police stations."

But PNG's Cybercrime Unit has just seven officers to investigate offences across a country of about 10 million people.

"That is insufficient," Assistant Commissioner Ette said.

Hodges Ette says AI-related crimes are becoming an increasing concern for investigators. (Supplied: PNG Department of Information and Communications Technology)

To help manage the workload, police are shifting less complex online offences to local police stations so specialist investigators can focus on more serious cybercrime.

The assistant commissioner said investigators were already seeing many AI-generated deepfakes.

"I personally saw one early this week," he said last week.

"There was a photo of three girls standing together, fully clothed.

"A couple of days later, the same photo appeared again, but this time the three girls were naked."

He said cases involving AI-generated sexual images were becoming an increasing concern for investigators.

'The level of stress is so serious'

Assistant Commissioner Ette said the psychological impact on victims can be devastating.

"I am aware of several instances where girls, particularly young women, have committed suicide," he said.

"The level of stress mentally is so serious."

He said victims need better access to counselling and support alongside stronger laws.

"It's frightening. I am a father of two girls," he said.

"I'm always apprehensive when I open Facebook."

Scammers are paying Meta to spread fake ABC News articles A $350 million scam is targeting Australians.

Colm Gannon, who heads the International Centre for Missing and Exploited Children Australia, said many Pacific communities still underestimate the risks posed by AI.

"People do not think within the Pacific Islands that it's going to affect their day-to-day wellbeing," he said.

"What we're seeing is AI becoming a commodity where young people, sometimes without realising it, are being sexually exploited and made vulnerable online."

He said governments should adopt a victim-centred approach, working with technology companies to remove abusive content quickly and provide support for victims.

World.title: Former student allegedly sets school on fire and posts on social media
World.content:
A former student of a NSW Central West school has been charged with setting the site on fire and posting the incident to social media.

The Cowra High School was closed this morning after its administrative block sustained extensive damage from the blaze last night.

A 17-year-old boy was arrested at a home in the town about 10pm and charged with damaging a property by fire and uploading it to social media.

He was refused bail and will appear in a children's court today.

'Extensive' damage to school building

Fire and Rescue NSW (FRNSW) acting superintendent Peter Murray said the agency received numerous Triple Zero (000) calls just after 7pm reporting a fire on the school grounds.

Three FRNSW trucks supported by the state's Rural Fire Service were on scene in about 10 minutes to find the administrative building alight.

"It was a substantial fire, the damage was extensive to that part of the building," he said.

" Crews worked pretty hard and were able to fortunately contain it to that part of the building. "

It took about half an hour to control the fire, which caused smoke damage to nearby structures.

"To initially knock this down and get what we call fire control — to be fairly certain it hasn't expanded any further — within 30 minutes is quite good," said Mr Murray.

No injuries were reported from the blaze.

Police officers commenced an investigation into the fire, which led to the arrest of the teenager later that evening.

He was charged with damaging property that exceeded $15,000 by fire, posting a video about the incident online, and breaking and entering to destroy property valued at more than $60,000.

School closed

Cowra High School Principal Anthony Hamer said in a statement that an "unexpected" fire occurred at the grounds last night.

"This fire has caused damage to some areas of the school," he said.

" We are currently working to have the entire school site safe for the return of our staff and students. "

He said students would learn from home today and would not be able to access the site.

"We look forward to welcoming our students back to school as soon as possible," he said.

World.title: Aussie world champs name new rugby sevens coach for LA Olympics
World.content:
Reg Tayler has been named head coach of the world champion Australian women's rugby sevens team, as the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics loom on the horizon.

The decision completes a succession plan following Tim Walsh's departure from the position after Australia clinched the World Championship in France last month.

Tayler was an assistant coach to Walsh, who has since become Rugby Australia's (RA) director of women's high performance.

Rugby Australia setting high standards Only three years out from hosting the Women's Rugby World Cup, Australia makes a key appointment it hopes will help deliver success on the international stage.

Tayler will guide Australia through its two-year build-up to the Olympics.

"The squad is determined for continued success through to the Olympics in Los Angeles," Tayler said in an RA statement.

"Our players are professional and dedicated to achieving a gold medal, and I am confident we will have the squad capable of that in 2028."

Tayler, who joined the Australian sevens program last year, has big shoes to fill.

Walsh not only led Australia to its recent World Championship victory but was also in charge when it won the inaugural Olympic gold in women's rugby sevens at the 2016 Rio de Janeiro Games.

It is the only time Australia has won Olympic gold in the sport.

Australia won the first women's Olympic rugby sevens gold on offer in 2016. (Getty Images/World Rugby: Dan Mullan)

Walsh, who coached Australia across two stints, will still have input through his newly created role as part of RA's strategy to align the sevens and Wallaroos programs.

He is confident Tayler will leave his mark as head coach, describing the appointment as a "seamless acquisition" for the squad.

"Reg is highly knowledgeable of the World Series circuit and has worked with many of our players coming through the pathways system," Walsh said.

"He's not going in cold, he completely understands the game and his expertise is going to be fully utilised by the program.

"It's a privilege and honour to retain Reg."

Tayler has previously coached the Australia A women's sevens team.

He also spent time working with Ireland's women's and men's squads between 2023-25.

Australia claimed the World Championship with victories in the final two legs of the series in Valladolid and Bordeaux.

World.title: Women with hormone condition may face higher risk of heart attack, stroke
World.content:
Women with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) have a "significantly higher" risk of cardiovascular disease than women without the condition, according to a new study.

The study, published today in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology, & Women's Health, analysed health insurance data collected from more than 2.4 million US women between 2000 and 2022.

It found women with PMOS (previously known as polycystic ovary syndrome or PCOS) were four times more likely to have cardiovascular events such as a heart attack or stroke than those without.

The paper's lead authors — reproductive endocrinologist Snigdha Alur-Gupta of the University of Rochester and Anuja Dokras, a professor of obstetrics and gynaecology at the University of Pennsylvania — said this was the largest study to explore the relationship between PMOS and cardiovascular risk to date.

Healthy eating and regular exercise may reduce the long-term heart disease risk for people with PMOS. (Unsplash: Jonathan Borba)

Dr Alur-Gupta and Professor Dokras said prior to the study, it was established that women with PMOS had an "increased risk of multiple cardiovascular disease risk factors" — such as type 2 diabetes.

But, they said, it was "notable" that even after taking into account obesity and other cardiovascular disease risk factors, or looking at data from younger women, a "higher hazard" remained for people with PMOS.

Dr Alur-Gupta and Professor Dokras said the research emphasised the importance of early heart health screening for people with PMOS, as well as other preventative measures, such as healthy eating and regular exercise.

"Our findings highlight the need for healthcare provider and patient education and awareness to improve early screening, counselling and long-term surveillance in this population," they said.

PMOS and cardiovascular health

PMOS, a common hormonal and metabolic disorder that affects 170 million women worldwide, can lead to infertility, metabolic conditions such as type 2 diabetes and mental health issues.

The condition was renamed from PCOS in May in a move that emphasised its hormonal and metabolic impacts, according to Helena Teede of the Monash Centre for Health Research Implementation.

The name of this health condition was 'very inaccurate'. Now it's changed Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) has been renamed polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), a move health experts say will lead to faster diagnoses and better treatment for women of all ages.

Professor Teede, who led the renaming initiative, did not contribute to the new study and said its link between PMOS and cardiovascular disease was significant, but not surprising.

She said women with PMOS experienced a disturbance of their endocrine system, which meant chemical messengers (hormones) were disrupted as they tried to communicate with other parts of the body.

"That disruption affects a whole body with many different manifestations," Professor Teede said.

"Hormone levels like insulin levels are associated with diabetes and heart disease, and they're all increased in this condition."

Helena Teede has led several studies on PMOS and spearheaded the condition's recent name change from PCOS. (Supplied: Monash University)

Heart Foundation senior manager for healthcare programs and clinical strategy Natalie Raffoul, who is a registered pharmacist and did not contribute to the study, said there hadn't been many high-quality studies probing the link between PMOS and cardiovascular health to date.

"Studies like this help us to recognise the lifelong care that is required after a diagnosis of PMOS, including regular screening for things like diabetes, which are well-known to be associated with the condition as well," she said.

Does the same risk exist in Australia?

In their study, US researchers used medical claims data from 413,450 pre-menopausal women with PMOS between the age of 18 and 50, comparing the data to more than 2 million women without the condition.

Dr Alur-Gupta and Professor Dokras said after factoring in risk factors — such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol and diabetes — cardiovascular disease risk only accounted for about a third of the relationship between PMOS and arteriosclerotic cardiovascular diseases that involve thickening of the arteries such as heart attacks and strokes.

The study was observational, which meant that although it identified a link between PMOS and cardiovascular disease, it didn't prove the condition caused it.

Women with PMOS have a higher prevalence of central obesity and insulin resistance, which is associated with an increased long-term risk of high blood pressure. (Unsplash: CDC)

While the study was conducted in the US, which has different demographics to Australia, Professor Teede said she expected the results would be similar here.

Dr Alur-Gupta and Professor Dokras agreed.

"As we've shown that the higher hazard exists even outside of these traditional risk factors, [we] do think that a higher hazard would be expected even in women with PMOS in Australia," they said.

Heart health screening needed

Dr Alur-Gupta and Professor Dokras said more research was needed to understand the potential biological factors underpinning the condition which could impact cardiovascular health.

"We showed through our analyses that the higher hazards are not solely attributable to cardiovascular risk factors," they said.

"Therefore, this association should be discussed even in patients without traditional risk factors such as hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and obesity."

ABC Health in your Instagram feed Follow @abchealth on Instagram, where we're busting myths and sharing practical, smart health advice.

Professor Teede and Ms Raffoul both welcomed the idea of increased screening and education for women with PMOS.

Professor Teede said her team recently analysed global heart disease guidelines and found "virtually none" mentioned PMOS as a potential risk factor.

"We should be aware these women are at high risk," she said.

"We should make sure we're focusing on prevention [of cardiovascular disease]."

World.title: Tate brothers face court for first time since Miami arrest
World.content:
Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate will fight extradition to the United Kingdom where the brothers are accused of rape and sex trafficking, their lawyer has said.

The Tate brothers appeared in federal court on Monday, local time, for the first time since their weekend arrest and are being held in federal detention.

In the coming weeks, a US district judge will consider whether they meet the conditions for extradition.

US magistrate Lauren Louis set another hearing for July 27.

The brothers, through their social media empire promoting wealth, male dominance and misogyny, are among the world's most polarising internet personalities.

Normally photographed in tailored suits and fitted shirts, they wore tan jail uniforms and handcuffs during the brief hearing in which neither said a word.

A court sketch of the Tate brothers before judge Lauren Louis in a Miami federal court on Monday. (Lauren Lacy via AP)

Their attorney, Joseph McBride, said they should remain in the US.

"We are, of course, objecting to extradition because Andrew and Tristan are innocent," Mr McBride said after the hearing.

" They've never done nothing wrong. They shouldn't be extradited for crimes they did not commit. "

Mr McBride said the brothers were surprised when they were arrested in Miami on Saturday and that the attempt to have them extradited was politically motivated.

"There's no question about it," he told reporters.

Joseph McBride says the brothers "should not be extradited for crimes they did not commit". (AP: Marta Lavandier)

Without providing any details, Mr McBride said the Tates' case "had a lot to do with" former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer's decision to step down, and said it was no coincidence the brothers were arrested after meeting "friends in Washington, DC".

"We went to see our Congress people in DC, and now we're getting arrested. This feels political," Mr McBride said.

He did not specify who the pair met with or what was discussed.

Prosecutors in Britain said the new charges relate to four new victims and were brought after authorities received evidence from Bedfordshire Police in south-eastern England.

The allegations, spanning 2010 to 2017, include rape, assault, trafficking and offences relating to "indecent images of a child and extreme pornography".

Mr McBride said none of the latest accusers have been identified, adding: "We'd like to know who's accused Andrew and Tristan of what."

Why the Tate brothers were arrested Everything you need to know about the arrest of the Tate brothers.

The brothers are already charged with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other alleged victims in the UK between 2012 and 2015.

Their lawyer said in a statement on Saturday that he believed the arrests were "green-lighted by a low-level functionary" at the Justice Department without input from leadership.

The Justice Department told The Associated Press that the arrests were approved by leadership of its Criminal Division.

The new allegations are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the Tates that has spanned the US, Britain and Romania.

The brothers have repeatedly denied wrongdoing.

Loading...

The dual US and British citizens moved to Romania in 2016 and were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation.

They denied those allegations, and the Romanian case has not gone forward because of legal and procedural problems.

Last year, they were allowed to leave Romania and flew to Florida.

The former professional kickboxers have millions of followers on social media and are vocal supporters of US President Donald Trump.

Andrew Tate, 39, first became known a decade ago when he was a contestant on the UK reality television show Big Brother.

He was booted from the show when a video appeared to show him assaulting a woman.

He has amassed over 10 million followers on X but has been banned from other platforms, including YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, for violating hate speech guidelines.

Andrew Tate has made widely condemned comments, such as saying women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for the attacks and sharing graphic descriptions of how he might attack women.

The Tate brothers have consistently denied allegations of abuse and human trafficking, claiming their violent and misogynistic statements have been taken out of context or were intended as jokes.

AP

World.title: Live: ASX to follow Wall Street lower, oil prices higher after Houthis threaten Saudi blockade
World.content:
Good morning, and welcome to the ABC's finance blog! I'll be guiding you through the latest market action for the next few hours.

It looks like the local share market will start its day modestly lower. ASX futures, which are a rough indicator of how the market may open, have risen by about 0.4%.

The Australian dollar has risen slightly to 69.96 US cents.

Houthi threat keeping oil prices high

On oil markets, Brent crude futures settled 0.9% higher at $US88.88 per barrel.

Mediators have passed Iran a proposal to de-escalate the war with the US that would offer a 10-day ceasefire to find ways to revive an interim deal reached last month. That's according to Reuters, quoting an unnamed senior Iranian official.

While traders are hoping there will be renewed US-Iran negotiations at some stage, there has been a new complication which could drive oil prices even higher.

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they were imposing a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, opening a new front in the US-Israeli war on Iran and widening the threat to global energy supplies and trade beyond the Gulf.

US markets continue to fall

The Middle East tensions also weighed on Wall Street's three major indexes, which finished trading lower this morning.

The technology-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell less than the S & P 500 and the Dow Jones as the chip sector recovered some of the prior week's losses.

The Dow fell 0.6% to 51,839 points, the S & P 500 lost 0.2% to 7,443 points and the Nasdaq slipped by less than 0.1% to 25,508 points.

Investors are also awaiting the release of profit results from America's tech giants later this week — and expectations are incredibly high.

Google's parent company, Alphabet, Tesla and Intel are some of the companies that will be reporting their June-quarter results in the next few days.

Anyway, please grab a coffee, tea or whatever you normally have in the morning, and I'll have more updates for you shortly!



- with reporting by Reuters

World.title: Whistleblower's fight to unmask one of WA's worst child abusers
World.content:
As one of Western Australia's most monstrous serial paedophiles approaches the end of his prison term, the whistleblower who helped bring his crimes to light is publishing her account of the story.

WARNING - This story contains descriptions of sexual abuse and self-harm that some readers may find distressing.

Dennis John McKenna abused 28 boys over the course of two decades while serving as warden of the St Andrew's Hostel in Katanning, 287 kilometres south-east of Perth in WA's Great Southern.

Made aware of the abuse shortly after arriving in town in 1985, Maggie Dawkins reported McKenna's horrific crimes to local police, a local councillor and state government authorities.

No-one listened, and she was run out of town.

The abuse continued for years as a result.

While the demolition of the site in 2024 wiped the location of McKenna's crimes from the map, Mrs Dawkins's account, entitled To Be Believed — A West Australian Scandal, captures the harrowing story of those who survived his abuses, and the serious failings of WA authorities to stop him.

The Katanning Residential College was bulldozed in 2025. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

Trusted with harrowing story

Mrs Dawkins became aware of the first of many of those stories shortly after arriving in Katanning in 1985, working for a government-backed youth employment and support program.

She said one boy approached her, trusting her with his and his friends' stories in the hope of halting the abuse.

"I'd never heard the word rapist. I didn't know what it was," she said.

Maggie Dawkins played a vital role in exposing Dennis McKenna. (ABC News: Shannon Pearce)

"This young man, who was clearly distressed and embarrassed and all those dreadful feelings of shame, was trying to explain to me that this was going on at the hostel on a regular basis.

"I didn't know how to cope with this."

But reports to her line manager, local police and a local councillor fell on deaf ears.

Local figures berated her for "besmirching" McKenna, who had recently been named Katanning's Citizen of the Year.

Confronting the abuser

Mrs Dawkins took matters into her own hands and confronted McKenna herself.

She said she approached him and he told her he had "friends in high places".

" As he was throwing me out of town, he told me he had friends in high places. He held all the cards. "

It was not until years later, when the Blaxell inquiry investigated abuse at the hostel, that Mrs Dawkins realised just how many people knew of the abuse and did nothing.

"It just made me sick. It was incredibly soul-destroying," she said.

"The kids and parents of the kids who attended the hostel never had a chance."

Years waiting for justice

Mrs Dawkins then spent the next five years trying to unmask the ongoing abuse inside the walls of St Andrew's, which was later rebadged as the Katanning Residential College.

McKenna used the hostel as a base to sexually abuse school-aged boys. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

In 1990, five years after she raised the alarm, Operation Paradox, a national police effort to raise awareness of child sex abuse and encourage victim survivors to come forward, resulted in multiple complaints against McKenna.

He was arrested soon after, and eventually found guilty of 19 offences.

Since then, McKenna has been charged with a further 44 offences for the abuse of 28 boys, and remains locked up at Acacia Prison in Wooroloo east of Perth.

McKenna is due to complete his prison sentence later this year. (ABC News)

Why come forward

Both Mrs Dawkins's brave fight and her account have been lauded by those who survived McKenna's abuse.

After a football game in August 1990, McKenna sexually abused Todd Jefferis.

The unvarnished story of the abuse and grooming he suffered features throughout the book.

St Andrew's Hostel survivor Todd Jefferis spearheaded the campaign to demolish the building. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Mr Jefferis said Mrs Dawkins's work provides a platform for other whistleblowers to speak out about abuse.

"It certainly tells the truth about what really went on and how far-reaching it was," he said.

" If you've been abused or are being abused, the ability to go and speak out and have someone believe you is incredibly important. "

McKenna's evil left a deep scar on Kaye Anderson's family.

Her eldest sons, Ray and Quenton, were targeted and sexually abused by McKenna in 1985.

Ray, Quenton, Bevan, Nathan and Damian Anderson. (Supplied: Kaye Anderson)

Mrs Anderson also lost sons Nathan and Damien, in what she believes to be a direct result of their older brothers' deaths.

She said Mrs Dawkins revealed more of the story than she ever understood.

"I absolutely applaud her for standing up to an absolute mongrel bastard," she said.

"I just pray to God that it will [encourage more people to come forward]."

Listen to Maggie Dawkins's interview with Nadia Mitsopoulos on 102.5 ABC Perth and on local radio across WA from 9am today.

World.title: The big surprise on Andy Burnham’s first day as UK PM? Trump wants to help him
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeUK politics The big surprise on Andy Burnham’s first day as UK PM? Trump wants to help him David Crowe Updated July 21, 2026 — 9:25am ,first published 7:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has vowed to “bring back hope” to the country after being elevated to the leadership in a meeting with King Charles, declaring that the public deserves better from a new generation of politicians. Britain’s new leader embarked on a cabinet reshuffle within hours of his appointment, while also speaking with Donald Trump and emerging from the call with an offer of help from the US president after months of tension between the key allies. Andy Burnham gives his first speech as prime minister outside 10 Downing Street. Getty Images Burnham promised to deliver help with the cost of living within his first 24 hours in the job, as he arrived at his official residence at 10 Downing Street to deliver his first remarks as prime minister in front of hundreds of reporters. “We have not been good enough, and we need to be better. We will be,” he said.



The formal transfer of power concluded after the previous prime minister, Keir Starmer, visited King Charles at Buckingham Palace for a private meeting in which he officially resigned. That meeting cleared the way for Burnham to visit the King soon afterwards and be invited to form government, elevating him to the top post. King Charles welcomes Burnham to Buckingham Palace, where he was invited to form government. Getty Images In a brief statement, the King confirmed that Burnham accepted the invitation and “kissed hands upon his appointment” – the traditional language used to describe a prime minister accepting the monarch’s invitation to lead government. Trump revealed the two leaders had a “good” conversation on topics including the “outstanding” relationship between the US and UK – a message that contrasted with his harsh criticism of Starmer for not supporting the war against Iran.



“The Prime Minister has got a big job ahead of him, but he will be able to do it and, of course, the U.S.A. will be there to help!” Trump posted. “We discussed North Sea Oil, Trade, the Military Alliance, Demining of the Hormuz Strait, and many other topics. The call was interesting, and went very well. I wished Prime Minister Burnham, GOOD LUCK AND GODSPEED!” Charles and Burnham. Getty Images Trump also said he and Burnham would meet in the “not too distant future”, but did not say more. One possible meeting point is the G20 leaders’ summit due to be held in Miami in December. Speaking outside Downing Street after the palace meeting, without notes or a lectern, Burnham said he was “acutely” conscious he was the seventh prime minister since 2016.



“It requires my generation of politicians to raise our game and rise to the new challenge,” he said. “Britain needs to show the world that we can regain our stability once again, and that is our challenge: to make politics work, to make it work better.” Burnham and his wife, Marie-France van Heel, wave as they enter 10 Downing Street. AP Photo/Thomas Krych The couple is greeted inside the official residence by top political staff and other advisers. Getty Images Burnham spoke directly to the main television camera to give a personal assurance to the British people that he would do better than previous prime ministers.



“I know people at home are fed up with politics. I hear you,” he said, promising to deliver a “circuit breaker” for a system he said had taken wrong turns since the 1980s. Burnham vowed to decentralise power from London, reindustrialise the economy, end rough sleeping, ensure stronger public control of key industries, build more homes and improve mental health support. Loading He said he would outline help with the cost of living, in a funded government policy, within his first 24 hours. “It’s about putting the right values and the right standards at the heart of government,” he said.



“I will put the care of people at the heart of everything I do. I will give this my all, and I ask you all to pull with me. “Let’s build a new national sense of unity, of common purpose, and positivity. Let us make this the moment when Britain starts to believe again – the moment we bring back hope.” Burnham said his generation of politicians needed to “raise our game”. Bloomberg Upon those words, he entered 10 Downing Street with his wife, Marie-France van Heel, to be greeted by top political staff and other advisers. Earlier, Starmer had left the official residence to give his final address as prime minister in front of dozens of ministerial colleagues, staff and family members including his wife, Victoria.



“My work is done. In 6½ years, I took our party from a historic defeat in 2019, changed it so it was fit to face the country, and won a landslide general election victory in 2024,” he said. “Since then, it has been the privilege of my life to serve you and this great country as prime minister, and I am confident that Britain is now stronger and fairer than it was two years ago.” Keir Starmer receives applause as he leaves No. 10 Downing Street. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth Starmer and his wife, Victoria, depart Downing Street. Getty Images Starmer said Burnham had his “full support”.



“As I now pass the baton to Andy Burnham, I wish him every success,” he said. “I go with good grace, I go with a smile, and I go proud of everything that we have achieved.” King Charles welcomes Starmer to Buckingham Palace, where he officially resigned as PM. Getty Images Sir Clive Alderton, left, principal private secretary to the King and Queen, and King Charles III’s Equerry, Major Ben Rigby, right, greet Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel at Buckingham Palace. Aaron Chown/Pool PA via AP The meetings at Buckingham Palace formally concluded a long fight within the Labour Party to replace Starmer after growing discontent over his leadership, and a year of planning by Burnham and his allies to take power within the party.



In being named to the top post on Monday, Burnham became the nation’s seventh prime minister since 2016. Related Article Updated

UK politics ‘Number 10 North’: PM-in-waiting vows major power shift out of London In a surprise move that appeared to be aimed at calming financial markets, Burnham named former defence secretary John Healey as the Chancellor of the Exchequer. Healey quit the previous government a few weeks ago over funding plans for his department. Ed Miliband was promoted from energy secretary to foreign secretary. He replaces Yvette Cooper, who was appointed health secretary. Shabana Mahmood remains home secretary. Wes Streeting becomes defence secretary. Burnham also restored former Labour deputy leader Angela Rayner to cabinet as housing minister, after she stepped down last year.



Labour has 403 seats in the House of Commons, giving it a comfortable majority. The Conservative Party has 117 seats, the Liberal Democrats have 71, Reform UK has seven and the Greens have five. Small parties and independents make up the rest. Related Article UK politics Four things to know about Andy Burnham, the man likely to be the UK’s next PM But the divisions within the Labour parliamentary party have weakened the government, while Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has made big gains in local government elections and has soared in the public opinion polls as a potential prime minister. Burnham’s rise began in earnest on May 19 when he overcame resistance from Starmer’s allies and gained party approval to run as the Labour candidate at a byelection for the seat of Makerfield, which he won on June 19. Starmer announced on June 22 that he would resign. With Labour MPs making it clear they wanted a new leader, Starmer set up an internal party timeline to decide his replacement. When party officials called for nominations, Burnham was the sole candidate – an extraordinary development given he had become a member of the House of Commons only days earlier.



While Burnham is the seventh prime minister in roughly a decade, he is also being described as the sixth prime minister in 10 years. Former Conservative prime minister David Cameron stepped down on July 13, 2016 – 10 years and one week ago. He was followed by Theresa May, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak from the Conservative Party. They were followed by Starmer and Burnham. World.title: Two million adoring fans greet Spain’s returning World Cup champions
World.content:
SportSoccerFIFA World Cup Two million adoring fans greet Spain’s returning World Cup champions Suman Naishadham and Tales Azzoni July 21, 2026 — 9:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Madrid: Spain’s World Cup-winning soccer team returned home on Monday, and an estimated crowd of almost 2 million was on hand to celebrate the squad through the streets of Madrid. The 26 players and their coaching staff met with the country’s royals, and then with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, after arriving in the Spanish capital a day after beating Argentina 1-0 in the final in New Jersey. Loading “Thank you to the coaches and players for the style of play, the effort and the victory,” Sánchez said. “We have truly enjoyed watching you play.” The squad then boarded an open-top bus for a raucous parade through central Madrid. “Stars shine together” was written on the bus, which also carried photos of the footballers.



Players – carrying the World Cup trophy and wearing shirts with the words Somos Campeones (We Are Champions) – danced and interacted with the fans along the route. “It’s been an emotional and proud experience to represent a wonderful country with such passionate and devoted fans,” Spain’s coach Luis de la Fuente said before the parade started. “We are filled with joy.” Spain captain Rodri sits atop the bus carrying the winning World Cup players through the streets of Madrid. Getty Images The squad travelled down Madrid’s historic avenues from near Moncloa Palace, the prime minister’s official residence, to Cibeles Square, where authorities told local media that some 120,000 people were on hand for a ceremony. Players were introduced one by one before entering the stage set up at the square. Each picked the song to be played when they came in. Álex Baena, celebrating his 25th birthday, entered with the World Cup trophy.



Coach De la Fuente was thrusted into the air by his players after being introduced. The coach was among those who sang along to the song being played for them. The ceremony ended with the whole Spain squad lifting the trophy again, just like at the awards ceremony on Sunday, but now in front of the local crowd. Some of the estimated two millions fans who gathered for the World Cup parade on Monday (Madrid time). Getty Images Groups of fans had begun securing their spots near Cibeles late Monday morning ahead of the team’s arrival, bringing umbrellas to protect against the sun and temperatures of up to 35 degrees. The square is where previous Spain teams and their supporters have typically gathered to celebrate. It’s also the traditional celebration spot for Real Madrid when it wins titles.



Officials estimated a total of 1.8 million people welcomed the team in Madrid. Spain walked off with the trophy on Sunday (Monday AEST) after Ferran Torres scored the winner in extra time to secure its second World Cup title — and first since 2010 in South Africa. Martin Zubimendi and Spanish teammates soak in the adoration of fans in Madrid. Getty Images The team was congratulated by the leaders of the three countries that co-hosted the tournament — US President Donald Trump, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. After the final whistle, Madrid erupted into celebrations, with thousands of supporters pouring into the streets from bars and restaurants, many draped in Spanish flags or wearing the team’s colours.



Crowds packed the capital’s Puerta de Sol and other major squares — singing, dancing and setting off flares while car horns blared. Many celebrated Sunday’s victory long into the wee hours of Monday morning. Lamine Yamal was a popular member of the Spanish team that won the World Cup. Getty Images “I’m very happy. I’ve slept three or four hours, but for the team, I’ll do whatever it takes,” 19-year-old Victor Álvarez said. The men’s victory, combined with the Women’s World Cup won by Spain in 2023, makes the European nation the first to hold both titles simultaneously.



“Honestly, it was very exciting. We preferred not to go to any bar or anything, to experience it at home, focused and very happy, very joyful,” 59-year-old civil servant Gema Rodero said. Related Article Analysis

FIFA World Cup Rodri touched the heavens, descended into hell, then won the Golden Ball Celebrations were dampened, however, after local authorities reported that a 13-year-old in Salamanca, northwest of Madrid, had died after a fountain he had climbed onto with friends to mark the victory had collapsed. For many young supporters, the triumph is their first time witnessing the men’s team lift the trophy – and the national delirium that has followed. Spain is markedly different from 2010, when the Iberian nation was beset by a debt crisis, 20 per cent unemployment and nationalist regions fighting to win more autonomy.



The economy is expanding, the unemployment rate has halved, and the country is forecast to again be among the Eurozone’s fastest-growing major economies. Nationalist and separatist tensions have considerably cooled. AP

World.title: US launches new strikes after Iran-backed Houthis declare blockade of another key oil route
World.content:
Updated WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war US launches new strikes after Iran-backed Houthis declare blockade of another key oil route Nayera Abdallah , Eman Abouhassira and Timour Azhari Updated July 21, 2026 — 8:49am ,first published 5:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dubai/Riyadh: Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said they would impose a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, opening a potential new front against the US in its war with Iran and raising the threat to global energy supplies and trade beyond the Gulf. The Houthis made their announcement despite signs that Tehran and Washington want to resume diplomacy to halt a worsening cycle of attacks that has all but wrecked a fragile interim agreement signed last month. An image released by US Central Command shows service members aboard the amphibious assault ship USS Boxer supporting flight operations from the Arabian Sea. CENTCOM Iran’s Foreign Ministry said mediators had presented “proposals” to Tehran, signalling that diplomatic contacts remain active, but gave no details. Oil prices rose briefly after the Houthi statement, but later fell back as traders held out hope of a diplomatic breakthrough. The insurance cost of shipping goods through the Red Sea rose on the increased risks for merchant shipping.



Even so, the US President Donald Trump ordered a new round of strikes against Iran – the 10th consecutive night of attacks – that started about 6am on Tuesday (AEST). “The strikes are designed to further degrade Iranian military capabilities used to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz,” US Central Command said in a statement. Shortly after, Iranian state television said an explosion had been heard in the coastal cities of Bandar Abbas, Chabahar and Konarak. Air defence systems were also activated near Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant, Mehr reported. About 8am on Tuesday (AEST), the Iranian army said it had targeted US missile systems at Kuwait’s Arifjan base with surface-to-surface missiles, Iranian state TV reported. Earlier, Kuwait’s state news agency reported sirens were sounding.



Meanwhile, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre said it had received multiple reports that a tanker had been struck by unknown projectile in Strait of Hormuz, near Limah in Oman. Iran had been pressing the Houthis to close the Bab el-Mandeb gateway to the Red Sea if the US continued to attack Iranian power infrastructure. The full closure of the Bab el-Mandeb strait would reduce global oil supply by 7 per cent as it would leave most of Saudi oil exports unable to leave the region. The disruption would add to the huge cut to oil flows from the war in the Gulf, which has already reduced shipments by 10 per cent of global supply. In their statement, the Houthis’ armed forces said they were declaring “a maritime embargo against the criminal Saudi enemy, based on the equation of ‘an eye for an eye’, effective immediately” in response to what they called “an unjust and oppressive siege” imposed on Yemen by the Saudis.



Saudi Arabia on Tuesday (AEST) condemned the Houthi naval blockade announcement and their statements accusing Riyadh of “besieging” the Yemeni people. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said it would respond to Houthis threats to ships with “force” and began to implement safety measures for its ships passing through Bab el-Mandeb Strait. “Such threats are a blatant violation of international law and falls under acts of maritime piracy,” the coalition said US President Donald Trump exits Air Force One on Sunday. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin “The question now is whether [the Houthis] will begin targeting vessels heading to Saudi ports. At this stage, there’s no clear answer,” said Mohammed Albasha, a Yemeni analyst and founder of Basha Report, a Washington-based risk advisory firm. “Even if no ships are attacked, the announcement alone is likely to disrupt shipping and create uncertainty for Saudi ports. Whether the Houthis move from threats to direct action remains the critical issue.” The group fired missiles at Saudi ​Arabia last week after accusing the kingdom of bombing an airport under their control, piercing a four-year truce in the conflict between ‌the kingdom and the Iran-aligned group



Meanwhile, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Monday (Iran time) that Tehran had received a proposal from mediators for a 10-day ceasefire in efforts to salvage the interim deal, intended to pave the way to a lasting agreement to end the war that began on February 28 with US-Israeli attacks on Iran. Neither the ministry nor the official who spoke to Reuters gave any details on the putative ceasefire discussions. Two Pakistani government sources said separately that Iranian Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni had asked Pakistan to resume its mediation role in the conflict. He later arrived in Islamabad for further talks. In this photo released by the Pakistan’s Interior Ministry, Iran’s Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni, left, meets with his Pakistani counterpart Mohsin Naqvi, right, in Rawalpindi, Pakistan, on Monday. Pakistan’s Interior Ministry via AP The diplomatic push followed another night of US strikes on Iranian cities and attacks by Iran’s Revolutionary Guards on US military assets across the region. Trump, under mounting political pressure at home over rising petrol prices since the war began and Iran effectively closed the vital Strait of Hormuz, defended the recent strikes on Iran as honouring the deaths of up to three American service members in recent Iranian attacks.



Two US Army soldiers killed in Iranian attacks on Jordan were identified on Monday as First Lieutenant James Feehan, 25, of Ewa Beach, Hawaii, and Private Isabella Gonzales, 19, of Carrollton, Texas, were killed in Jordan in Friday’s attacks. Official also said this week that they had found unidentified remains that could be those of a third soldier reported as missing in the Jordan attacks An American service member was also killed in northern Iraq on Saturday during a “controlled detonation” of unexploded ordnance from a downed Iranian drone. First Lieutenant Tyler James Feehan and Private Isabella Gonzales were killed by an Iranian attack in Jordan. US Army Space and Missile Defence Command via AP “Every time Iran kills an American Soldier they will pay for that killing many times over! This directive has been passed on to Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Daniel Caine, and every Leader in the Military,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday. The Pentagon on Monday (US time) revealed that nearly 100 US troops had been injured in the war over the past two weeks. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a post on X that most of the injuries were minor concussions and “96 per cent” had since returned to duty.



The war has killed thousands of people, mostly in Iran and Lebanon, part of which has been occupied by Israeli forces following attacks on Israel by Hezbollah fighters who said they were acting in solidarity with Tehran. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun is due to meet Trump at the White House on Tuesday to present a plan on how to disarm Iran-aligned Hezbollah and secure an Israeli withdrawal. Israel also still has forces in Gaza following two years of war ignited by the Palestinian militant group Hamas’ attack on southern Israeli communities on October 7, 2023. Hamas said on Monday it had named top negotiator Khalil Al-Hayya as its overall leader, a move that an analyst said could signal a tougher stance by the group towards calls for it to disarm. Loading US Central Command said its ninth consecutive night of strikes against Iran aimed at weakening its ability to attack commercial vessels in the strait. The US military also said it redirected seven commercial vessels and disabled one as part of a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

World.title: Surgeon banned for six months after patient death, botched colonoscopies
World.content:
NationalDoctors at work Surgeon banned for six months after patient death, botched colonoscopies Kate Aubusson July 21, 2026 — 8:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A surgeon has been found guilty of professional misconduct over her treatment of 13 patients, including a man who died after she operated on the wrong end of his colon, and a woman whose bowel cancer tumour she missed during a rushed colonoscopy. Dr Liu-Ming Schmidt had her medical registration suspended for six months by the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal, which found that the surgeon had spent as little as five minutes performing colonoscopies on patients at Albury Wodonga Health on the NSW and Victorian border. Dr Liu-Ming Schmidt had her medical registration suspended for six months. Schmidt was the subject of a 2023 investigation that found a series of incomplete colonoscopies performed or supervised by the surgeon between 2018 and 2022. The investigation led to recall of roughly 2000 of Schmidt’s colonoscopy patients, and 1084 underwent repeat colonoscopies. Seven patients were diagnosed with colorectal cancer.



The tribunal’s decision, published on Friday, included details of what one doctor providing evidence called Schmidt’s “catastrophic error” during a surgery in November 2019, which contributed to the death of her 79-year-old patient. Related Article Health Colonoscopy ‘recall’: Almost 2000 Albury-Wodonga patients at risk, watchdog says Schmidt was on call when the man arrived at the hospital with a life-threatening bowel perforation. During an emergency surgery, Schmidt brought out the wrong end of the man’s bowel to attach to a colostomy bag, causing a complete mechanical bowel obstruction. “But most egregious, in our opinion, is Dr Schmidt’s failure to then closely monitor the patient after the operation,” the tribunal’s decision read. Schmidt admitted she did not see the patient for several days despite knowing he was acutely unwell, and she was working in the same hospital. When she was then alerted to her error, she failed to adequately disclose it to the patient and his family.



Another complaint in the case brought by the Health Care Complaints Commission (HCCC) concerned a woman known as Patient A, who first saw Schmidt in 2017 after a positive bowel screening result, suffering abdominal pain and a change in bowel habits. Schmidt performed four colonoscopies on Patient A between November 2017 and January 2022. The woman was referred back in January 2022 with iron deficiency anaemia and abdominal bloating – potential symptoms of bowel cancer. On February 14, Schmidt performed a gastroscopy and colonoscopy. About three months later, Patient A was admitted to hospital with severe iron deficiency anaemia, and a PET scan identified an abnormal mass in her caecum – the pouch-like beginning of the large intestine and the furthest point reached by a colonoscope. Another surgeon performed a colonoscopy on Patient A and identified a 5.5-centimetre adenocarcinoma. “This type of cancer could not have grown to this size in only three months,” the tribunal’s decision read.



The tribunal agreed with an expert witness that Schmidt failed to detect the tumour during her February colonoscopy, which was performed too quickly. Her records did not show that her colonoscopy had reached the caecum. Related Article Exclusive

Cancer The medical procedure some patients are having too often and others aren’t having enough Schmidt admitted to all the matters in the complaint, which included failing to take an adequate amount of time to perform colonoscopies for eight patients and adequately capture images during the procedures. The time it took Schmidt to perform seven of these colonoscopies ranged from 10 to just five minutes. She spent 16 minutes performing both a colonoscopy and gastroscopy on one patient. Colonoscopy withdrawal alone should usually take about eight minutes. All but one of these patients came from a random sample selected by Albury Wodonga Health who underwent colonoscopies performed by Schmidt.



The HCCC’s medical expert told the tribunal that rapid withdrawal during colonoscopy would lead to lesions being missed. The expert also raised concerns that Schmidt’s poor or infrequent imaging of the caecum during several procedures suggested that her colonoscope had not reached this section of the bowel – a requirement for a complete colonoscopy. “We find that Dr Schmidt’s conduct was of a very serious nature and demonstrated a significant departure from accepted standards,” the tribunal’s decision read. “It is sufficiently serious to justify suspension or cancellation of her registration.” The HCCC had sought to have Schmidt’s registration suspended for one year, but the Tribunal opted for a six-month cancellation, noting she had diligently tried to address the areas of concern that led to the complaints. “[H]er success in doing so is illustrated by the support of many colleagues, several of whom have observed her in the operating theatre,” the decision read. Following the January 2023 investigation, Schmidt stopped practising for one year. She then returned to practice with conditions, including limiting her surgical procedures, eventually completing a colonoscopy recertification program and only undertaking colonoscopies under supervision. World.title: ‘Baked bean cans’: Emirates boss to reject Boeing planes
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation ‘Baked bean cans’: Emirates boss to reject Boeing planes Christopher Jasper July 21, 2026 — 8:04am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Boeing has been dealt a fresh blow after Emirates said it would refuse to take delivery of 10 aircraft, claiming that the much-delayed jets would be better off being turned into baked bean tins. The Dubai airline has ordered a total of 270 new 777X planes from Boeing at $US440 million ($629 million) apiece, with the first jet built in 2019. But repeated delays stemming from design modifications has meant Emirates is still waiting for the planes seven years later. Emirates president Sir Tim Clark said the company was unwilling to take the 10 aircraft because the design of the 777X had undergone so many significant changes that bringing them up to the latest standard would not be feasible. Bloomberg Sir Tim Clark, the president of Emirates, said the initial batch of 10 of the jets required such a patchwork of changes to update them that they were not fit for purpose. “We’re not taking that batch and that’s it,” he told The Telegraph at the Farnborough International Airshow. “As far as we’re concerned, what they do with them is up to them.”



Clark said he understood that Boeing had been trying to find a home for the aircraft, before adding: “Heinz would be interested – baked bean cans.” Related Article Exclusive

Aviation Some A380s grounded amid emergency inspections for wing spar cracks His refusal to take the planes will serve as a new setback to Boeing, which has been rocked by a string of safety crises in recent years. Clark said Emirates was unwilling to take the 10 aircraft because the design of the 777X had undergone so many significant changes that bringing them up to the latest standard would not be feasible. The 777X has suffered numerous problems that have pushed back entry into service from 2020 to next year at the earliest.



Those issues have included a thrust control issue that halted test flights in 2024 and an incident in 2020 that saw an aircraft’s nose pitch up without pilot input, delaying the programme by years. Clark said the airline was also concerned by the earlier-than-expected structural failure of a 777X during a ground-based stress test of the airframe. Emirates’ refusal to take the planes will serve as a new setback to Boeing, which has been rocked by a string of safety crises in recent years. AP He added: “The modifications for the airframe have been so significant since the early flights. And don’t forget we had a static-test failure as well.” He added: “I went on the first one in 2019, which was fully configured except for our first-class cabins, and here we are in 2026. It’s now seven years on. We’re not taking them.”



His comments came after it emerged one of the planes earmarked for Emirates had already been scrapped. The 400-seat plane was quietly “disassembled” in 2025 after sitting dormant for six years on an airfield close to Boeing’s Seattle manufacturing centre, The Air Current reported. Stephanie Pope, the head of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, said changes were made to the aircraft “as the maturity of the design progresses”. She said: “If you look at those early airplanes, you’ve then got to weigh how much change it’s going to take and the benefit from that. “We are always looking at how much that change is going to cost and what will be the capability of the airplane, and making sure we’re getting the right solution not only for Boeing, but for our customer.”



Related Article Billionaires Bezos’ whirlwind visit: How do the rich and famous get to the beach so fast? Flight tests on the 777-9, the first version of the new 777X plane, should be completed by the end of this year, after which the model will need to show it is capable of flying for long distances over water on a single engine, according to analysts at Jefferies. That should pave the way for the first aircraft to be delivered to Lufthansa before the end of 2027. Asked when British Airways expected to receive the first of 24 planes it has on order, Sean Doyle, its chief executive, said simply: “Good question.” Telegraph, London The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: Officials got three of seven calls wrong at the weekend. Apart from that, the NRL was happy
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Officials got three of seven calls wrong at the weekend. Apart from that, the NRL was happy Christian Nicolussi Updated July 21, 2026 — 7:54am ,first published 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sydney Roosters forward Nat Butcher should not have been penalised for a high tackle, Melbourne were denied a legitimate try, and Manly’s Reuben Garrick was offside when he scored against the Titans. Aside from those three clangers, the NRL was more than satisfied with a string of other controversial calls made by referees and the bunker over the weekend. Loading This masthead pinpointed at least seven contentious calls in five games that were heavily criticised by coaches, players and commentators. They did not include queries St George Illawarra had with Valentine Holmes being penalised for an obstruction and Setu Tu being denied a try by a bunker ruling.



We revealed the bunker’s decision-making efficiency rate sat at an impressive 98 per cent just a month ago. But fans have been in the dark about the reasoning behind refereeing calls since the NRL scrapped head of football Graham Annesley’s weekly press conference a couple of years ago. In the hope of achieving some clarity, we asked the NRL for its thoughts about the weekend calls. Were Penrith robbed? The Panthers thought they had won a repeat set – and a chance to win the game – with two minutes of Thursday night’s match left after Brisbane’s Josiah Karapani was dragged into touch. Referee Todd Smith ruled a knock-on, which Penrith successfully challenged – but the bunker ruled Smith had blown the whistle before Karapani was taken into touch. Because it was a “mutual infringement”, Karapani was instructed to play the ball, rather than Penrith receive the ball back.



Penrith coach Ivan Cleary said after the game: “If we get the ball there, and we should have got it ... it’s just one of those nights”. The NRL, however, formed the view the decision was technically correct because the whistle was blown simultaneously as Karapani was being pushed into touch. If anything, Penrith could have been penalised for the second effort. Roosters Butchered Coaches Trent Robinson and Craig Bellamy both took issue with a few calls during Friday night’s Storm-Roosters clash.



Robinson was stunned Butcher was penalised for a high tackle on Alec MacDonald, which allowed Melbourne to march downfield and score two minutes later. Nat Butcher’s ‘hit’ on Alec Macdonald. Nine “It was completely laughable,” Robinson said of the penalty. The NRL agreed it should not have been given. Did Warbrick knock on? Bellamy could not understand why the Storm were denied a try in the first half, when Will Warbrick appeared to knock a ball back from a kick, only for Gerard Sutton to rule it a knock-on.



Bellamy broke into one of his famous colourful rants in the coach’s box. After several slow-motion reviews, the NRL were satisfied Warbrick got his hand in front of the ball and knocked it back. Walker shot clock Roosters halfback Sam Walker appeared to have taken a dropout after the shot-clock buzzer sounded in the 67th minute, which would have given Melbourne a penalty kick from in front to level the scores.



Loading “Six to eight weeks ago, we got done for taking too long with a line drop-out,” Bellamy said. But the NRL was satisfied the Walker kick and shot-clock buzzer were simultaneous, so Sutton was entitled to wave play-on. Similar situations occur on occasions with scrum-clocks. Was Dom Young taken out? Cronulla opened their account against the Knights with a try to Will Kennedy on Friday evening, but Ronnie Mulitalo appeared to deny Newcastle winger Dominic Young a fair chance at leaping for the ball.



Braydon Trindall sent the ball up, Mulitalo chased, but barely got off the ground – yet still did enough to impede Young. The NRL was comfortable Mulitalo had not taken his eyes off the ball, never looked at Young and had both arms extended in a catching position before he jumped, which meant there was a genuine contest, and no need to rule a “disruptor” penalty. Red V see red The Dragons have worked hard to address their sluggish second-half starts, so you could forgive them for being cranky when the Warriors went ahead in the 44th minute via Dallin Watene-Zelezniak from what they felt was a forward pass.



“It’s just not right,” co-captain Damien Cook said. “I feel sorry for the fans that have to watch that. But it’s happened too many times to us.” The NRL was comfortable it was not a forward pass, and other camera angles not shown on the live broadcast supported this view. Did Garrick jump the gun? Titans skipper Tino Fa’asuamaleaui made a beeline for referee Adam Gee after Reuben Garrick scored for Manly in the second half, wanting to know if the Manly centre was offside.



“It happened to Max Plath in Origin, that was the call; are you serious?” Fa’asuamaleaui asked Gee, referring to the Maroons being denied a try in similar circumstances in Origin III only a few weeks earlier. The decision did not cost the Gold Coast the win – and just as well, because the NRL, based on the available footage, believed Garrick was “marginally offside”.
