World.title: Officials got three of seven calls wrong at the weekend. Apart from that, the NRL was happy
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Officials got three of seven calls wrong at the weekend. Apart from that, the NRL was happy Christian Nicolussi Updated July 21, 2026 — 7:54am ,first published 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sydney Roosters forward Nat Butcher should not have been penalised for a high tackle, Melbourne were denied a legitimate try, and Manly’s Reuben Garrick was offside when he scored against the Titans. Aside from those three clangers, the NRL was more than satisfied with a string of other controversial calls made by referees and the bunker over the weekend. Loading This masthead pinpointed at least seven contentious calls in five games that were heavily criticised by coaches, players and commentators. They did not include queries St George Illawarra had with Valentine Holmes being penalised for an obstruction and Setu Tu being denied a try by a bunker ruling.



We revealed the bunker’s decision-making efficiency rate sat at an impressive 98 per cent just a month ago. But fans have been in the dark about the reasoning behind refereeing calls since the NRL scrapped head of football Graham Annesley’s weekly press conference a couple of years ago. In the hope of achieving some clarity, we asked the NRL for its thoughts about the weekend calls. Were Penrith robbed? The Panthers thought they had won a repeat set – and a chance to win the game – with two minutes of Thursday night’s match left after Brisbane’s Josiah Karapani was dragged into touch. Referee Todd Smith ruled a knock-on, which Penrith successfully challenged – but the bunker ruled Smith had blown the whistle before Karapani was taken into touch. Because it was a “mutual infringement”, Karapani was instructed to play the ball, rather than Penrith receive the ball back.



Penrith coach Ivan Cleary said after the game: “If we get the ball there, and we should have got it ... it’s just one of those nights”. The NRL, however, formed the view the decision was technically correct because the whistle was blown simultaneously as Karapani was being pushed into touch. If anything, Penrith could have been penalised for the second effort. Roosters Butchered Coaches Trent Robinson and Craig Bellamy both took issue with a few calls during Friday night’s Storm-Roosters clash.



Robinson was stunned Butcher was penalised for a high tackle on Alec MacDonald, which allowed Melbourne to march downfield and score two minutes later. Nat Butcher’s ‘hit’ on Alec Macdonald. Nine “It was completely laughable,” Robinson said of the penalty. The NRL agreed it should not have been given. Did Warbrick knock on? Bellamy could not understand why the Storm were denied a try in the first half, when Will Warbrick appeared to knock a ball back from a kick, only for Gerard Sutton to rule it a knock-on.



Bellamy broke into one of his famous colourful rants in the coach’s box. After several slow-motion reviews, the NRL were satisfied Warbrick got his hand in front of the ball and knocked it back. Walker shot clock Roosters halfback Sam Walker appeared to have taken a dropout after the shot-clock buzzer sounded in the 67th minute, which would have given Melbourne a penalty kick from in front to level the scores.



Loading “Six to eight weeks ago, we got done for taking too long with a line drop-out,” Bellamy said. But the NRL was satisfied the Walker kick and shot-clock buzzer were simultaneous, so Sutton was entitled to wave play-on. Similar situations occur on occasions with scrum-clocks. Was Dom Young taken out? Cronulla opened their account against the Knights with a try to Will Kennedy on Friday evening, but Ronnie Mulitalo appeared to deny Newcastle winger Dominic Young a fair chance at leaping for the ball.



Braydon Trindall sent the ball up, Mulitalo chased, but barely got off the ground – yet still did enough to impede Young. The NRL was comfortable Mulitalo had not taken his eyes off the ball, never looked at Young and had both arms extended in a catching position before he jumped, which meant there was a genuine contest, and no need to rule a “disruptor” penalty. Red V see red The Dragons have worked hard to address their sluggish second-half starts, so you could forgive them for being cranky when the Warriors went ahead in the 44th minute via Dallin Watene-Zelezniak from what they felt was a forward pass.



“It’s just not right,” co-captain Damien Cook said. “I feel sorry for the fans that have to watch that. But it’s happened too many times to us.” The NRL was comfortable it was not a forward pass, and other camera angles not shown on the live broadcast supported this view. Did Garrick jump the gun? Titans skipper Tino Fa’asuamaleaui made a beeline for referee Adam Gee after Reuben Garrick scored for Manly in the second half, wanting to know if the Manly centre was offside.



“It happened to Max Plath in Origin, that was the call; are you serious?” Fa’asuamaleaui asked Gee, referring to the Maroons being denied a try in similar circumstances in Origin III only a few weeks earlier. The decision did not cost the Gold Coast the win – and just as well, because the NRL, based on the available footage, believed Garrick was “marginally offside”. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Warmer than average June drives down demand for electricity
World.content:
This past June has been the warmest on record, driving down demand for electricity as wholesale prices fall.

Contact Energy's June operating report says New Zealand's electricity demand was down 0.04 percent on June 2025. In contrast, demand was up 1.1 percent in June 2024 over 2023.

Weather appeared to play a big part as the 10.6C nationwide average temperature for June 2026 was 1.9C above the 1991-2020 June average.

At the same time, Electricity Retailers and Generators Association said wholesale prices were sitting at some of their lowest winter levels in more than a decade.

"We are definitely starting to see the downward trend ourselves," Major Electricity Users' Group (MEUG) executive director Karen Boyes said, adding the milder winter was helping to bring down prices, though many of its members were locked into long-term contracts.

"It's a positive direction, but it's hard because a lot of these businesses do long-term contracts, so there is not many of the membership currently coming off," she said.

"But there are some who are starting to look. So we are steadily hoping to see some positive stories, like being mentioned - 30 percent drops. We'd love to see that."

While weather was playing its part, Boyes said July and August were the coldest winter months.

"We've also got really great lake levels, so things are looking positive. The weather conditions are working in our favour at present."

Boyes said she was hoping prices continued the downward trend, as the industry was yet to fully recover from 2024's peak prices.

"So we're still getting back down towards where the average was over the last 15 years.

"We've also seen some of MBIE's (Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment's) industrial data, which shows that prices have dropped between 2025 and 2026. So there's definitely some positive signals there."

Still, she said the industry was concerned about other power charges.

World.title: Pilot escapes unharmed as light plane crashes in Canterbury
World.content:
A light plane has crashed in rural Canterbury, but the pilot has escaped unhurt.

Fire and Emergency says the plane came down on Station Road near Kirwee just after 10am on Tuesday.

Three fire crews from Kirwee, Burnham and Rakaia attended the crash.

World.title: Will light pollution disrupt our connection with Matariki?
World.content:
The season of Matariki is a time to look to the future and plan ahead, but not everyone in Aotearoa will have a clear view of the star cluster in the future.

Victoria University of Wellington lecturer Dr Bridgette Farnworth told RNZ light pollution in New Zealand is increasing, on average, at a rate of 3.2 percent per year.

"Now that doesn't seem like a lot, but when we consider it to the global average, the global average is only 2.2 percent. So for me as a wildlife biologist, I kind of am looking at this as a potential emerging conservation issue for New Zealand."

Estimates indicate about 97 percent of the population lives under skies affected by light pollution, she said.

Victoria Campbell (Ngāi Tahu) is the general manager of the Dark Sky Project, the joint venture which organises stargazing tours at Mount St John near Tekapo in the southern alps.

She told RNZ without conversations on the way we use light, it is probable that many people won't be able to physically view Matariki because of light pollution.

"I know that unless you have advocates championing for good lighting practices, that indeed, people will build infrastructure, will continue without having that lens of good lighting practice, and that will result in us not having that ability to see Matariki and our stars from those environments."

The VIIRS satellite summaries showing upward light detected from 2012 to 2021 for Auckland. From the following publication: Cieraad, E., & Farnworth, B. (2023). Lighting trends reveal state of the dark sky cloak: light at night and its ecological impacts in Aotearoa New Zealand. New Zealand Journal of Ecology, 47(1), 3559. Supplied/Dr Ellen Cieraad

Matariki is a small and faint star cluster among brighter, more prominent stars.

Campbell said DarkSky International (DSi) certified places, such as MacKenzie, Wairarapa and Rakiura/Stewart Island, can be an exemplar of how light is used.

"I have a goal of Aotearoa becoming a dark sky nation. So I'm not opposed to light and development and progress, but what we can do is do that in line with some really good lighting practices that mean that we can preserve the integrity of the sky and still use light the way that we need to. But, in a more deeper level, we really should be having conversations about light because it does have wellbeing impacts on us as humans."

Dark sky areas can also help people grow a connection with the night sky, she said.

"I would hope that once people do experience that and also start to explore the knowledge that sits behind our connection to the stars, then I think the value of our stars and our ability to be able to connect them and learn from them will do us some good."

Victoria Campbell. Supplied / Ngāi Tahu

Campbell said there are some simple solutions to alleviating light pollution, including switching to amber tone lighting as well as shielding street lights to direct light downwards.

"We can look at having lighting regulations in place through our city councils and they have that connection to consent and planning. And so the Mackenzie District Council, for example, operating with the Aoraki Mackenzie International Dark Sky Reserve Board, they work collaboratively so that the infrastructure that is going in the Mackenzie region is within regulations that allow us to continue to have dark sky status."

Farnworth said combating light pollution can start small, for individuals that might mean turning porch lights off or closing curtains in the evening.

For businesses it might mean putting advertising lights on a timer. "Seabirds, they're not buying your product at three o'clock in the morning," she said.

And finally for councils and the government, she would like to see the start of a conversation about lighting in public spaces.

"Can we consider both public safety and ecology as well? So the two can go hand in hand together. And I think that's the pathway forward that we are looking at, which is really great for a country that's committed to conservation and New Zealand really can do that."

The VIIRS satellite summaries showing upward light detected from 2012 to 2021 for Christchurch. From the following publication: Cieraad, E., & Farnworth, B. (2023). Lighting trends reveal state of the dark sky cloak: light at night and its ecological impacts in Aotearoa New Zealand. New Zealand Journal of Ecology, 47(1), 3559. Supplied/Dr Ellen Cieraad

Looking down to protect wildlife from light pollution

Farnworth said light pollution changes animal behaviour drastically. Insects, such as moths, are attracted to light, but other native species avoid lit spaces and the light doesn't need to be that bright to stop them from entering a particular area, she said.

"We can also look at how light affects other responses, so animal communication, for example. So some of the birds in New Zealand's very famous dawn chorus, for example, they'll start singing earlier if they're exposed to light at night."

Many New Zealand native animals are nocturnal and some that are particularly affected include our most iconic species, she said.

Wētā avoid illumination, while pūriri moths are attracted to it.

"These are huge, big moths the size of your palm of your hand, and they are really attracted to lighting. And the thing about pūriri moths is that they spend six years in their larval stage underground before they'll turn into adults and they only live for a couple of days and they're flying off to find a mate.

"So if they get distracted by maybe a garden light or a billboard, they'll probably just be a little bit dazzled by the brightness basically until they die. So when we think of specific light pollution effects we can think of that kind of being as the ultimate Tinder date gone wrong."

Stargazing tour at University of Canterbury Mt John Observatory in Tekapo (MAKI YANAGIMACHI)

Farnworth said many seabirds are very sensitive to lighting. The endangered Hutton's shearwater can become disorientated by artificial lights, often leading to crash landings on roads and being hit by cars.

"The bats in New Zealand, these are critically endangered species and some of the research is showing that they will reduce the activity around where areas are illuminated. So we're basically pushing them out of really important zones that they need to be in.

World.title: Struggle to hear at parties? You're not alone
World.content:
*Correction: This story has been updated to correct names and clarify comments.

When I was 25, I thought I was losing my hearing. I could hear clearly in normal situations, but I struggled at parties and networking events where many people would be speaking at the same time.

After countless times standing in a circle with people laughing at a clearly very funny joke that I could not even hear, I took myself to get a hearing test.

There I was, prepared to be told that I need to live with a hearing aid for the rest of my life. But instead, I was told that my hearing was perfectly fine.

The good news was that I didn't need to worry about what colour I wanted for my hearing aid, the bad news was I continued to feel alone at parties.

But it turns out that it's not just me. Scientists have long studied people's ability to focus on a targeted speech in noisy environments, a phenomenon known as the cocktail party effect.

In research, cocktail party means a noisy setting where there could be a large quantity of people speaking at the same time, and there could be other environmental noises such as clinking of the glass, traffic and buzz from machines.

Clara Zhang, PhD candidate at the University of Auckland's Acoustics and Vibration Research Centre, has been looking into listening in noise.

"My research is on improving the perception of non-native speakers in noise. Cocktail party is a very typical noisy environment, and non-native listeners are typically more disadvantaged when they're listening in noise."

Zhang said the effect was first defined and named in the 1950s, and affects both native and non-native listeners.

She said noisy environments made it harder to isolate the speech from the background noise, even if it's being made by the person right in front of you.

Pouria Bahmani Kolour (right) organises language exchange events around Auckland. Pouria Bahmani Kolour / Supplied

It's easier for native listeners as their ears are sharper at distinguishing the sounds. But for non-native listeners like me who grew up speaking a different language, everything muddles into one big pot of boiling noise.

In the 2023 census, 24 percent of those living in New Zealand said they spoke a second language other than English or te reo Māori.

Pouria Bahmani Kolour, who organises language exchange events around Auckland, is also familiar with the problem.

"Many people, many immigrants have the same common problem. Some people actually get very frustrated. They blame themselves for not studying enough, not trying hard. Some people don't actually care, they just let it slide."

He said their events were set up afterhours in a quiet cafe, and hopefully prepared participants for noisier events in the future.

"We are trying to make a calm environment for the people who participate to be able to actually hear each other and speak."

Bahmani Kolour's native language is Farsi and he's a strong believer in "practice makes perfect".

He said his listening had improved significantly since attending four language exchanges a week.

Zhang said while practicing the language helped, asking for help was also important.

"I think studies have shown that non-native listeners, even if you have a lot of experience and you are very proficient, you still can't quite reach the native behaviour, so I think maybe you want to ask the speaker to come a bit closer to you or ask them to speak slower."

She said organisers could also mitigate the effect, by choosing a venue with better acoustic settings, for example, using a larger space that allow groups to scatter.

Audiologist Angela Loucks Alexander said some treatment and training may also help.

Specialising in Auditory Processing Disorder, Loucks Alexander, said some native-listeners who were not experiencing hearing loss may also find themselves unable to hear clearly.

Audiologist Angela Loucks Alexander says trainings used to help those with Auditory Processing Disorder can also help non-native listeners in noisy settings. Angela Loucks Alexander / Supplied

"Auditory Processing Disorder is a hearing problem that has less to do with the ears and more to do with the brain, it's difficulties in understanding what you hear. People can go in and have a test done and find out that their hearing sensitivity is within normal limits, but they may have a hard time understanding what they hear."

She said five to 15 percent of the population had the disorder, which affects both children and adults, and could present more in some groups than others.

Loucks Alexander said while non-native listeners may not be suffering from the disorder, they could still benefit from the training that was used in the treatments.

"So auditory processing can be improved because the brain is plastic, and we can actually train the brain in how to hear better in noise. I just want people to know who have these difficulties that there is hope."

She said the number of professionals who could help with the disorder had been growing, and she had set up a map to help those to find the right help.

Currently, most treatments required private funding, but Loucks Alexander hoped that with more research and awareness, this could change.

"When they can't hear and understand, they don't feel heard and understood, and I think this is a huge problem here in New Zealand."

I'm not sure whether I will seek treatment yet.

But speaking with the experts does make me feel... heard.

World.title: Inflation rises to highest level in two years
World.content:
Consumer prices rise 1.5% in June quarter, annual rate hits two-year high of 4.1%

Quarterly CPI rise driven by fuel prices, offsets some cheaper food

Higher fuel, electricity, housing drive annual increase

Middle East conflict the key reason for fuel spike, new fighting may keep inflation higher for longer

Underlying inflation measures towards 3%, RBNZ expected to keep raising cash rate

Inflation hit a two year high as the full impact of the Middle East war made itself felt on prices.

Stats NZ data showed the consumer price index rose 1.5 percent in the three months ended June, with the annual inflation rate rising to 4.1 percent from 3.1 percent in March.

It was the highest annual rate since December 2023, and the quarterly increase the highest since September 2023.

Higher petrol prices were the biggest contributor, rising 20 percent in the quarter, with diesel up 48 percent.

"Together petrol and diesel accounted for almost two-thirds of the 1.5 percent quarterly increase," prices spokesperson Nicola Growden said.

The higher petrol prices accounted for about a quarter of the annual inflation rate.

Excluding food, fuel and household energy the quarterly inflation rate would have been 0.4 percent and the annual rate 2.5 percent.

Domestic inflation takes back seat

Domestic prices - non-tradables - such as power, rents and rates were overshadowed by the rise in fuel prices, but still rose 3.4 percent for the year, and by 0.6 percent for the quarter.

Building a new house and electricity prices were two significant items to rise.

Construction of a new house was 1.6 percent for the quarter, the highest in more than three years, and electricity up 4.4 percent.

"Respondents reported that the higher costs for materials, subcontractors, fuel, and labour contributed to rising prices for new housing," Growden said.

Electricity prices rose 12 percent for the year, and local body rates were nearly 9 percent higher. These offset falls in real estate services, audio visual equipment, and some food items such as milk and cheese.

More RBNZ rate rises to come

The inflation numbers were at the top end of economists' expectations.

Various measures of underlying inflation pointed to an annual rate in a range between 2.5 and 3.0 percent.

RBNZ governor Anna Breman recently said the central bank was expecting inflation to peak in the just ended quarter at 3.9 percent.

But she warned the resumption of hostilities was raising the risk that inflation pressures would spill over and become more entrenched.

The RBNZ raised the official cash rate by 25 basis points to 2.5 percent two weeks ago, which Breman likened to taking the foot off the accelerator.

Financial markets are betting on at least two more rises in the official cash rate to 3 percent this year.

World.title: Auckland planning chair says proposed changes will remove density around local centres
World.content:
The chair of Auckland Council's planning committee Richard Hills says proposed changes to new intensification rules will remove density around local centres and focus it near frequent transport services.

On Tuesday, councillors will decide whether to make changes to the proposed Plan Change 120 (PC120) before it goes out to public consultation for a second time.

Auckland Council is required by central government to enable development capacity for 1.4 million dwellings in the city.

In June, councillors agreed to send two versions of PC120 to local boards and iwi authorities for feedback - Plan A and Plan B, which provided for 1.4-1.6 million dwellings and 1.5-1.7 million dwellings respectively.

The feedback from local boards was largely that "about a third wanted A, about a third wanted B, and about a third wanted a mix of both or didn't say", Hills said.

The big change most local boards wanted was to remove density around local centres, "those are smaller centres in their communities, not the town centres, not the metro centres".

"There were other local boards who asked for things that can't be changed, so a change to a walkable catchment or a change to a town centre that's required under the law to stay."

The chair of Auckland Council's planning committee Richard Hills. Alexia Russell

The proposed changes to go before councillors on Tuesday were a blend of Plan A and Plan B, and focus housing density where infrastructure was already in place, he said.

"...we're largely landing in the place where we're doing all the legal requirements, but adding density, so that's six-storey developments around frequent transport corridors - the really, really busy bus routes, mostly heading into the city."

Building heights would also lift to 10- to 15- stories around most train stations on all lines within 10km of the city centre, not just specific Western line stations specified in law, Hills said.

The exception is Meadowbank train station, where it's proposed to reduce building heights to a maximum of six stories due to its valley location and poor access.

Other proposed amendments include reducing building height limits on the southern end of Takapuna Metropolitan Centre from 15 to six stories, and extending the walkable catchments around Akoranga and Smales Farm bus stations so they join up.

It is also proposed to further reducing the development potential for properties at risk of natural hazards, based on updated data, Hills said.

A law change in April, has enabled the council make changes to the overall plan, or withdraw parts of it.

Hills said removing local centres from the proposed intensification plan would leave just 15 percent of urban Auckland impacted by the plan change.

The plan to intensify in areas with existing infrastructure was in contrast to what's been happening with fast track consenting where 1000- to 2000-home developments have been given the go-ahead in areas with no infrastructure, he said.

"I think for most Aucklanders I hear, we should only be putting housing where there is good transport, water, community infrastructure like libraries and that's what the plan shows.

"It remains to be seen what councillors and iwi representatives will make of the proposed changes tomorrow," Hills said.

North Shore councillor John Gillon has proposed a separate amendment, largely based on Plan A.

World.title: Former owner of The Captain Cook Hotel who paid minor for sex appeals prison sentence
World.content:
A Dunedin entertainment industry figure who paid a 15 year-old for sex is appealing against his prison sentence.

Michael McLeod, who is the former owner of Dunedin pub The Captain Cook Hotel, was last week jailed for two years and three months for contracting the minor for sex and drug charges.

He previously admitted to supplying methamphetamine and cannabis.

In sentencing, judge David Robinson described his actions as sickening and unconscionable.

The High Court has confirmed an appeal has been lodged.

World.title: US bill targets birthright citizenship in CNMI, Guam
World.content:
A Republican congressman has introduced legislation that would end automatic United States citizenship for many people born in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), Guam, and other US territories from 2027, drawing strong opposition from a territorial rights advocacy group.

The End Birthright Citizenship for Territories Act, introduced by Virginia Republican rep Morgan Griffith, would amend federal law so that people born in Puerto Rico, Guam, the US Virgin Islands and the CNMIon or after 1 January 2027, would no longer automatically receive US citizenship under current statutory provisions.

The bill argues Congress has the authority to change citizenship laws applying to the territories.

In a statement announcing the bill, Griffith said the recent US Supreme Court decision in Trump v Barbara "leaves the door open for Congressional action on citizenship in the American territories".

"Just like Congress possesses the power to grant the territories Constitutional rights in statute, we have the power to take them away in statute," Griffith said.

The proposal has drawn criticism from Right to Democracy, an advocacy organisation focused on US territories.

"This dangerous and unconstitutional legislation highlights the problem with the Insular Cases and the idea that Congress has the power to simply turn constitutional rights on and off at will in U.S. territories," Neil Weare, the organisation's co-director, said.

"This is a concern we've been warning about for a long time, and here it is in black and white."

Weare said the bill's wording was broader than what he described as Griffith's stated aim of addressing so-called "birth tourism".

"The proposed amendments to federal statute are sweeping, and could mean that anyone born in a U.S. territory starting in 2027 would no longer be recognized as a US citizen, indeed, may not be a citizen of anywhere," Weare said.

"While Rep Griffith says his legislative intent is to focus on addressing so-called 'birth tourism', the actual text of the legislative amendments does not contain any limiting language and could deny citizenship to anyone born in a territory moving forward."

Another Right to Democracy co-director Adi Martinez Roman said the issue extended beyond politics.

"The question of federal power over citizenship in US territories is not a partisan or ideological issue - it is one of fundamental rights in a democracy," Martinez Roman said.

Martinez Roman argued the proposal could also conflict with the Northern Mariana Islands' Covenant with the United States.

"The legislation is also especially troubling because it seeks to unilaterally amend the citizenship provisions negotiated in the Northern Mariana Islands' Covenant, which under Public Law 94-241 require 'mutual consent,' to change," Martinez Roman said.

"This is just the kind of federal action the Covenant was negotiated to prevent."

According to Right to Democracy, the proposal follows comments by US vice president JD Vance after the Supreme Court's Trump v Barbara decision, in which he reportedly said limiting birthright citizenship in the territories by executive action was "a great idea" and that "we're certainly looking at that."

World.title: Football world 'devastated' by death of English icon Keegan
World.content:
Former England captain and manager Kevin Keegan has died aged 75.

Keegan's family and Newcastle United revealed in January that the two-time European Footballer of the Year was undergoing cancer treatment, without disclosing details of his illness. His death was confirmed by Newcastle overnight.

Last month, Keegan, who was nicknamed "King Kev" and "Mighty Mouse" and was one of the most influential figures of his generation in English football, revealed he had stage four cancer.

Fans lay flowers at St James' Park, Newcastle United's home ground, in memory of Keegan after his death. (Getty Images: Owen Humphreys)

"We are devastated to learn of the passing of Kevin Keegan, one of the most iconic, influential and deeply loved figures in our club's history," Newcastle said in a statement.

"As a player, he brought world-class talent, ambition and belief to St. James' Park, helping to transform perceptions of what Newcastle United could be.

"As a manager, he ignited our city. Kevin gave supporters hope and pride, and led a team whose style, spirit and passion captured the imagination of football fans around the world. He was so much more than an entertainer."

Glittering career as player and manager

Keegan became one of English football's biggest superstars in his time with Liverpool from 1971-77. (Getty Images: Harry Ormesher)

Keegan began his career at Scunthorpe United before joining Liverpool in 1971.

He made 323 appearances for Liverpool in all competitions, scoring 100 goals over six seasons. He won three First Division titles, the FA Cup, two UEFA Cups and the 1977 European Cup during a glittering spell at Anfield.

After moving to Hamburg, Keegan was named European Footballer of the Year in 1978 and 1979, becoming the only British player to win the Ballon d'Or twice. He later returned to England to play for Southampton and Newcastle before retiring in 1984 at the age of 33.

Keegan scored 21 goals in 63 appearances for England between 1972 and 1982, captaining the side 31 times.

He moved into management at Newcastle in 1992, guiding the club into the Premier League and transforming it into one of England's most entertaining sides.

Keegan's team came agonisingly close to winning the 1995-96 Premier League title before they were overtaken by Manchester United.

Although the title race did not go Keegan's way, his rant aimed at United manager Sir Alex Ferguson in the heat of the race went down in football folklore.

After leaving St James' Park in January 1997, he had a brief spell at Fulham before taking charge of England in 1999 following Glenn Hoddle's departure.

He resigned after Euro 2000 and a defeat by Germany at Wembley Stadium, famously saying he was "not good enough" to do the job, at a media conference. He won seven of his 18 matches in charge.

Keegan later managed Manchester City before leaving the club in March 2005 and initially announcing his retirement from football. He made an emotional return to Newcastle in 2008, though his second spell at the club lasted only eight months.

A lasting legacy

A statement from Keegan's family, quoted by British media, said on Monday: "It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75.

"The former England player and manager had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments."

Tributes poured in for Keegan, with Liverpool saying in a statement: "Our 'Mighty Mouse', his legacy at Liverpool will be forever etched in history."

England Football wrote on X: "We are incredibly saddened by the news that Kevin Keegan OBE has passed away," while former Newcastle striker Alan Shearer wrote: "My Hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy Boss".

Reuters

World.title: PM backs bid for future NT AFL team, no promises on funding
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has backed the prospect of an AFL team in the Northern Territory, but has stayed tight-lipped on whether his government would help fund it to get off the ground.

With a 20th AFL licence up for grabs, the NT has been touted as one of the top options to take it home, with Western Australia and the ACT also billed as possible contenders.

It comes as Tasmania prepares to enter the AFL with the Devils in 2028, bringing the competition a step closer to becoming truly representative of each state and territory.

This year's Tiwi Islands grand final marks the first time a sitting PM has ever attended the iconic match. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Despite being known as a breeding ground for some of the competition's most exciting talent, from regions like Gove and the Tiwi Islands, the NT has never had a top-tier team.

Mr Albanese visited the Tiwi Islands on Sunday, the first time a prime minister has travelled to the islands north of Darwin in more than 25 years, where he voiced his support for an NT team.

"I'd love to see a team here in the territory, as I'm sure all Territorians would," he said.

"It's a while off, [but] we'll continue to talk and engage with the AFL as well."

Anthony Albanese met with local players at the Tiwi Islands grand final on the weekend. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Mr Albanese was asked whether the Commonwealth would help finance an AFL team in the NT as it has done to help create an NRL team in Papua New Guinea.

"I don't run the AFL, so I'll wait, and certainly any submissions from the AFL [for funding] would be welcome," he said.

"We'll engage constructively with the AFL as well.

" The Northern Territory has a great history of producing great footballers. "

'We have the raw talent'

Reacting to the prime minister's comments, Northern Land Council (NLC) chair Matt Ryan said an AFL team would bring huge social benefits to the jurisdiction.

'Work to do': AFL targets Indigenous player boost The AFL is considering a range of measures to boost the number of Indigenous players in the league following a significant decline in recent seasons.

"We have the raw talent, and I think we can do it," he said.

"I would push that 100 per cent."

When asked if the NLC would be prepared to consider helping with funding the establishment of a team, alongside possible federal financial support, Mr Ryan said, "I think we should all chip in".

"It's our team and I think we should sponsor or support them," he said.

Mr Ryan said he believed the establishment of an NT team would help offset the falling number of Indigenous players in the league.

Tiwi Islands women's footy player Mara Munkara, who played in the weekend's grand final, said an NT team would "mean a lot to the Tiwi people".

"It could bring excitement, everyone happy, everyone around Northern Territory," she said.

Mara Munkara says an NT AFL team would bring a lot of excitement to the Territory. (ABC News Pete Garnish)

A task force has been formed in the NT to try to build the case a local team to be created.

A business case published in 2024 included the recommendation for the federal government to fund construction of a new stadium in Darwin's CBD, to help bolster the jurisdiction's chances for a team.

The AFL has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Ex-league star Dureau dies at 39 after long cancer battle
World.content:
Former Newcastle NRL halfback Scott Dureau, who became a Super League star with the Catalans Dragons, has died after a battle with cancer. He was 39.

The Dragons confirmed Dureau's death last night, amid reports he had died of brain cancer.

"A former iconic player of the club, he had been courageously battling the illness for several years," the Dragons' statement said.

"Beyond the exceptional player that he was, Scott was a man cherished by all those who had the privilege of knowing him.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"His talent and numerous achievements on the field, but above all his humility and kindness, will forever be etched in our memories.

"In these painful moments, president Bernard Guasch and the entire club extend their most sincere condolences to his wife Libby, his two daughters Imogen and Everly, his family, and all his loved ones."

Dureau played 42 games over four seasons with Newcastle before teaming with French club the Catalans Dragons for four years, chalking up 97 appearances.

He was named in the British Super League's "Dream Team" in 2011 and 2012 and won the Albert Goldthorpe Medal, the competition's equivalent of the NRL's Dally M medal, in the second of those seasons.

After his retirement in 2015, Dureau took up a coaching role with the Knights.

He had been battling cancer for more than decade, having retired from playing after a tumour was removed from behind an eye.

AAP

World.title: 'I love my name': Swans star on having the best name in the AFLW
World.content:
Sydney Swans' star youngster Zippy Fish was not surprised her name garnered some attention last season.

"Growing up, everyone was like, 'Is that actually your name?' Like, 'Yeah, it's my name,'" Fish laughed, talking to ABC Sport ahead of the upcoming season.

"I thought it would be quite a big feature [coming into AFLW].

"I love my name. Well, my full name is actually Zipporah, but I actually kind of forget that myself sometimes, because everyone just calls me Zippy … Very grateful for my name."

The attention Fish attracted after being drafted was immediate. She announced herself on the AFLW stage in her first game against Richmond last year, equalling the all-time AFLW record for most disposals in a debut match, with 26 touches.

Zippy Fish became known for her run off halfback and blistering speed. (Getty: Darrian Traynor)

Her blistering speed and ability to launch off halfback made her an instant fan favourite.

This was then cemented by her easy-going nature.

In her first post-match boundary interview with Fox, she said: "I don't really get nervous for anything really, I just went out and did my thing."

Over the course of her first season at the Swans, a new moniker developed. She started to be called "Zippy Ya Ya".

"That nickname came from [fellow Swans AFLW player] Imogen Brown, and it was so random, how it got out of here [the club]," Fish said.

"She does this thing, she just puts 'Ya Ya' at the end of everyone's name. And it just stuck on my name."

Halfway through the season, fans made this into a shirt.

Zippy Fish with the fan-made "Zippy Ya Ya Fan Club" shirt. (ABC: Marnie Vinall)

Her teammate Jasmine Grierson bought the shirt from League Tees. The team had a fines wheel last season and if someone spun the wheel and landed on it, they had to wear the shirt for the day.

Fish said she never landed on it.

While her move to the Swans is one she says she is deeply grateful for — it's hard to catch Fish without a giant smile plastered on her face — she does admit there are times she gets homesick.

The now-20-year-old is from Newman, a small country town in the Pilbara region of Western Australia, approximately 13 hours north-east of Perth.

When drafted to Sydney, she had to move across the width of the country as a teenager.

"It was definitely tough. I'm a big family person, and I love my family, and obviously my boyfriend's back there, so it sucks. But I think it's made me grow as a person," Fish said.

Zippy Fish won the Rising Star in 2025 after a sensational debut season. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

She was drafted from the East Fremantle Sharks at pick number five after running in the WAFL as a teenager with Molly O'Hehir, now at the Melbourne Demons, and Claudia Wright, now at the Brisbane Lions.

You can often hear draftees say how coming into AFLW is a bit of a surprise because you go from playing against girls to playing against women. But Fish said the Western Australian league prepared them well.

"I'd always been around footy and I watched a lot of W, so kind of knew what I was going into," Fish said.

What can we expect from her this season?

"Same as last year, pretty much, I reckon," she said.

"Just a little bit of run off halfback, maybe try and get forward and kick some more goals. And you'll probably just see me smiling out on the field, having a ball."

Fish will have a chance to become even more of a household name as she represents Australia in the upcoming Australia vs Ireland AFLW representative game in August.

She will be one of just two Swans players donning the green and gold, alongside fellow fan-favourite Chloe Molloy.

World.title: Tribunal upholds three-match ban for Crows forward Darcy Fogarty
World.content:
The Crows have failed in their challenge to Darcy Fogarty's three-match striking ban at the AFL Tribunal, the panel finding Fogarty had time to decide to swing his arm at Sydney's Harry Cunningham.

Fogarty was charged after his high hit on Sydney's Harry Cunningham in the second quarter of Adelaide's game with the Swans at the SCG.

Cunningham jumped to try to get the ball deep inside Sydney's defensive 50, and Fogarty came in and caught the Swans player high.

Cunningham was ruled out of the game with concussion and will miss this week's match against cross-town rivals GWS.

The hit was assessed as careless conduct, severe impact and high contact.

The Crows argued that Fogarty's actions did not constitute a strike, and that even if they did it should be high, not severe impact.

AFL counsel, Andrew Woods KC, said the actions were careless and a breach of the duty of care. He said it was no surprise the incident resulted in a concussion.

The contact "was flush, it was direct, and it was on a player whose eyes were on the ball, so he was vulnerable in that moment".

"Cunningham goes to ground, he is visibly severely impacted," Woods said.

"He remains on the ground and requires the help of support staff to get up and exit the field."

After deliberating for less than 20 minutes, the panel returned and chair Jeff Gleeson said they were "comfortably satisfied" that Fogarty had indeed committed the offence of striking.

"Fogarty had time to consider how he would tackle Cunningham in those circumstances. He chose to do so by swinging his right arm forcibly in the direction of Cunningham's upper body and head," Gleeson said.

Fogarty will now miss Crows matches against Collingwood, Essendon and Richmond.

Look back at proceedings in our live blog.

World.title: Electric Tiwi football final sees back-to-back victory for Imalu Tigers
World.content:
Just minutes into the men's Tiwi Islands football grand final, black-and-yellow-clad supporters jumped the sideline fence and started storming the field prematurely, caught up in the excitement of their first goal.

The Imalu Tigers had not yet won the flag, but their devoted supporters never gave them a reason to doubt their hopes of securing back-to-back premiership glory.

Some Tigers fans were so passionate, they ran onto the field each time their team scored. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

For the thousands of people living on the Tiwi Islands, Aussie Rules is much more than a friendly sport. It's a religion, and it all culminates on grand final day.

And for the many visitors attending the grand final game at Wurrumiyanga Oval on Bathurst Island, about 80 kilometres north of Darwin, it is a once-in-a-lifetime experience.

Tapalinga Super Stars players and supporters hug after their win in the women's grand final match. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Each year, hundreds of tourists charter planes and catch ferries across to the Tiwi Islands to watch some of Australia's most promising upcoming AFL players battle it out in front of their home crowds.

This year, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was one of them, becoming the first Australian leader to attend the game while in office.

The Tigers' opponents, the Ranku Eagles, also had plenty of supporters. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Victory for Imalu Tigers, Tapalinga Super Stars

Despite the opposing team, the Ranku Eagles, having the home-ground advantage, Melville Island's Imalu Tigers had the real upper hand, with droves of loyal supporters dominating the fence lines.

With reigning premiers Imalu only having lost a single game this season, it was always going to be a David-and-Goliath battle.

The men's grand final game was close early on before the Tigers pulled away. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

At half-time, it appeared the Eagles stood a chance, with the Tigers only narrowly in front by 12 points.

But in the third quarter, Imalu doubled their lead and soon became unstoppable.

For the second time in as many years, the Tigers took home the premiership cup, claiming victory in a thrilling 11.9 (75) to 7.8 (50) win against Ranku.

The winning Tigers team lifts the cup. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

One young Tigers fan told the ABC he hopes to be playing alongside his male relatives next season.

"It's the sport we grew up with and we just love playing it," he said.

"We love to beat people in it. It can get a bit rough, but yeah, we love it."

The Imalu Tigers had a dominant season in the lead-up to the final. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

In the women's division, it was a tight contest until the end between the Tapalinga Super Stars and the Jikilarruwu.

It was tit-for-tat for much of the first half of the game between the two sides, before Tapalinga created some distance in the third quarter, leaving Jikilarruwu trailing by 10 points.

As the final siren sounded, cheers were met with tears as the Super Stars won the game, defeating Jikilarruwu Thunder & Lightning 8.9 (57) to 4.8 (32).

Player with the Tapalinga Super Stars pose with the premiership cup. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Huge day of art trade

Grand final day is the largest social event on the Tiwi Islands' social calendar, attracting hundreds of tourists to the community from around the country.

With art centres open amid the influx of visitors, for the islands' artists, the event also doubles as their biggest day of trade and an opportunity to pour money back into the local economy.

Artist Romolo Kantilla said it was also an important time to share their culture.

Romolo Kantilla says the grand final is an opportunity for Tiwi Islands people to share their culture through art. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"It's a very special day for Tiwi people, it's a big day and we get everyone from the mainland and it's a good time to come see the art," he said.

"The art is based on creation stories, totem and country.

"Art is always part of us Tiwi people."

World.title: Breakthrough win for Bernard Tomic after lean tennis times
World.content:
Bernard Tomic is back in the winner's circle with the Australian veteran cracking his first Challenger Tour title in eight years.

Reaching the final of the Lincoln Challenger tournament in Nebraska, the 33-year-old showed some grit to save a championship point before downing Estonian Mark Lajal 4-6, 7-6 (4), 7-6 (3).

With a world ranking of 206, down from a career-high of number 17 back in 2016, Tomic started as the underdog against 23-year-old Lajal, who is ranked world number 159.

The crafty Queenslander nailed his service games, on target with 72 per cent of first serves as well as nine aces to cause headaches for his rival.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Tomic also had a three-set battle to book his place in the final, downing American wildcard Spencer Johnson 6-7 (5), 6-3, 6-2.

It was his fourth Challenger Tour title, with the last coming in Mallorca in Spain in 2018.

A quarter-finalist at Wimbledon back in 2011 and former junior champion, Tomic recently lost in the second round of qualifying, falling to fellow Australian Chris O'Connell 6-4, 6-4.

On the main ATP Tour, his most recent singles title was at the ATP 250 event in Chengdu in 2018.

AAP

World.title: Spain's World Cup win a reminder collective spirit trumps solo stars
World.content:
You could see it in the Spanish players as they floated euphorically, each kissing the top of the trophy.

You could feel it from the fans in the stands as they straddled that blurry line between overwhelmed and overjoyed.

And you could hear it rumble through Spain, as a nation united through something which in reality should not mean this much but means more than almost anything else.

Nick Hornby summed it up best in his classic football-themed memoir Fever Pitch.

"I fell in love with football as I was later to fall in love with women: suddenly, inexplicably, uncritically, giving no thought to the pain or disruption it would bring with it."

Argentina felt its force too, the scenes of Lionel Messi in tears, fans distraught, Leandro Paredes losing control and lashing out.

Lionel Messi was crushed after the defeat. (Getty Images: Michael Regan)

In that moment they thought may a love like this never find me.

World Cup football can twist and torment, ripping out your heart and stamping on it till you feel like it can never be repaired.

It can also make you fall head over heels and erase all the hurt you ever felt before.

La Roja ruthless in victory

Spain captain Rodri takes in the magnitude of the achievement. (Getty Images: Alex Pantling )

Spain coach Luis de la Fuente spoke about it in his own terms before the semi-final against France, drawing on inspiration from Julius Caesar, and the idea of having to suffer to achieve great things.

And this was a game that was a struggle for all, it lacked the overall quality and excitement you might expect from a final.

Argentina was stubborn and produced heroic defending in the box, but again questionable roughhousing tactics, eventually resulting in Enzo Fernández's send off.

The reigning champions showed little initiative to create much of anything until the final minutes of extra time as their dream dissipated in the warm New Jersey air.

Spain, having only conceded one goal all tournament, and with 20 shots to two in the decider, might not have produced its flashiest performance, but it was its most important.

This is what La Roja has done throughout the past six weeks, control the ball effortlessly, win it back almost immediately, build pressure through well-organised and committed structures, and wait till late to put it all to bed.

Ferran Torres celebrates the goal that proved to be the decider in the World Cup final between Argentina and Spain. (Getty Images)

The Spaniards were particularly effective in shutting out Messi, who saw little of the ball and was quickly dispossessed or forced into errors when he did have it.

Turns out he can be stopped; it just takes the most exceptional defensive team of this tournament to do it.

The European Champions are now World Champions for the second time, unbeaten for 38 straight matches, a magnificent footballing dynasty growing with every game, becoming the first country to simultaneously hold the men's and women's World Cups.

"I'm so proud of this generation of footballers who have grown up with this philosophy, remained true to it, made it even better and set an example as a team and a family," Spain coach Luis de la Fuente said.

"They're excellent, world-class footballers with exceptional talent. I'm very moved. Looking back and thinking about them, we've won everything, absolutely everything, with this generation of players."

Spain's collective triumph

Celebrations in Madrid will continue long after tonight. (Getty Images: Chris McGrath)

Argentina is a team built around one player, the likes of whom we have never seen before.

Spain is built around a collective approach, filled with exceptional players, but all who work in harmony, allowing each other to shine in different moments.

Like Mikel Merino with his repeated winners off the bench, or Rodri holding the side together as the linchpin in midfield, or Ferran Torres with his vital assists, and today's match-winning strike.

"I think in the end the goal came from 47 million people, not just those of us that are here," Torres said.

"Today destiny was written, it was made for us to win. We're far from our people today but we tried to be as close as possible to them.

"A huge relief [to score]. I've been criticised throughout the whole tournament but as I said before, destiny was written."

It says so much that Lamine Yamal, 19, seen by most as Messi's heir, did not play much of an influential role in this final, or at any stage during the tournament.

Lamine Yamal did not quite have the breakout tournament some predicted. (Getty Images: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu)

He was not a passenger, but was certainly not a conductor, and that can only breed even further confidence, and strike further fear into other nations, as he goes from boy to man.

This World Cup started slowly for Spain, a scoreless draw with the tournament's best underdog story, Cabo Verde.

But as the superstars like Messi, Kylian Mbappé, Erling Haaland, Harry Kane, and Jude Bellingham took all the headlines and dominated social media algorithms, Spain was the quiet, conscientious achiever.

That all changed with the terrifyingly efficient dismantling of France in the semifinals, and now a completely deserved win in the final.

"This generation of players is an example for Spanish sport, for the Spanish youth," de la Fuente said.

"Together we are much stronger, and that is why we don't forget anyone."

A team forged through fire, built on discipline and togetherness, now enjoying its love story.

Tech.title: Here are the 30,000 songs Sony is suing Udio’s AI music generator over
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Sony Music Entertainment has filed another lawsuit against Udio, accusing the AI music generator of infringing the copyright of more than 30,000 of its songs, ranging from Elvis Presley’s Hound Dog to Beyoncé’s Say My Name, and Harry Styles’ As It Was. The lawsuit, filed in a New York court on Monday, claims that this list represents “only a small portion of Plaintiffs’ works that Udio infringed,” as reported earlier by Music Business Worldwide.

In 2024, Sony, along with Universal Music Group and Warner Records, filed a lawsuit against Udio and the AI music-maker Suno. After gaining access to Udio’s training data through discovery, Sony claims it identified additional songs using an “audio fingerprinting” technique. Sony filed a request to add more than 30,000 songs that Udio allegedly “copied and ingested into its generative AI models,” but a judge later rejected the company’s motion, leaving the scope of the original lawsuit at 333 works.

Sony has now made the more than 30,000 songs the subject of its new lawsuit, which the company says it could expand. It claims Udio “admitted that its generative AI models were ‘constructed by showing the program a vast amount of different kinds of sound recordings,’” including from YouTube. UMG and Warner Music Group have since settled with Udio and are now partnering with the company as the music industry embraces AI.

You can read the full list of songs Sony is suing Udio over in this filing. The company is asking to block Udio from infringing its works, as well as for up to $150,000 per work infringed.

Tech.title: The FCC is planning to retroactively ban disguised DJI gadgets
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Last October, we told you how the FCC had given itself the power to retroactively ban gadgets that have already received its approval to be imported and sold in the United States. Now, the FCC’s getting ready to wield that power for the first time, by cracking down on the “DJI front companies” suspected of sneaking the Chinese company’s tech past its foreign drone ban.

For example, we highlighted a deal on Xtra’s version of the DJI Osmo Pocket 3 just two weeks ago, a product that already got FCC approval before the drone ban ever came down, and a proudct which Amazon offers with next-day shipping. If the FCC’s retroactive ban goes into effect, that product should disappear from all major online retailers and Xtra’s own website, and the company may even need to write off however many cameras are still sitting in US warehouses like Amazon’s.

The Xtra Muse and the DJI Osmo Pocket 3 — too close to even call it a “clone.“ Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

The ban wouldn’t affect gadgets that have already been purchased, and it wouldn’t happen immediately. The FCC’s currently taking public comments for 30 days first. While the FCC has “tentatively” concluded that these companies are selling equipment that should be banned over national security fears, it claims it’ll listen to “specific evidence” otherwise.

But that should maybe be taken with a grain of salt: the FCC largely ignored public comments about net neutrality and lied about a cyberattack. It’s also worth pointing out that the US government has never provided specific public evidence that foreign drones pose a national security threat to begin with, or why other products like cameras should be caught up in that ban. If you want to comment anyhow, you can do so with an “Express Filing” here.

In the meantime, the FCC says it has “temporarily deferred the grantee codes of these companies,” a phrase that it does not define. (A former FCC official tells The Verge he’s never heard that phrase before; we’re asking the FCC if that means these companies can’t get future gadgets authorized for import and sale.)

The specific companies that the FCC is targeting include Cogito Tech, Fixaxo Technology, Lyno Dynamics, Skyhigh Tech, Spatial Hover, SZ Knowact and WaveGo Tech (both of whom are behind Skyrover), and Xtra Technology, none of which responded to the FCC’s requests for information. It also includes agricultural drone brand XAG, which did reportedly reply to the FCC once, but not with the information that the FCC asked for.

All save XAG were brought to the FCC’s attention by Konrad Iturbe, who figured out how to track the “FCC front companies” last year. The FCC also cites our story about Xtra.

Today, the FCC is also announcing that it’s parting ways with one of the Chinese test labs that helped some of these products make it to market: SGS-CSTC Shenzhen. While SGS-CSTC did reply to the FCC to claim it’s not controlled by the Chinese government, as the China-owned CSTC only has 15 percent ownership of the lab, US law currently considers another entity to have control if it has 10 percent or more or a company — at least when it comes to authorizing radios for use in the US.

On July 10th, the FCC said it might take even more actions against the eight “DJI front companies” if they didn’t reply by today, July 20th. We’ll let you know what we hear.

Tech.title: The Odyssey turned me into an IMAX believer
Tech.content:
After seeing Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey for the first time early last week, I came away impressed, but somewhat conflicted about two of the film’s more fantastical set pieces. While those scenes were beautifully crafted and tremendously acted, there was something a little bit off about the way they hit my eye. I spent days wondering what, exactly, wasn’t quite working for me during that first theatrical viewing, and I thought that might have just been splitting hairs. But it wasn’t until I saw the movie again over the weekend — this time in IMAX — that the issue became crystal clear.

Though I’d heard all of the buzz about The Odyssey being the first feature shot entirely with 70mm film IMAX cameras, I thought a lot of it was clever marketing hype meant to activate Nolan’s cinephile fan base. I hadn’t considered how watching the film in larger format would make for a markedly different viewing experience. But The Odyssey really is a movie that needs to be seen in IMAX if you want to get a true sense of the story Nolan is telling.

Spoiler warning: This story contains spoilers for The Odyssey (which, to be fair, is an adaptation of Homer’s almost 3,000-year-old epic poem).

There are many scenes throughout The Odyssey that look perfectly fine when the film is displayed in the 35mm format. Majestic, wide shots of Odysseus (Matt Damon) and his men at sea make you appreciate the Mediterranean’s expansiveness, and you can feel the soldiers’ claustrophobic tension as they hide within the Trojan horse. Even though you can see that the film is cropped, Odysseus’ disastrous encounter with the Laestrygonians gives you a sense of how gigantic they are compared to the wandering Ithacans. But The Odyssey’s scenes involving some of the story’s more gargantuan monsters take on a different gravity when they’re displayed in IMAX because of how much more visual information there is to take in.

When I saw The Odyssey in 35mm — which is projected in a widescreen, 2.39:1 aspect ratio — I knew that the Cyclops Polyphemus (Bill Irwin) towered over the humans who marched into his cave searching for food. But when I saw a standard IMAX screening of the film — whose 1.90:1 aspect ratio is smaller than the 70mm’s 1.43:1 ratio — I had a much clearer understanding of the creature’s stature and the subtle nuances baked into Irwin’s physical performance. Because the IMAX screening projected a taller image, I was able to spend more time taking in details that were easy to miss the first time around, like the way Polyphemus has to hunch in order to keep his head from hitting the cave’s ceiling.

The substantive difference between the two screenings became exceedingly obvious once I saw the Cyclops chasing Odysseus and his men down a mountain for a second time. In 70mm, you can see more of the monster’s upper body as it lumbers through trees in a fitful rage, which brings an added sense of danger and urgency to the chase scene. I had a similar experience seeing the soldiers rowing past a whirlpool not knowing that they were drifting directly into the sea monster Scylla’s reach. The 35mm screening shows you that Scylla’s humongous, but the IMAX screening’s added real estate makes it easier to understand how she’s able to snatch her victims up before any of them realize that she’s lurking in the cliffs above them.

By shooting The Odyssey completely in 70mm, Nolan crafted a film whose size and visual detail could make it feel immersive in ways that most modern features aren’t. But he also chose a format that makes it difficult for most theatergoers to see the movie in its most impressive form. Because there are only about 40 theaters globally (25 in the US) that are able to screen 70mm IMAX films, the vast majority of people will probably never get a chance to take The Odyssey in as Nolan intended. This and the fact that standard IMAX screenings are more expensive than standard movies have prompted some to accuse the director of being anti-art and contributing to the culture of obsessive format purism.

One could also argue that Nolan is using The Odyssey to show IMAX and theater owners that there is a genuine public demand for films shot in 70mm. The current shortage of 70mm screenings of The Odyssey is due to the fact that IMAX hasn’t been able to produce new projectors. Speaking to Variety, IMAX CEO Richard Gelfond explained that the company has largely been focused on retrofitting old projectors, but there aren’t many movie exhibitors willing to take on the construction costs it would take to build the 1.43:1 screens necessary to display 70mm films. If IMAX and various theater chains were willing to pony up the cash for projector part development and venue expansion, 70mm screenings could become more common. But for the time being, the industry seems comfortable using the format’s scarcity as an effective marketing tool.

That marketing strategy has worked for The Odyssey — a highly anticipated project from one of the world’s most revered filmmakers. But Nolan’s star power clearly has a lot to do with the movie’s box office success. There aren’t that many other directors who could get people journeying across the country just to see one of their features. It also helps that the movie is actually worth seeing, especially in IMAX.

Tech.title: SpaceX in your index fund, explained
Tech.content:
is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Index funds are touted as one of the safest ways to invest. Rather than picking and choosing individual stocks, index funds let you bet on the market as a whole. So what happens when a company like SpaceX — a giant gamble, and, in my opinion, terribly overpriced — is fast-tracked into the Nasdaq-100? Does it suddenly threaten the stability of index funds based on the Nasdaq-100? Can a $1.77 trillion IPO crater the retirement funds of regular people who would ordinarily have no interest in investing in Elon Musk’s meme stock?

The answer has less to do with SpaceX and more to do with index funds — how they work, their history, and why they’ve been treated as one of the least risky ways to interact with the stock market. So I talked to Burton Malkiel, one of the people most responsible for the rise of the index fund.

“If I were buying individual stocks, I would think twice about buying SpaceX, which is tremendously overhyped,” he tells me. But SpaceX isn’t a reason to avoid index funds, he says. To explain why, here’s a dive into index funds, how SpaceX interacts with them, and how it all might play out.

What is an index fund?

An index fund is an investment vehicle that seeks to match a specific market benchmark, such as the S&P 500 or the Nasdaq-100. It was popularized in part by Malkiel’s 1973 book A Random Walk Down Wall Street. The “random walk” of the book’s title means that the past prices of a stock don’t predict the future, and because it is hard to predict the future, it is very difficult to beat the overall market returns over a long period of time. For that reason, most of us might as well just invest in the overall market and trust it will increase in value as a whole. “A very small minority of stocks are responsible for the whole return, and experts can’t pick them any better than the index as a whole,” Malkiel told me.

The strategy of index fund investment has been endorsed by Warren Buffett, who has suggested that the average investor is best served by putting 90 percent of their money in “a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund.”

And they are very popular! In 2024, the assets under management in passive investing, such as index funds, outpaced that of active funds, according to Elise Ryan of State Street Investment Management.

Why are people worried about SpaceX specifically?

Shortly before SpaceX went public, the Nasdaq changed its rules for the Nasdaq-100, so that a newly public company that’s large enough can join the benchmark on its 15th day of trading. That rule change was requested by SpaceX, Reuters reported.

When SpaceX joined the Nasdaq-100, on July 7th, index funds had to buy in. Interestingly, at close on July 6th, the stock was down. There’s some structural reason for that — namely, that everyone knew the index funds would have to buy in, and so banks and hedge funds most likely did some fun trades. Index rebalancing funds made out like bandits. Finance is fascinating and full of monsters.

There’s reason to believe that the index fund buying is part of the reason SpaceX had its initial IPO pop, according to research from Harvard Business School. What’s more, SpaceX is the initial entry into indexes for a number of expected mega-IPOs. Anthropic and OpenAI are expected to make their debuts later this year.

What does the index fund inclusion mean for SpaceX?

Some degree of price stability. New IPOs often fluctuate wildly. For instance, Facebook’s shares dropped 25 percent the Monday after its 2012 IPO, tripping breakers to halt trades.

Beyond the fluctuations from the market itself, a lot of people will soon be able to sell SpaceX shares that aren’t yet on the market. SpaceX employees are subjected to “lockup periods,” where they can’t immediately cash out and sell their stock following the IPO. Those periods are going to expire, and doubtless some people will want to sell shares. The index funds are likely to “help absorb some of the selling,” thus keeping the price from dipping too low, according to The Wall Street Journal.

How important is SpaceX in these index funds?

The company has a market cap of more than $1.5 trillion as of this writing, which is obviously enormous. But the IPO sold less than 5 percent of the company’s shares. Because of the way the Nasdaq adjusts its index, SpaceX will be treated like a much smaller company.

But remember, next month more SpaceX shares will be released from lockup. People with 180-day lockups can sell more shares than were initially sold in the IPO after SpaceX publishes its second quarter financial results, notes Bloomberg’s Matt Levine. Those results are expected in mid-August. That will make it more important in those index funds — though whether the price will fluctuate much is anyone’s guess, as short sellers are also anticipating the lockup releases. These market mechanics may explain some of the stock’s short-term price fluctuation, even though the company hasn’t had much major news occur.

SpaceX may take up more room in index funds as more shares are sold. But it might not, as selling usually drives down the price.

Why are people mad about SpaceX in index funds?

Musk has the majority of the voting rights for SpaceX. In other companies, shareholders can theoretically influence outcomes through shareholder proposals. With SpaceX that isn’t true. Other companies can be sued by shareholders for bad behavior, but SpaceX has limited shareholders’ litigation rights. One way to avoid a company that has made these choices is to sell the stock — but the inclusion in index funds means that’s harder.

But wait. I don’t vote on the corporate governance for companies in my index funds. Why does corporate governance matter to me?

You don’t, but the big indexers do. That means a lot of power is concentrated in just a few hands. It’s one of the worries people have about index funds. There are some other criticisms of index funds, too — that they buy high and sell low when they rebalance, for instance — and some investors believe they distort the market, making big companies even bigger. That’s why some analysts have called index funds “worse than Marxism.” Coming from capitalists, that’s a pretty big insult.

But still — if you believe those big indexers are sophisticated investors who are working on your behalf, you want them to make choices in corporate governance. To, for instance, vote against acquisitions that might be bad for shareholders, or install problematic members of the board of directors.

It seems like if you add up all these mega-IPOs along with the existing tech companies, there’s a lot of AI concentration in the index funds. Should I worry about that, in case AI is a bubble that pops?

Even before SpaceX entered the Nasdaq-100, most of its biggest companies were already AI-heavy — like Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Google parent Alphabet, Broadcom, and Meta.

One of the biggest criticisms Malkiel hears about index funds is that the market is extremely concentrated, so that 10 companies are worth more than 30 percent of it. But he doesn’t view that as an argument against index funds. “The market’s always been concentrated,” he says.

“We’ve overhyped every technological change in history,” Malkiel adds. Railroads were overhyped, and so was the internet in the ’90s, and doubtless we are overhyping AI right now. That’s not a reason to be scared of index funds. “You’ve got to remember that it’s a very small minority of stocks that are responsible for all the return in the market,” Malkiel says. “That’s why you shouldn’t be terribly worried.”

What else are people worried about?

SpaceX isn’t getting fast-tracked by the S&P 500, another major index with its own governance rules. That may create significant differences in returns between index funds tracking the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100. (I, for one, look forward to seeing how that plays out.)

I suspect that most of the growth in SpaceX’s value has already been realized — which is why we have a megacap IPO in the first place, so that all the private investors can cash out — but as with Tesla, SpaceX is a meme stock with a sizable interest from retail investors. That decouples its performance from its fundamentals, effectively making it difficult to predict how the stock will actually do.

Does SpaceX’s size and inclusion suggest people should simply buy SpaceX stock directly?

No, says Malkiel. “If I were buying individual stocks, I would think twice about buying SpaceX, which is tremendously overhyped,” he tells me. But people wouldn’t be better off by avoiding an index fund in order to avoid SpaceX.

Over time, the market has produced a return of about 10 percent a year. But the majority of companies aren’t responsible for that return, Malkiel says. Only 4 percent of stocks give that rate of return, and everything else underperforms. If you own an index fund, you will definitely own a bunch of the stocks that lose money, but you’ll also own that crucial 4 percent. “We know experts can’t determine which ones are going to be good,” he says. “The point is, we don’t know which ones are going to be the best and which ones are going to fail.”

Besides, if you have an index fund with SpaceX in it, and SpaceX loses value, the fund rebalances with fewer SpaceX shares, since SpaceX is proportionately less of the overall market. Lots of companies, including those that are in index funds, go bankrupt every year. The focus isn’t on losses — it’s about gains.

Are there other SpaceX schemes I should be aware of?

SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell donated shares of the company to Trump Accounts, which are investment accounts for children. The president said the donation was worth $325 million. That is perhaps more alarming than the index funds, because it ties SpaceX very closely to political power.

Let’s say I want to avoid owning SpaceX shares at all. How can I do that?

Besides preferentially investing in the S&P 500 index funds, you might also choose to invest in environmental, social, and governance funds. They generally have higher fees than index funds and don’t perform as well, but if not having SpaceX in your portfolio is a high priority, that might be a way to avoid it — since Musk’s control of SpaceX means the company flunks the “G” part of the requirement. (It may also flunk the “E” part, environment, thanks to the pollution from rockets and AI.) Different ESG funds have different criteria, but someone trying to avoid SpaceX because of Musk might end up with Tesla in their ESG fund — for its electric vehicles, Malkiel says.

Tech.title: Get Borderlands 3, Risk of Rain 2 and 13 other great PC games for $15
Tech.content:
Brad Bourque is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The aptly-named “2K Megahits 2026 Bundle” from Humble includes 15 Steam games for $15. It’s a smattering of the publisher 2K’s biggest games of the 2010s, including BioShock Infinite, Risk of Rain 2, Borderlands 3, and XCOM: Enemy Unknown. The bundle will be available until August 7th, though the bundle page notes that keys for some games are already starting to run low. All of the games work on Windows, while some support MacOS and SteamOS.

One of my personal favorite games, Risk of Rain 2, is included in the bundle. In the third-person roguelike, you’ll face off against increasingly difficult waves of enemies, fighting to stay alive as long as you can and collecting power-ups and useful perks before extracting to the next zone to do it all again. It’s just challenging enough to make victory satisfying, and fun to play alone or with friends. You also get 2012’s XCOM: Enemy Unknown, a legendary turn-based strategy game that’s usually $15 on its own, to give you a sense of the bundle’s value.

The bundle also notably includes three games from the Borderlands universe. Borderlands 3 Special Edition is a traditional looter-shooter FPS, Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands adds RPG elements like an overworld map and spellcasting, and Tales from the Borderlands is an interactive episodic visual novel from Telltale Games. You’ll also get a variety of shooters, including BioShock Infinite, Duke Nukem 3D, Bulletstorm, plus Hidden and Dangerous from the turn of the millenium.

Part of the proceeds from the bundle benefit Covenant House, an organization that benefits young people facing homelessness, as well as the publisher and Humble. You can adjust how you pledge is split between the beneficiaries by clicking the button that says “adjust donation” under the checkout button.

You can find the full list of games in the bundle below:
